items.title: T-MUON: Tensorizing Muon via t-SVD for Large Language Model Pre-training
items.content: arXiv:2610.24938v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. We show that the exact T-MUON update is a steepest-descent direction under the $\star_M$-spectral norm and establish a convergence guarantee. Across GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu, head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform consistently achieves lower validation perplexity than AdamW, Muon, and variants using DFT, DCT, or DST transforms. These gains persist in additional experiments with longer context lengths and larger token budgets, although the preferred tensorization mode varies across settings.
items.author: Dongyang Li, Mingsong Yan, Zheng Zhang, Sui Tang
items.summary: T-MUON generalizes the Muon optimizer using t-SVD tensor decompositions, grouping structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defining Muon-style updates via the M-transform. The authors prove the exact update is a steepest-descent direction under the star-M spectral norm with convergence guarantees, and evaluate on GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M parameters up. This extends the rapidly growing orthogonalized-optimizer line for LLM pretraining.
items.reasoning: Timely contribution to the hot Muon/orthogonalized optimizer area with genuine theoretical grounding (spectral-norm steepest descent guarantee) and scaling to LLaMA-style pretraining. The gap over existing tensor-aware Muon extensions may be incremental, and full-scale validation matters for real impact.

items.content: arXiv:2610.25119v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.

items.title: Distributionally-Robust Policy Learning with Observational Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.25591v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Policy learning from observational data is fundamental to applications ranging from personalized medicine to welfare-program targeting, but standard approaches optimize empirical performance and may fail when the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution. We study \emph{distributionally-robust policy learning}: given observational data, we seek a policy $\pi \in \Pi$ that maximizes the worst-case policy value over an $f$-divergence ball of radius $\rho$ around the data-generating distribution. We propose an estimator built on cross-fitted doubly-robust scores for the conditional treatment effect, paired with a DRO solver that handles \texttt{KL}, $\chi^2$, and \texttt{CVaR} ambiguity sets. We establish two convergence guarantees. First, the estimated policy attains the standard $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ rate on its DRO regret, and inherits the doubly-robust property -- the rate continues to hold whenever either the outcome model or the propensity model is consistently estimated, even at slow nonparametric rates. We then propose a sample-splitting bias-correction algorithm derived from the Lagrangian dual, and show that under a Tsybakov-style margin condition on the treatment-effect, the estimator attains a fast rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-(1+\alpha)/(2+\alpha)})$ , interpolating between $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ and $\widetilde{O}(1/n)$ as the margin parameter $\alpha$ ranges over $[0,\infty)$. To our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate a margin condition into the analysis of distributionally-robust policy learning, and the first to obtain fast rates in this setting. Empirically, on synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments calibrated to a welfare-to-work program, distributional robustness yields meaningful improvements over empirical welfare maximization when training and test distributions differ.

items.title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.25856v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.

items.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
items.content: arXiv:2610.26722v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

items.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
items.content: arXiv:2610.24872v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.

The paper proposes per-class label counting as a free, label-free diagnostic check.

items.title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
items.content: arXiv:2610.24963v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target-aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target-relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model-specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population-level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.

items.title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25086v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.

This replaces two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation, reducing autoregressive decoding latency while preserving depth.

items.title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
items.content: arXiv:2610.24858v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

items.title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.25090v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.25090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}

items.title: Tricking Synthetic Image Detectors with Amortized Generative Attacks
items.content: arXiv:2610.25554v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Rapid advances in image synthesis have increased the need for reliable synthetic-image detectors, yet their robustness to transferable attacks remains incomplete and understudied. Existing evaluations generally examine whether an attack constructed against one detector transfers to another, but rarely isolate how its effectiveness changes when the attacked images originate from different generators. We conduct a systematic evaluation of three representative attacks: two iterative perturbation-based methods, MIG and MuMoDIG, and the amortized generative attack Tricker. Across four detectors and five generators spanning diverse architectures, we introduce a two-axis evaluation protocol that independently varies the surrogate detector used to construct or train the attack and the generator supplying its input images. We assess attack effectiveness, cross-detector transferability, perceptual quality, runtime, and interaction with common post-processing operations. We revisit Tricker and show that its data and training requirements can be substantially reduced, enabling broader and more efficient evaluation. Our results demonstrate that transferability is not a detector-only property: the input-generator distribution strongly influences both evasion effectiveness and attacked-image quality. MIG and MuMoDIG exhibit pronounced dependence on the detector--generator pair, whereas Tricker provides more uniform white-box evasion and image quality. We additionally observe that post-processing maintains the asymmetric transferability topology. These findings expose a neglected dimension of attack evaluation and motivate transfer-aware protocols that jointly account for detector and generator variation. We will release our code, evaluation data, and trained attack models with a responsible-use statement.

items.title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.26216v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently. Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer--diffusion training. Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction: generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents. We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Robust Alignment and Reconstruction VAE (RoAR-VAE). Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.

items.title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.23880v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.

items.title: Humanoid SRL: Augmenting Humanoids with Supernumerary Limbs for Coordinated Loco-Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.25628v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid robots are envisioned to perform diverse human-level tasks through their anthropomorphic morphology. Their dual-arm configuration enables a broad range of everyday actions. Yet, as in humans, this morphology can constrain loco-manipulation when both arms are occupied or additional contacts are required beyond their reach. Supernumerary robotic limbs (SRLs) offer a way to extend these capabilities, but their integration requires the added limb to be coordinated with whole-body motion and balance. In this study, we develop and integrate a supernumerary arm into a humanoid platform to investigate how morphological augmentation reshapes its feasible action space. Through quantitative analysis and hardware experiments across two configurations, we show how the additional limb expands whole-body interaction capabilities by enabling manipulation and support to be coordinated beyond the constraints of the native dual-arm configuration. To control this augmented morphology, we leverage model-based trajectory optimization (TO) to generate dynamically feasible motions for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) controllers. The controllers are trained in simulation and transferred to hardware in a zero-shot manner, enabling coordinated whole-body skills for contact-rich tri-arm loco-manipulation. We further show vision-guided autonomous execution on selected tasks using diffusion policies trained from hardware demonstrations. Our findings suggest that humanoid morphology need not be restricted to human-like forms, but can be reimagined as an extensible design space for robotic augmentation.

items.title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
items.content: arXiv:2610.26390v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.

items.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
items.content: arXiv:2610.24006v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.

items.title: WAQS: Weight Absorption for Quadratic Probing and Affine Steering
items.content: arXiv:2610.24367v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. We introduce \textbf{WAQS} (\textbf{W}eight \textbf{A}bsorption for \textbf{Q}uadratic probing and affine \textbf{S}teering), a framework that obtains state-dependent steering, without additional inference-time computation. WAQS models a concept with a quadratic probe, whose gradient yields an affine, activation-dependent steering direction. We show that this affine intervention can be folded exactly into adjacent linear transformations through an offline weight update. Moreover, we prove that quadratic functions form the maximal class of smooth concept scores whose gradient-based interventions are affine and therefore exactly absorbable into linear layers. Under a Gaussian representation model, our formulation admits an interpretation as the difference of class-conditional Mahalanobis pulls and naturally generalizes linear discriminant and difference-in-means steering. To scale to high-dimensional representations, we introduce a low-rank parameterization of the quadratic term. Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy steering tasks, quadratic steering matches or improves upon constant linear steering while preserving model utility, with the absorbed implementation introducing no additional inference-time operations. Our results suggest that quadratic probes provide a practical middle ground between static linear steering and computationally expensive dynamic nonlinear interventions.

This advances lightweight model control as an alternative to fine-tuning.

items.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
items.content: arXiv:2610.24471v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.
items.author: Meng-Chen Wu, Umesh Bodhwani
items.summary: This paper organizes the pluralistic alignment literature around a two-layer taxonomy separating Overton, Steerable, and Distributional pluralism, and distinguishing whose preferences define the reference from what evidence demonstrates success. It clarifies how existing work conflates distinct questions about desired behavior, reference populations, and evaluation. As a survey/position paper it should help structure a growing research area.
items.reasoning: A valuable conceptual contribution to alignment research, addressing the underexamined problem of representing human preference diversity rather than collapsing it. Taxonomies influence field direction, but as non-empirical work its impact hinges on community uptake.

We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.

items.title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference
items.content: arXiv:2610.24611v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets.

items.reasoning: Addresses a practical pain point (expensive agent benchmarking) with a principled Bayesian approach and a clear theoretical connection to variance reduction. Niche application area limits broad impact, but the method could generalize to agent evaluation broadly.

items.title: Teaching Code Agents to Ask Without Leaking Private Code
items.content: arXiv:2610.24824v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Local coding agents can extend their reach by consulting a stronger cloud model. Such consultations, however, often expose the repository's private identifiers, file paths, and source code. Host-side masking hides recognized identifiers but leaves the surrounding code and the agent's phrasing unchanged, while training for less disclosure risks suppressing consultation or producing questions too vague to answer. We propose utility-verified abstraction (UVA), which teaches the agent to describe private entities by their role and type while retaining the technical details an expert needs. From solved repair trajectories, we rewrite each question into this form and keep the rewrite only if it discloses fewer private entities and the repair, replayed from the same execution state with the repair trajectories. Across two benchmarks, the trained agent consults more often than before training. On repository-level issue repair, it solves 37.6% of issues, against 25.3% for the same model working alone, a gain from the training as a whole rather than from consultation alone. Its questions disclose 3.7-fold fewer private entities and 1.4-fold less verbatim code than the untrained agent's questions to the same expert.

items.title: MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.24955v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. We introduce MemPrice, which treats active context as a shared resource and dynamically allocates it across memories and representation levels. MemPrice turns accumulated memory pressure into an adaptive price on context, encouraging detail only when its estimated retention value justifies the additional footprint. This pressure persists across memory refreshes, allowing the contents of memory to evolve while preserving long-run control over context usage. We show that irreversible compression can force linear worst-case regret against hindsight following its own memory trajectory, and introduce a same-state benchmark to evaluate allocation on MemPrice's realized memory states. MemPrice enforces the hard context budget at every round and regulates long-run occupancy through adaptive pricing, without prior knowledge of the interaction horizon. Under priced-frontier regularity, its average allocation-regret bound against this benchmark vanishes when accumulated estimation error is sublinear. We evaluate the framework under matched memory budgets on LongMemEval, LoCoMo, AppWorld, and WebShop across three foundation models, spanning both query-blind memory construction and goal-directed agent context management.

items.title: DAGLoop: Aligning Method Design with Experimental Feedback in Automated AI Research
items.content: arXiv:2610.25089v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated AI research agents aim to improve machine learning methods by iteratively proposing, implementing, and evaluating candidate methods. Existing work uses the outcome of each evaluation to determine how the next candidate should be revised for performance improvement. However, a candidate often combines multiple design decisions, and its overall outcome alone does not reveal which decisions produced their expected effects, whether their required conditions were satisfied, or which decisions should be retained or revised. Inspired by ablation studies in the machine learning community, we propose DAGLoop to test the expected effect of a design decision by comparing implementations with and without that decision while preserving the other decisions it requires. Specifically, DAGLoop translates each design decision's rationale into a testable expectation and pairs it with a targeted experiment, forming an experimental specification for assessing the expected effect under its required conditions. Using these specifications, we formulate ablation planning as the construction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from the candidate method's design: nodes associate decisions with tests, and edges encode dependencies. The DAG specifies which decisions each experiment must retain and supports joint tests when an expected effect requires several decisions to act together. Outcomes are recorded with the tested decisions, expectations, and conditions to form structured research memory. This memory guides the agent in retaining experimentally supported decisions, revising unsupported ones, and planning further experiments when the evidence is unresolved. Experiments on dozens of research tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements achieved by DAGLoop across diverse executable research settings. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/deng34567/DAGLoop.
items.author: Dengyuxing Wang, Yonggang Zhang, Qianshu Cai, Huajiang Zheng, Jun Song, Yangqiu Song, Yike Guo
items.summary: DAGLoop improves automated AI research agents by applying ablation-style analysis to candidate method revisions, testing each design decision in isolation rather than relying only on overall evaluation outcomes. This lets the loop determine which decisions actually produced expected effects and should be retained or revised. The approach addresses credit-assignment ambiguity in iterative machine learning method discovery.
items.reasoning: A sensible and novel framing that imports ablation methodology into autonomous research agents, targeting a real weakness in current self-improving loops. Impact depends on experimental validation quality, which the abstract suggests but does not fully demonstrate, and the approach may add substantial compute cost per iteration.

items.title: Stepwise Reasoning Verification: Don't Generate, Classify!
items.content: arXiv:2610.25441v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Verifying the reasoning of large language models is increasingly important as they are applied to complex mathematical and scientific problems. Existing work focuses on large decoder models and reports mixed results for generative and discriminative verifiers, leaving unclear which paradigm is more effective and whether large models are necessary. In this work, we cast stepwise verification as a natural language inference task: the problem and partial solution prefix form the premise, while the next reasoning step serves as the hypothesis to be classified as entailed or non-entailed. This formulation enables error localisation at individual reasoning steps and direct comparison of encoder classification, decoder classification, and decoder verdict generation across model scales and annotation budgets. Across five reasoning datasets, a 0.15B encoder classifier outperforms most generative verifiers with up to 4B parameters. On identical decoder backbones, classification outperforms generation from 0.5B to 4B parameters and matches it on the strongest 7B backbone---reaching comparable performance with roughly one tenth as many annotated problems. Our findings establish classification as a parameter- and data-efficient approach to stepwise verification and show that strong verification does not require large generative decoders.

items.title: P(Yes): 15$\times$ Improvements via Test-Time Scaling of Decision Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25474v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Decision models answer typed questions, such as multiple-choice or yes/no questions, with a probability for each option. We add test-time search to frozen decision models, with no training: we show the model a complete proposed answer, read off its probability of saying "Yes" to the proposal's correctness, and search for answers that it rates higher. The search is done either by editing one answer at a time or by joint optimization, which changes several answers at once. Search raises accuracy for every model and test set we tried, and the gains are largest for exact correctness on logic puzzles, where every answer in a task must be right. On 128 such puzzles, it takes Qwen3.8-27B from 2 to 30 exactly correct puzzles ($15\times$) and its per-blank accuracy from 27.8% to 48.5%. On a shared set of 47 puzzles, searching over each model's own Yes/No score raises the per-blank accuracy of StartLux Instant, Perplexity Decider, Clef, and JEV, which we reach only through its public API, by 4.0 to 13.0 percentage points, and raises the number of puzzles they get exactly correct, out of 47 and averaged over three search seeds, from 10 to 35, 9 to 26, 2 to 11, and 9 to 31.7 respectively.

items.summary: This work adds training-free test-time search to frozen decision models by reading the model's probability of endorsing a proposed answer and iteratively editing or jointly optimizing answers to raise that probability. Accuracy improves across all tested models and datasets, with the largest gains on logic puzzles requiring exact correctness, where Qwen3.8-27B improves from 2 to 30 fully correct puzzles. It demonstrates that decision-model probabilities can serve as an effective search signal.

items.title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
items.content: arXiv:2610.25764v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

items.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.25871v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

It also addresses drift awareness, aiming to reflect real-world clinical reasoning beyond individual-sample prediction.

As a domain-specific foundation model, its impact depends on validation breadth and deployment evidence, which the abstract does not fully establish.

items.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25959v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.

The goal is to move beyond single-scene, task-specific embodied systems.

items.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.26310v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.

items.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
items.content: arXiv:2610.26844v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Bi-Approximate CHC Solving
items.content: arXiv:2610.23771v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Constrained Horn clause (CHC) solvers often struggle to discover deep counterexamples whose derivations may require extensive rule unfolding. Although large language models (LLMs) can propose long-range symbolic relations, prior work on formally checked LLM-assisted verification has mainly focused on generating inductive invariants and concrete traces. We exploit this broader capability through Derivation Power Under-approximations (DPUs). Each DPU is a solver-certified under-approximation of the relation induced by a multi-step CHC derivation. An LLM proposes each DPU with symbolic intermediate-state witnesses that enable SMT validation without introducing additional quantifiers. Validated DPUs can be composed and reused soundly. Building on this mechanism, our LLM-assisted framework HornCraft combines invariant generation for over-approximation with DPU generation for under-approximation in CHC solving. On 260 linear and nonlinear integer-arithmetic CHC-COMP benchmarks left unresolved by a 30-minute Spacer run, HornCraft returns certified verdicts for 228 instances. It certifies 42 instances as unsafe, compared with 22 when DPU construction and reuse are disabled.

The formally checked design is a strength, though impact depends on empirical solver gains not fully visible in the abstract.

items.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2610.23935v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.

items.summary: DScout observes that higher mean accepted tokens in diffusion-drafted speculative decoding need not yield higher throughput due to prefix-acceptance and latency effects, and introduces two factorizations guiding drafter training (inclusion, weighting, prediction losses) and inference for throughput. This better aligns diffusion drafters with the actual acceptance dynamics of verification.

items.title: How Much Can We Prune? Exploring the Performance Limits of Visual Token Pruning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23974v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.
items.author: Janghoon Cho, Shubhankar Borse, Reza Pourreza, Juntae Lee, Jihwan Bang, Munawar Hayat, Fatih Porikli
items.summary: This work reframes visual token pruning for vision-language models as selecting one shared visual-token subset under a fixed budget across a broad question distribution, using offline search to establish upper bounds on achievable performance. It aims to distinguish intrinsic pruning limits from limitations of current selection algorithms.
items.reasoning: The complementary offline-search perspective provides a valuable oracle-based calibration for an active research area, potentially redirecting effort in token pruning research. The analysis-first methodology is strong, though the scope is limited to image understanding tasks.

items.title: Agentic Interpretation: Harness-Governed Evidence Construction for Software Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.23996v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Software agents answer behavioral questions about code, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure. These tasks require repository-wide evidence, yet most scaffolds leave intermediate findings in free-form trajectories, making them hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from final answers. We present Agentic Interpretation (AgInt), a framework for harness-governed evidence construction. The model proposes typed records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and persists them, reports unresolved requirements, and licenses answers under task-specific rules. The resulting certificate gives the model persistent external state and leaves an auditable decision record. Formally, append-only certificate states form a grounding lattice ordered by record inclusion, where each admitted record extends the state by union.   We evaluate AgInt with four models on SWE-bench-Live and DeepSWE for patch acceptance and Defects4J and GitBug-Java for fault localization. AgInt outperforms the plain agent and Agentic Code Reasoning on all reported patch-acceptance metrics and ranks responsible lines higher while inspecting fewer irrelevant lines in fault localization. For GLM-5, reject-class F1 rises from 0.256 to 0.543 on SWE-bench-Live, All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400 on Defects4J, and wasted inspected lines fall from 31.5 to 11.7 on GitBug-Java. A matched-template control separates the mechanism: the persistent scaffold drives most fault-localization gains, while the certificate body and gate govern patch-acceptance calibration. With execution licensed, AgInt produces harness-reproduced witnesses for 293 of 475 null-dereference candidates versus 253 for a matched shell agent, and 62 of 117 resource-leak candidates versus 58. Across reported efficiency measurements, it uses 35% fewer executions and reduces cost per candidate by 59%.

items.title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
items.content: arXiv:2610.24469v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.

Introduces truncLongPPL, scoring only a truncated prefix with measured cost savings and near-equal downstream performance.

items.title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.24952v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.

items.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.25069v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). items.title: Vision as Proprioception: Estimating Humanoid Robot Pose from Video
items.content: arXiv:2610.25288v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.

items.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
items.content: arXiv:2610.25447v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_\theta$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_\theta)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

items.summary: This paper improves machine unlearning for masked diffusion language models, which generate text by iterative token unmasking with bidirectional context. Building on the first MDLM-specific unlearning method that matches a frozen prompt-masked anchor via KL divergence, the authors identify limitations of the anchor-based approach and propose an enhanced method balancing forget-set removal with capability preservation.

items.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2610.25603v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.

It offers rare field evidence on how parallel AI deployment reshapes human work behavior.

items.title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25735v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.

items.summary: Adapts a calibrated measurement methodology to detect degradation of certified safe behaviors (deception, power seeking, sycophancy) as models undergo fine-tuning or setting changes, applying it to two open-weight models. items.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)
items.content: arXiv:2610.26190v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.

It uniquely addresses cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. Automated judge profiles are calibrated to practitioners and clinicians.

items.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
items.content: arXiv:2610.26339v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
