items.title: Real-Time Radar Semantic and Panoptic Scene Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.26816v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robust scene understanding under varying environmental conditions is essential for safe autonomous driving. While cameras and LiDAR degrade in adverse weather and poor lighting, Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) spinning radar provides dependable 360{\deg} perception at extended ranges with minimal compute cost. However, real-time FMCW radar scene understanding is challenging due to complex signal returns, limited temporal resolution, and scarce annotated datasets. We introduce StreamRPS, a novel framework for streaming FMCW radar panoptic segmentation, comprising an automated label-generation pipeline via LiDAR scene completion and a real-time streaming network for semantic and panoptic segmentation. Our encoder-decoder streaming architecture comprises a radar-specific hierarchical Transformer encoder and task-specific decoders for semantic or panoptic prediction. Our encoder introduces a stem to capture range-dependent signatures, anisotropic patch embeddings to preserve angular resolution, and axial polar attention to separately model the periodic azimuth and bounded range axes. We further introduce azimuth roll rotation augmentation to simulate ego-vehicle rotation during training. Comprehensive experiments on the SAX and BOREAS datasets validate both our auto-labeling methodology and streaming segmentation network against established baselines. We outperform the strongest baseline by at least 1.4pp while processing sectors at over 400 FPS in a 4-sector streaming setting. We additionally provide manual annotations for 100 SAX radar scans, enabling independent evaluation of the entire framework.

items.summary: StreamRPS enables real-time semantic and panoptic segmentation of FMCW spinning radar for autonomous driving, combining an automated label-generation pipeline via LiDAR scene completion with a streaming encoder-decoder network. Radar offers reliable 360-degree perception in adverse weather where cameras and LiDAR degrade, but scarce annotations have limited progress. The label-generation pipeline plus real-time network is a practical advance for all-weather perception.

items.title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token
items.content: arXiv:2610.26857v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
items.author: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
items.summary: VideoMaMa++ improves diffusion-based video matting by solving chunk-boundary inconsistencies that cause flickering edges and discontinuous transparency in long videos. It represents RGB and mask conditioning as separate interacting token streams and introduces a preserve-and-refine token to carry information across chunks. This enables temporally consistent matting beyond the 6-24 frame limits of diffusion backbones.
items.reasoning: Video matting is practically important for media production, and the token-based cross-chunk consistency mechanism is a clean technical solution to a real limitation of diffusion-based matting; scope is somewhat specialized.

items.title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
items.content: arXiv:2610.26538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated six models from two vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for five of six models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 3.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for five models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, three models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin, but no model reached the pre-set 30% limits of agreement. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model (4.2 points) and changed the others by less than 1 point. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.
items.author: Xiaomeng Li
items.summary: Evaluates six frontier multimodal LLMs, including Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 variants, on estimating consumed energy from meal photos using 802 weighed-intake meals from a controlled feeding trial. Counterintuitively, before/after photo subtraction underestimates intake, and small average errors hide wide individual errors. It is a valuable reality check on using general-purpose LLMs for dietary assessment.

items.title: Retrieval-triggered Action Projection Adjustment for Frozen VLA Policies: An Empirical Study and Failure Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.24573v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.

In CALVIN evaluations, the initial reduction in near-collision proxy events was not reproduced in an independent replication cohort, and the paper includes a candid failure analysis.
items.reasoning: Notable primarily for its scientific honesty: a rigorous replication study showing a proposed memory-augmentation method's benefits did not reproduce is more informative than many positive results. The method itself is modest, but the empirical rigor and failure analysis add real value to the VLA literature.

items.title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2610.25534v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.
items.author: Zhenqi Wu, Trung Tien Dong, Aditya Penumarti, Mohamed A. Fouad, Menna A. Fouad, Mingyang Mao, Jane Jaejeong Shin, Xiaomin Lin
items.summary: AQUAACT addresses the data scarcity blocking autonomous underwater manipulation by recording pilot joystick commands alongside camera observations, mirroring how underwater tasks are flown today, to create a dataset suitable for training vision-language-action models. It also provides a closed-loop benchmark to evaluate learned policies on underwater tasks such as inspection and reef survey. The dataset bridges the gap between land VLA progress and underwater deployment.
items.reasoning: Fills a genuine data gap for underwater robotics, an underrepresented domain for VLA learning, and the joystick-level recording design matches real operational practice. Dataset and benchmark contributions are valuable, but overall impact depends on community adoption and the scale of data collected.

items.title: PhantomTac: Hijacking Robotic Tactile Systems with Deploy-and-forget Tags
items.content: arXiv:2610.26174v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control. Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion. In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors. The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object. Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker. Such an attack scheme is "deploy-and-forget" -- the attacker can deploy the tag and leave. When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object. Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object. Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device. We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design. End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm. Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.

items.title: Certifiably Correct Fr\'echet Means in Orbit Spaaces
items.content: arXiv:2610.24191v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study Fr\'echet means in orbit spaces of finite orthogonal group actions. Since computing these means is NP-hard in general, we take inspiration from group synchronization to develop tractable spectral and semidefinite relaxations. Pairwise alignment certifies global optimality and we develop a semidefinite certificate that can extend beyond this condition. For Gaussian data modulo sign, we prove that our certificate succeeds in a high-noise regime where alignment fails. Numerical experiments evaluate these methods in various settings, including summarizing ensembles of districting plans and clustering time series

items.title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities
items.content: arXiv:2610.23866v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce GardenBench, a benchmark with 11 test suites that evaluate the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a range of tasks. By systematically prompting LLMs with various lightweight queries, we document day-to-day changes in model performance, including run costs and times, that other benchmarks miss. This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. Our main contribution is an innovative, lightweight, and inexpensive benchmark, designed to be consumer-facing and for everyday tasks.

items.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
items.content: arXiv:2610.24349v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.

items.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.24454v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.

items.title: Concordance Plausibility Check for Intervention-Conditioned Human Digital Twins
items.content: arXiv:2610.24577v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Intervention-conditioned human digital twins predict treatment alternatives that cannot be observed in the same patient. Ordinary predictive accuracy therefore cannot establish counterfactual credibility. We propose the Concordance Plausibility Check (CPC), a claim-centered framework combining real-world evidence, qualified simulation and clinical knowledge. CPC matches evidence to the causal claim, audits contradictions and shared dependencies, and reports Pass, Fail or reason-coded Indeterminate.

items.title: DialogMem: Evaluating Dialogue-Grounded Embodied Memory in 3D Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.24767v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.

items.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
items.content: arXiv:2610.25111v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.

The work highlights exploration-exploitation failures as reasoning gets cheap relative to physical experiments.

items.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25675v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.

This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity while handling activation outliers for low-bit LLM quantization. It improves accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over global transformation methods.

items.title: CVaR-RMD: CVaR Selection Pressure for Robust Metaheuristic Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.25697v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. We propose CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs and ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk over heterogeneous evaluation conditions. Across three combinatorial optimization domains, CVaR-based selection improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while maintaining competitive mean performance. These gains persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks

items.summary: This paper introduces CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs but ranks candidates by conditional value-at-risk rather than mean performance. items.content_html: arXiv:2610.25697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. We propose CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs and ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk over heterogeneous evaluation conditions. Across three combinatorial optimization domains, CVaR-based selection improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while maintaining competitive mean performance. These gains persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks

items.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
items.content: arXiv:2610.25996v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.
items.author: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
items.summary: This position-style paper argues that LLM agents fail on long-horizon procedural tasks because they lack explicit procedural memory, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. The authors propose Goal-Oriented Graphs, a symbolic representation encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable structure, and discuss construction challenges and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning. It offers a neurosymbolic roadmap for making agent know-how explicit, accessible, and modifiable.
items.reasoning: The neurosymbolic framing of procedural memory is a useful conceptual contribution to the agent memory literature, and Goal-Oriented Graphs provide a concrete representational direction. However, as an argumentative/principles paper, it appears to lack strong empirical validation, which limits demonstrable impact. Its value lies in framing and future research direction rather than immediate results.

items.title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
items.content: arXiv:2610.26066v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.

items.title: LLMs Prompted for Legal Context Refuse More: Overrefusal from Small On-Premises LLMs in Criminal Legal Context
items.content: arXiv:2610.26211v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Confidentiality requirements increasingly push legal professionals toward small, on-device LLMs that keep case data in-house, used for everyday tasks such as summarization, translation, and reformulation. Following standard prompting guidance, a user naturally states their role (``I am a lawyer...''). We show that this innocuous habit has an unexpected cost: such authority framing can make the model selectively refuse legitimate requests, introducing bias through uneven access to assistance. We evaluate four modern small open-weight LLMs on benign legal-domain prompts to measure this over-refusal.   Surprisingly, we find that authority-style prefixes (''I am legal counsel working for a national supreme court'', ''I'm a defense lawyer'') systematically increase refusal rates by 2--20x over the no-prefix baseline, while a known role-play jailbreak prefix shows mixed effects, sharply increasing refusals in some models and barely shifting them in others. The finding suggests that small on-prem deployable LLMs are unstable under contextual framings that a real institutional user might naturally introduce, and further investigation is essential to minimize opportunities for bias.

Evaluating four modern small models on benign legal prompts, it reveals that standard prompting guidance (declaring your role) introduces bias through uneven access to assistance. This has direct implications for legal professionals adopting confidential on-device LLMs.
items.reasoning: Practically important and counterintuitive finding about how role framing triggers over-refusal, highly relevant given growing on-device LLM adoption in sensitive professions. Evaluation covers multiple models and a well-motivated domain, though limited to four small models and no mitigation is proposed.

items.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.26554v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.

items.title: Composable Parametric Demographic Injection for Values Survey Simulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23867v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as simulated respondents in computational social science, yet accurately reproducing population-specific heterogeneous response distributions remains challenging. Existing methods such as demographic prompting are sensitive to prompt design and increase inference overhead, while parameter-based methods struggle to reuse demographic information efficiently, limiting generalization to unseen combinations. In this regard, we propose PARADE, a composable PARAmetric DEmographic injection framework that represents each demographic attribute value with a reusable and composable LoRA module. Specifically, PARADE separates task-common survey capability from demographic-specific value shifts via a shared Task LoRA and attribute-level Demographic LoRAs, with composition calibration to reduce parameter interference. At inference time, target population models can be constructed on demand by recombining the relevant modules, including demographic combinations not observed during training. Extensive experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench across three backbone models show that PARADE achieves strong population-level distribution alignment while maintaining competitive predictive performance, reducing KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline.

This improves generalization to unseen demographic combinations over prompt-based approaches while reducing inference overhead.
items.reasoning: A clever parameter-efficient mechanism for a growing area (LLM social simulation), with a clean architectural separation that improves composability and cost. Impact is meaningful but scoped to survey simulation use cases.

items.title: Beyond Prediction: A Component-Level Study of Concept Recovery in In-Context Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23936v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to make accurate predictions from demonstrations, but prediction success alone does not reveal the extent to which the underlying concept has been recovered. Existing evaluations typically assess recovery at the level of the whole concept, making it difficult to identify which components are recovered and to separate model limitations from ambiguity in the demonstrations. We introduce a component-level framework for concept recovery that decomposes concepts into their defining components and uses controlled structural interventions to evaluate both component-level and whole-concept recovery under identifiable demonstrations. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and three composition forms, we find that models often achieve high prediction accuracy despite poor whole-concept recovery, with systematic over-specification of relevant attributes and level constraints. Individual structural components are generally insufficient for whole-concept recovery, whereas jointly specifying complementary components, particularly relevant attributes and their level constraints, substantially improves recovery. However, this improvement is fragile: a single plausible but unnecessary level constraint can substantially disrupt recovery. Finally, joint supervision of recovery and implicit prediction substantially improves recovery while preserving prediction performance, with the learned capability transferring across composition forms. Overall, our component-level analysis provides a more diagnostic view of what models recover from demonstrations than the existing holistic view.

items.title: PeekKV: The First Content Token Already Knows Which Heads Matter
items.content: arXiv:2610.23939v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
items.author: Minyoung Go, Yongjun Park
items.summary: This paper addresses KV cache compression in LLM serving by studying how active attention heads shift between prefill and decode stages, showing that head importance identified in prefill is unstable across workloads. It proposes leveraging the first content token during decode, where active-head composition is stable, to identify important heads for non-uniform cache compression.
items.reasoning: KV cache compression is a practically important efficiency topic, and the finding that head composition stabilizes along the decode path is a useful empirical insight with a clean methodological motivation. However, the contribution is incremental within a crowded subfield.

items.title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
items.content: arXiv:2610.24131v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.
items.author: Jianing Shi, Zaibin Zhang, Shijun Lei, Zhenfei Yin
items.summary: This paper studies whether communication structures (peer visibility, update timing) in LLM teams improve symbolic regression for scientific law discovery, decomposing team performance into candidate generation and selection stages. Counterintuitively, distributing budget across independent trajectories beat coordinated teams, and communication policies like Ring actually reduced mean held-out fitting score. The work matters because it challenges assumptions that LLM agent collaboration structures inherently help scientific discovery.
items.reasoning: Rigorous controlled comparison with measurable gains (Q differences), addressing a timely question about multi-agent LLM scientific search. Findings are negative/contrarian, which is valuable but scope is limited to symbolic regression.

items.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
items.content: arXiv:2610.24321v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.
items.author: Aakriti, Manoj Cherukumalli, Prathamesh Patil, Leonidas Tsepenekas, Amit Varshney, Penghang Liu, Elizabeth Fons, Vamsi Potluru
items.summary: Morpheus-2.0 is a compact encoder-only time-series foundation model representing targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid, with dual-axis attention running variable and time relations side-by-side in every layer. It handles varying schemas, horizons from orders of magnitude apart, and sampling rates from seconds to years without fixing horizon and resolution at training time. The industrial authorship (Fons, Potluru, Varshney suggest finance-oriented provenance) targets universal forecasting.
items.reasoning: Architecturally distinct take on universal time-series forecasting addressing real limitations of current foundation models (fixed horizon/resolution, isolated series processing); impact depends on empirical results versus established baselines.

Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.

items.title: When Opposite Premises Translate Identically: A Source-Conditioned Diagnostic for Multilingual Commonsense Items
items.content: arXiv:2610.24428v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multilingual reasoning comparisons depend on translated premises preserving the relations in their English sources. Automatic translation scores can rank source-target pairs, but an acceptance decision alone cannot certify a counterfactual benchmark field. We test a source-contrast diagnostic for ACCORD premises: reverse the English polarity, translate both arms independently, count identical target outputs, and score each arm against its own source. Across 71 matched question identities at two containing-item depths, five target languages, and three translation checkpoints, Swahili has 63, 113, and 67 exact collisions among 710 pairs per checkpoint. At a human-reference-calibrated threshold, round-trip NLI passes both arms of 3 of the 113 NLLB-3.3B collisions, while LaBSE passes 78. Each collision proves at least one unfaithful translation, but does not identify its arm. These controlled measurements do not establish screening accuracy on spontaneous translation errors or a language-by-hop reasoning effect; the study has no native equivalence labels or answer-model evaluation.
items.author: Shuai Wang, Rui Hu
items.summary: Presents a source-contrast diagnostic for validating multilingual counterfactual benchmarks: reverse the English premise polarity, translate both versions, and detect target-language collisions where opposite premises produce identical translations. Across five languages and three translation checkpoints it finds substantial collision rates, especially for Swahili, undermining the validity of translated commonsense benchmarks.
items.reasoning: A methodologically careful benchmark-qauality study with practical implications for anyone building multilingual evaluation sets. Scope is narrow (one benchmark family, five languages) and impact is primarily on evaluation methodology rather than model development, but the collision diagnostic is a reusable tool.

items.title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
items.content: arXiv:2610.24590v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.
items.author: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan, Yang Li, Tiange Fu, Xiaoyuan Fu, Guiyang Luo, Jinglin Li
items.summary: Proposes Scene-Adaptive VLA, a framework using dynamic layer routing to adapt the structure of vision-language-action models to driving scene complexity, reducing inference compute for onboard deployment while preserving driving capability and explainability. It targets structural adaptation, which the authors argue is underexplored relative to sequential approaches like chain-of-thought and token adjustment.
items.reasoning: Combines two active threads -- VLA models for autonomous driving and conditional computation -- in a way that addresses real energy and latency constraints on vehicles. Novelty of dynamic routing itself is limited, but the application and framing are timely; empirical strength determines ultimate impact.

items.title: LLM Trojans that Increase Response Lengths and Cost
items.content: arXiv:2610.24784v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Management of the token-based costs of using LLMs has emerged as a significant problem. Some frontier-model providers charge five times per response token than per prompt token, while others offer prefilling discounts for prompt tokens. In this paper, we devise a defense against a new data-poisoning attack that plants a Trojan which increases the length of the response (and hence the cost to the user) when its trigger is present in the prompt. In particular, we demonstrate how a subtle Trojan may trigger on semantically similar instructions of an instruction fine-tuned LLM.
items.author: Zhengxing Li, Guangmingmei Yang, Nader Alfares, David J. Miller, George Kesidis
items.summary: The paper describes a new data-poisoning attack that implants a Trojan into instruction-tuned LLMs, causing inflated response lengths and higher token-based costs when a trigger appears in the prompt, including triggers on semantically similar instructions. The authors also propose a defense against this economically motivated backdoor attack.
items.reasoning: Novel attack surface tying LLM security to real monetary cost, a practically relevant concern given token pricing; combining an attack characterization with a defense strengthens the contribution, though the scope is limited to a specific poisoning scenario and lab conditions.

items.title: LLM Agents as Suppliers of Physical System Models: Calibration and Acceptance in Modelica
items.content: arXiv:2610.25019v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: To procure a model of a device, a client hands a supplier a description, sometimes with recorded data or a target response, and accepts the model against this handover. We let LLM coding agents act as the supplier on handovers with data, building Modelica models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet, and ask what acceptance certifies. Several agents reach the noise floor, but a handover admits a set of models: the description leaves parts of the structure open, and the data narrow it only to the agreed accuracy. We therefore accept by membership in this set, not by matching one reference, and add layers above behaviour: a physical invariant exposes an energy-creating model at the noise floor. Interpretability becomes a property of the delivered model, tested on a variant, read where none exists and shaped through the handover. Most failures are fits delivered with a systematic residual on their own fitting data, where the handover left open how close is close enough. In a follow-up, stating a threshold makes the agents compare against it, and more deliveries pass. The argument applies wherever a handover underspecifies a model meant to be read, not only run.
items.author: J\"org Frochte, Herbert Schmidt
items.summary: This paper studies LLM coding agents acting as suppliers that build Modelica simulation models of physical systems (four simulated systems plus a real switching magnet) from client handovers with data. Rather than accepting models by matching a single reference, the authors formalize acceptance as membership in the set of models consistent with the specification, and layer additional checks such as physical invariants that can expose an energy-creating model that still fits data to the noise floor.
items.reasoning: A novel and practically motivated framing of LLM agents in engineering workflows, connecting model acceptance theory to a real domain (Modelica physical modeling). The set-membership acceptance and invariant-layering ideas are thoughtful, though the evaluation scope is modest with only five systems.

items.title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
items.content: arXiv:2610.25362v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.

All test data is validated by native speakers, and preference optimization is used to steer culturally appropriate behavior.
items.reasoning: A substantial resource contribution filling a real gap in cultural alignment beyond factual knowledge, with careful native-speaker validation and broad author credibility in Arabic NLP. Impact is significant for the Arabic NLP community though narrower for the field at large.

items.title: PRIMA: Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter for Zero Shot Social Bodily Behavior Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.25482v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.
items.author: Mingcong Ding, Babette B\"uhler, Tim F\"utterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Enkelejda Kasneci
items.summary: PRIMA is a lightweight adapter module that injects a human body-structure prior into frozen vision-language models to enable zero-shot recognition of fine-grained social bodily behaviors like grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling. Pose information is used only as a training-time supervisory signal, so no pose estimation is needed at inference, and the design supports adaptation to new behavior taxonomies without retraining the base VLM. This addresses a real gap, since VLMs prompted with text alone often confuse subtle postural distinctions.
items.reasoning: The approach is sensible and well-motivated: using pose as training-time supervision while keeping inference pose-free is an elegant efficiency choice, and targeting fine-grained social behavior recognition is a comparatively underexplored application for frozen VLMs. However, the paper is an application-focused adapter method rather than a fundamental advance, the abstract does not report benchmark-beating SOTA numbers, and the social-signal-analysis niche limits breadth of impact. Author credibility is reasonable with an academic group, but it is not a major-lab release.

items.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25626v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.

items.summary: Proposes MapSteal, a framework that lets a smaller student model autonomously and recursively acquire knowledge from a black-box teacher LLM, expanding query targets from a small set of roots without predefined queries or student feedback. The structured scheduling and deduplication make the extraction systematic, which doubles as a demonstration of a realistic model-extraction attack surface for deployed LLMs.
items.reasoning: Novel angle on knowledge stealing by removing the need for predefined targets, with security relevance, but the work appears to be an early-stage academic contribution from academic authors rather than a demonstrated large-scale extraction of a frontier model.

items.title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25846v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.
items.author: Debojeet Ghosh, Shreyansh Kumar, Ayushman Garg
items.summary: Pre-registered audit comparing three confidence channels, verbalized confidence, hidden-state probes, and semantic-entropy-style answer agreement, across five Qwen2.5 models on retrieval and reasoning benchmarks. Findings include that probes on prefill states become informative much earlier in layer depth for retrieval (about 7%) than for multi-step reasoning (about 28%), showing the channels are not interchangeable measures of knowing what one knows.
items.reasoning: Methodologically careful, pre-registered measurement-validity study with practical implications for abstention and uncertainty estimation; the model scale is modest and findings are correlative, but the multi-channel comparison fills a real gap.

items.title: Adaptive Decoding Methods for Token-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.25860v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
items.author: Zhaonan Li, Zelei Cheng, Amritansh Mishra, Chia-Hsuan Lee, Mann Patel, Sambit Sahu, Ben Zhou, William M. Campbell
items.summary: This paper studies how rollout decoding support should evolve during RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), proposing a schedule that widens from top-K=10 to K=20 to full support as the token budget grows. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the adaptive schedule beats matched fixed-K baselines by about 1.8 points on interpolated validation performance. It matters because decoding policy is an underexplored lever for RL training efficiency.
items.reasoning: Solid empirical study on an important efficiency question for RLVR training, with controlled comparisons and consistent gains across three runs, but the scope is limited to a 4B code setting and the contribution is a schedule rather than a new algorithm.

Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.

items.title: Toward Online Robust Zero-Sum Markov Games with Function Approximation
items.content: arXiv:2610.26286v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Online robust zero-sum Markov games pose a coupled operator-learning and game-solving problem: from nominal interaction data, the learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator while maintaining strategic coverage and controlling stage-game approximation error. Existing robust reinforcement-learning theory does not yet provide such an operator-learning perspective beyond specialized multi-agent settings. We develop an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Our analysis is organized around the robust Bellman residuals induced by the candidate value class and yields a regret reduction that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification. Under explicit interpretable assumptions, we obtain conditional theorem interfaces for general and projected function approximation, together with closed results in several structured regimes, including tabular, epochwise cross-fit linear, self-normalized pure-online linear / finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS truncation. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and the return-gap trade-off predicted by the framework.

items.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.26801v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.

items.title: Compaction-Aware Reinforcement Learning For Ascend Triton Kernel Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23950v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.

items.title: SPADE-KD: Peer-to-Peer Collaborative Learning under Heterogeneous Settings
items.content: arXiv:2610.24013v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.

items.title: PAC Learning with Query Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2610.24332v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study realizable multiclass PAC learning with query feedback, where each training example provides a single binary response indicating whether its true label belongs to a chosen subset from a fixed query family. Our main contribution is the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that captures both the structure of the hypothesis class and the ability of the available queries to distinguish labels. This parameter generalizes the bandit DS dimension, which it recovers under singleton queries. We establish a sample-complexity lower bound of $\Omega(D/\varepsilon)$ and an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(D^2/\varepsilon)$, suppressing factors polylogarithmic in the number of labels and the failure probability. When the available queries can split every candidate set into two parts of comparable size, we improve the upper bound to $\widetilde{O}(D/\varepsilon)$, yielding a characterization up to logarithmic factors.

items.title: Near-Optimal Regret for Semi-Bandit Learning of Monotone Stochastic Problems
items.content: arXiv:2610.24446v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We consider the task of learning an (approximately) optimal policy for stochastic optimization problems where the true distributions are unknown. In each period, the algorithm plays a policy for the stochastic problem and observes semi-bandit feedback, i.e., it only receives new samples from the random variables that were selected by the policy. We obtain an algorithm that works for a large class of ``monotone'' stochastic problems, including prophet inequality, Pandora's box, series testing, stochastic knapsack and stochastic matching. We obtain $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT})$ regret for ``weakly'' monotone problems and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nT})$ regret for ``strongly'' monotone problems, where $T$ is the number of periods, $n$ is the problem dimension (number of random variables) and $k$ is the maximum support size of any random variable. This improves over previous regret bounds by a $\sqrt{n}$ factor. In fact, our dependence on $n$ and $T$ is the best-possible due the $\Omega(\sqrt{nT})$ lower bound for multi-armed-bandits. Our main technique is the use of Hellinger distance in bounding the ``error'' between the true and learned distributions, and the use of a constant-factor chain rule for the Hellinger distance of dependent random variables.

Bounds are O(sqrt(nkT)) for weakly monotone and O(sqrt(nT)) for strongly monotone settings.

items.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations
items.content: arXiv:2610.24737v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Mat\'ern kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.

items.title: A Symmetry-Matching Approach to Blind-Spot Reduction in Sparse Autoencoders
items.content: arXiv:2610.24908v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language models can treat semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable at the representation level, creating blind spots that standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) objectives do not target. In safety-critical settings such as clinical dosage extraction, legal clause interpretation, or financial amount verification, such failures can propagate silently into downstream decisions. We study this problem as one of feature-basis orientation. Building on a symmetry-matching view from algebraic error-detection theory, we add a differentiable $V_{\mathrm{Gini}}$ regularisation term to SAE training that penalises uneven perturbation response within a specified family. Across GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Qwen 2.5, a frozen multi-seed evaluation shows that $V$-regularisation raises both relative and absolute lower-tail responses while reducing response-profile imbalance, with no material general-text reconstruction degradation. JumpReLU and minimum description length (MDL) objectives remain close to the Standard SAE profile under the same protocol. Family-geometry controls show that the effect is not explained by template duplication or a single dominant perturbation family, and held-out probes plus null-calibrated separation tests evaluate how far the representation-level change carries to downstream discriminability. A zero-shot audit on out-of-distribution clinical radiology minimal pairs finds the relative weak-tail lift in all evaluated model-by-family cells, not perfectly rank-aligned with the trained statistic, and a held-out family audit finds it on family kinds never used in training. Together, the results show that perturbation-aware SAE training can reorient feature bases toward safety-relevant input changes while leaving downstream validation as a separate empirical step.
