items.content_html: arXiv:2610.25595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.

items.title: Learning Goal-Conditioned Subgoals through Frozen Hierarchical World Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.26179v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hierarchical world models plan over long horizons by passing predicted states from a coarse model to a lower-level controller. Choosing these states can be expensive: the upper-level planner repeatedly differentiates through candidate macro-action trajectories. We replace this search with a lightweight goal-conditioned network trained through the frozen high-level predictor. The network supplies a conditioning vector, while the predictor generates the next latent waypoint. Training uses hindsight goals and state-prediction losses on offline trajectories, without search-solution targets or macro-action labels. Inference retains an autoregressive high-level rollout, but requires no high-level candidate optimization. We evaluate this approach on the shared-latent HWM checkpoints distributed with H-JEPA, using three backbone seeds and three head initializations per backbone. With a common evaluation protocol, mean success is 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze. The method improves over the corresponding HWM search baseline on three environments and has the same mean on Push-T. Dedicated measurements on an NVIDIA L40S give 1.28-4.39x end-to-end speedups for batched evaluation. Ablations identify state-adaptive conditioning as a consistent contributor, while predictor-mediated subgoals and unrestricted conditions have environment-dependent benefits.

items.title: Foundation Model Driven Optical Flow
items.content: arXiv:2610.26690v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We investigate how frozen pretrained visual and depth representations support dense optical flow when coupled with a supervised matching network. Building on TTSFlow, this paper studies Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) feature decoding and one coarse-to-fine refinement stage. Our method fuses features from frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 models and estimates optical flow through a trainable transformer-based matching pipeline. After optical-flow training on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D, it achieves 2.37 endpoint error (EPE) on the Sintel training split, Final pass, compared with 2.52 for the FlowSeek (T) configuration reported here. Our RoCo-Spring 2026 entry, RoCo-29.VSAI, obtains a robustness-balanced score of 1.1038, Spring EPE of 1.411, and RobustSpring proxy EPE of 4.739, with a lower balanced score than seven of the twelve listed reference baselines. These results characterize the complete pipeline, which reuses frozen foundation backbones and performs one refinement stage. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/Visual-and-Spatial-AI-Lab/FFlow}

items.title: ChairNav: Cross-Embodiment Pre-training and Personalization for Long-Horizon Wheelchair Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24012v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Developing autonomous electric wheelchairs capable of long-horizon sidewalk navigation is critical for accessible personal mobility, yet existing approaches either focus on indoor map-based navigation or rely on expensive, complex sensor stacks to achieve full autonomy. In this work, we propose to tackle outdoor sidewalk navigation by leveraging visual navigation foundation models and large-scale navigation datasets, which offer strong generalization using lightweight hardware. To this end, we present ChairNav, a novel framework that adapts a general visual navigation model into a personalized electric wheelchair navigation system using a three-stage data pyramid. To address the scarcity of in-domain data, ChairNav first pre-trains on large-scale cross-embodiment datasets transformed into the wheelchair domain, followed by mid-training on a small number of wheelchair demonstrations to eliminate remaining domain gaps. Finally, a post-training stage refines the deployed model from user interventions to personalize its behavior. We deploy ChairNav on a commercial electric wheelchair equipped with an RGB-D camera and an onboard NVIDIA Jetson compute module. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of each stage in our data pyramid: pre-training reduces lateral ADE by 18%, and post-training increases the mean distance between user interventions from 29.2 m to 57.4 m. Further evaluation on kilometer-scale urban sidewalk routes shows that our system operates autonomously for 93.4% of total driving time, demonstrating its potential for everyday accessible mobility. Demo video and more details are at https://vail.cs.ucla.edu/ChairNav/.

items.summary: ChairNav adapts general visual navigation foundation models into personalized electric wheelchair navigation for long-horizon outdoor sidewalk navigation using a three-stage data pyramid: pre-training on large-scale navigation datasets, then in-domain adaptation, then personalization. It targets accessibility-critical mobility with lightweight hardware rather than expensive sensor stacks. This addresses an underserved, socially important application of embodied AI.
items.reasoning: The accessibility focus and cross-embodiment pre-training strategy are commendable and practical; impact is meaningful but the approach builds on existing navigation foundation models rather than introducing new methods.

items.title: Stress-Query and Temporal Reliability of Vision-Language Models as copilots in Autonomous UAV Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23877v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Integrating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into autonomous UAV navigation enables high-level semantic reasoning but introduces critical temporal bottlenecks that can destabilize flight control. This paper presents a systematic benchmark that evaluates the operational trade-offs among model scale, hardware constraints, and flight reliability. By subjecting the system to extensive stress tests on both a high-performance workstation and a constrained integrated-graphics laptop, we isolate the kinetic impact of inference latency against reasoning accuracy. Our findings reveal a performance dichotomy: lightweight models struggle with structural hallucinations that break deterministic state machines, while heavyweight models induce trajectory overcorrections due to inference lag. We demonstrate that a mid-weight architecture strikes the optimal balance, successfully rehabilitating navigation in degraded environments without compromising real-time stability across different hardware profiles.

It isolates the kinetic impact of inference latency against reasoning accuracy and finds a dichotomy: lightweight models suffer structural hallucinations that break state machines, while heavyweight models cause trajectory overshoot from latency. A useful empirical guide for deploying VLMs in real-time control.

items.title: MicroSplat: Towards Automating 3D Small-Scale Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2610.23899v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on. The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame. Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing. We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm. After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended. It performs calibration, plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm's own poses. We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions.

items.summary: Presents MicroSplat, a system producing 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions of sub-millimeter objects using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator rig, handling the extreme field-of-view and depth-of-field constraints of macro optics that violate standard 3DGS assumptions. It automates capture and processing that previously required human-in-the-loop photogrammetry. Applications include circuit-board inspection and specimen digitization.
items.reasoning: A practical and creative extension of 3DGS into the micro scale with real automation value; niche applications and hardware dependence moderate the score.

items.title: Touch Where It Matters: Learning Local Tactile Policies for Fine-Grained Gripper Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.24485v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual imitation policies can organise task motion, yet contact-rich object use demands gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing. We study fine-grained gripper control as a local feedback problem within ongoing task execution. Our approach assigns tactile feedback a dedicated control role during contact-rich task stages. We introduce ContactPolicy, a learned local controller that takes over the gripper while a visual base policy continues to control the arm. ContactPolicy combines tactile and force histories with current robot state to jointly predict gripper increments and their modulation, updating the gripper target from each new observation. An Intent policy manages control handover between the visual base policy and ContactPolicy. Real-world experiments on container opening, object handling, and tool operation show improved task success over both the Visuomotor Policy and Tactile-Force Policy baselines. Execution analysis illustrates how the gripper adjusts contact within an ongoing task, including periods of target retention and fine-grained changes as interaction conditions evolve. Arm-state ablations and failure analysis further examine how execution context supports local regulation. These results support task-local tactile policies for fine-grained gripper control within visual manipulation.

items.title: Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy in Remote Manipulation Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.25436v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Shared autonomy is a control paradigm that combines human cognitive abilities with robot precision to enable effective remote manipulation in complex environments. A key challenge is how to adapt the level of autonomy using information extracted from the human, task, and/or environment. In this paper, we propose a novel arbitration strategy that dynamically adjusts the level of autonomy in the system using the entropy of a belief distribution derived from a multimodal intent inference. Human intent is modeled with a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which updates beliefs over goals given real-time operator gaze data and robot arm motion during teleoperation. We then formulate the blending of human input and autonomous control as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem, where the system's autonomous behavior is guided by the belief distribution. This approach enables continuous, gradual transitions across the full spectrum of autonomy levels, from direct teleoperation to full autonomy. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments to compare the performance of our proposed algorithm against two MPC-based shared autonomy methods. Compared to the baselines, our approach achieved reductions of at least 61% in object retrieval time, 44% in trajectory length, and 60% in human control input. Participants reported high perceived control, predictability, intent recognition, and responsiveness, along with low workload.

items.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24051v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.

Four state-of-the-art T2I models are evaluated across nine classes of constraints from single attributes to multi-object relationships.

items.title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.24383v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.24383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

items.title: MM-LeJEPA: Correlated Gaussian Regularization for Multimodal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
items.content: arXiv:2610.24681v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LeJEPA derives an isotropic Gaussian embedding target by minimizing, under its task assumptions, a Fisher information criterion that controls the task-averaged squared prediction bias. This enables unimodal self-supervised learning without reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. However, its isotropic task prior does not account for the cross-modal structure of multimodal tasks that read shared content. We introduce MM-LeJEPA by extending LeJEPA's task assumptions to multimodal learning. Specifically, we model multimodal tasks as strength-weighted combinations of components that read independent information from the two modalities and components that read the same content from both. Under explicit gradient-moment, correspondence, and symmetry assumptions, we derive a correlated Gaussian target that minimizes a weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance constraint. An analytic transform adapts Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) to this target, yielding a two-term objective that combines distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction. The extension adds a single scalar hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation, and retains the simplicity of LeJEPA. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, our results are competitive with representative open-source methods. Code will be released.

items.reasoning: A principled theoretical extension of a recent self-supervised architecture to the multimodal regime, grounded in Fisher information arguments. Impact depends on empirical gains over established multimodal SSL baselines, which the abstract does not fully demonstrate.

items.title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.25281v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. To this end, we introduce new benchmark datasets constructed from CIKM, KDD, and SIGIR conference papers, with varied prediction settings, including impact forecasting for emerging concepts unseen during training. We propose MiroGraph, a Multi-agent reasoning framework with scientific concept Graphs, in which a feature designer agent designs predictive features for a given concept pair from structural, semantic, and trend perspectives, and then three LLM agents compute the actual feature values from the enclosing subgraph of the concept pair. Using these feature values, a classifier designer agent constructs a classifier that predicts the final impact labels. MiroGraph outperforms various impact forecasting and temporal link prediction methods.

items.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
items.content: arXiv:2610.25516v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.

It demonstrates that well-timed compaction can outperform both truncation and full-context for small models.

items.title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
items.content: arXiv:2610.25563v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.
items.author: Yichen Liu, Xiaochong Jiang, Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu

The proposed framework formulates device selection as a contextual bandit problem combining adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint selection. This addresses a real gap where prior work retrieves tools but never learns which eligible device returns useful observations.

items.title: ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25963v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Judgment models answer semantic questions by scoring a finite set of candidate outcomes. Can reusable programs turn these local decisions into powerful multistep reasoning? We introduce \method, a framework that jointly constructs judgment schemas and composition programs for frozen judgment models. A generative teacher designs the procedure offline; the judgment model resolves local semantic questions online, and the saved program composes its decisions into an answer. We study three allocations of design effort between humans and the teacher, focusing on construction through a shared interface. We instantiate the framework with Kev. On three selected BIG-Bench Hard tasks, nine independently constructed programs solve all 450 executions of 150 development inputs. A separate deployment study freezes three programs after development-set reference-agreement refinement and evaluates them on 600 held-out questions. These programs achieve near-perfect 99.67\% macro accuracy, versus 64.00\% for direct Kev and 68.80\% for final-answer-only Qwen3.5-4B. They attain comparable observed accuracy to Qwen's unrestricted response policy (99.07\%) with an \textbf{8.43-fold online speedup}: 0.255 versus 2.150 seconds per question. These results show how reusable programs can substantially expand the reasoning capability of a compact judgment model while keeping its parameters fixed.

items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
items.content: arXiv:2610.26185v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

items.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.26251v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. We propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension grounded in original benchmark data that enriches static benchmarks with structural diversity and enriches single-score black-box evaluation with multi-dimensional, capability-oriented assessment. CaFE first profiles the original benchmark and defines eight Structural Features (SFs) that characterize its temporal structure. For each SF, it resamples the original data according to its structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments the retained samples by varying the SF's salience, producing samples with different structural profiles. After filtering out out-of-distribution samples while preserving diversity, CaFE yields a refreshed evaluation set. TSFMs are then evaluated on this set using both conventional forecast-error metrics and intervention-response metrics, giving each model a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show that CaFE yields stable evaluation results and reveals per-feature strengths and weaknesses that a single aggregate score hides. Moreover, on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard. CaFE therefore makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest.

items.title: Remembering Has a Price: Learning Memory Worth under Resource Constraints
items.content: arXiv:2610.26453v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lifelong agents continually accumulate and reuse experience to improve after deployment, yet in practice they often operate under tight generation, interaction, and memory budgets. Under such stringent joint constraints, we find that existing lifelong-memory methods can become ineffective, with several sophisticated approaches offering little advantage over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a more fundamental problem: resource scarcity makes each memory decision more consequential. When only a small amount of past experience can be retained or reused and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving a relevant but ineffective memory can consume scarce context and hinder downstream execution. The key challenge is therefore not simply to retrieve relevant experience, but to determine which experiences are actually worth retaining and reusing. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight online memory framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback and applies it consistently to memory retrieval and bounded memory management. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods. These results suggest that effective lifelong adaptation under resource constraints depends not on remembering more, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/TokenWorth.

It proposes learning the value of memories, i.e., deciding what is worth retaining and reusing when resources are scarce.

The memory-value framing is conceptually valuable for lifelong agents, though empirical breadth is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Toward Structured Financial Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.26516v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Foundation models promise reusable capabilities and step-change performance gains across tasks. In finance, large-scale pretraining of domain-specialized foundation models can advance both goals. However, prevailing architectures and objectives do not by themselves address the combined demands of financial systems: partial observability, interacting entities, asynchronous events, changing regimes, action-dependent outcomes, and rare states with disproportionate consequences. Moreover, independently developed specialists may learn incompatible representations, while multi-domain monolithic alternatives couple data access, model updates, and governance. We therefore propose a structured-data-first research agenda centered on modular, domain-specialized financial foundation models connected by a representation fabric for reuse and composition across domains and tasks. These models should maintain persistent financial state across aggregation levels and time horizons, capture its dynamics, and simulate action-conditioned futures, while remaining calibrated across regimes and for tail outcomes. They must also learn efficiently under data and access constraints and provide faithful, traceable explanations. We identify research challenges, directions, and capability-oriented evaluation criteria.
items.author: Natraj Raman, Saumitra Mishra, Vamsi Potluru, Sumitra Ganesh
items.summary: A position/research-agenda paper from a JPMorgan-affiliated team arguing that financial foundation models require structured-data-first, modular architectures to handle partial observability, asynchronous events, regime changes, and rare high-consequence states. It critiques both incompatible specialist models and monolithic multi-domain alternatives on governance and representation grounds.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful agenda-setting paper rather than an empirical breakthrough; it articulates a coherent vision for domain foundation models in finance from credible industry authors, but its value depends on future validation.

items.title: StebBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.26679v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.
items.author: Hossein A. Rahmani, Bin Wu, Chaeeun Lee, Fanghua Ye, Sahan Bulathwela, Sujay Kumar Jauhar, Marzieh Fadaee, Nick Craswell, Emine Yilmaz

items.reasoning: A well-executed benchmark with diagnostic granularity that open-domain agent planning evaluations lack; credible evaluation-focused author team, though the domain (wikiHow procedures) constrains depth.

items.title: Zero-Shot Tabular Learning via Hypergraph Reasoning with LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.23923v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Tabular data are prevalent across diverse domains such as healthcare and finance. Zero-shot tabular learning aims to make predictions without labeled data. However, existing LLM-based approaches rely on row-wise prompting, resulting in high inference cost and limited use of inter-row dependencies. In this work, we propose TABHGR+, an efficient relation-aware zero-shot framework for tabular data that leverages LLM-generated rules to label and group rows. Specifically, based on column and task descriptions, we use LLMs to generate rules that assign weak labels to all rows. To refine these noisy weak labels, we construct a hypergraph by grouping semantically related rows using LLM-generated rules and perform hypergraph-based label propagation. Lastly, we further enhance the LLM-generated hypergraph for propagation, which is potentially sub-optimal, by assigning label-adaptive weights to hyperedges. By requiring only a constant number of LLM calls independent of dataset size, TABHGR+ substantially reduces inference cost while achieving higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.
items.author: Geon Lee, Kyungho Kim, Dongwon Choi, Juyeon Kim, Shinhwan Kang, Kijung Shin
items.summary: TABHGR+ uses LLM-generated rules to weakly label and group table rows, then refines noisy labels via hypergraph-based label propagation, enabling efficient zero-shot tabular prediction that exploits inter-row dependencies. This improves on row-wise prompting approaches in both cost and accuracy for healthcare and finance-style data.
items.reasoning: A sensible combination of LLM rule generation with structured hypergraph reasoning that addresses real weaknesses (cost, ignored inter-row structure) in LLM tabular learning. Competes in a busy area; strength is the structured refinement mechanism and strong author group.

items.title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.24005v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
items.author: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
items.summary: PACE targets ViT-free native multimodal LLMs that tokenize pixel patches directly, showing empirically that unlike ViT-based models they tolerate aggressive visual token compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. The paper proposes an analysis pipeline and Pareto-adaptive compression tailored to this setting.
items.reasoning: The observation that native ViT-free MLLMs behave differently under compression is a useful empirical finding for an emerging architecture paradigm, and the Pareto-adaptive method addresses an underexplored gap. Impact depends on how widely native MLLMs are adopted.

items.title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.24093v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.
items.author: Luciano Marchezan, Romain Lefeuvre, Kevin Delcourt, Benoit Combemale, Houari Sahraoui
items.summary: The study analyzes 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across pre-LLM, LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development eras using Software Heritage snapshots, measuring semantic and syntactic code similarity, SonarQube quality metrics, and evolution characteristics. It empirically investigates whether AI-assisted development reduces code diversity or degrades quality.
items.reasoning: A timely empirical question with a well-designed longitudinal methodology, though attributing observed changes to AI assistance across eras is inherently confounded by ecosystem drift. The findings are relevant to software engineering practice and policy around agentic coding tools.

items.title: Analyzing Repetition and Interference Effects in Memory-Constrained User Simulators
items.content: arXiv:2610.24232v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: User simulators can help evaluate and train AI systems to interact with humans at scale. To do so, evaluation of user simulators must measure behavioral parity with people. We evaluate whether memory-constrained user simulators are sensitive to two factors known to affect human information retention: repetition of a fact and interference from competing information. We find that some simulators achieve human-like overall accuracy, and replicate the magnitude of repetition and interference effects, but none match people's accuracy on particular questions: while humans misremember facts, models forget them, leading to different error patterns. We release this data as a challenge benchmark for future work on user simulators.
items.author: Cara Su-Yi Leong, Nicholas Tomlin, Tal Linzen
items.summary: This study evaluates memory-constrained user simulators against two well-documented human memory phenomena: repetition improving retention and interference from competing information. While some simulators match human overall accuracy and replicate effect magnitudes, none match human error patterns at the question level: humans misremember facts whereas models forget them. The released benchmark gives future simulator work a behavioral-parity target.
items.reasoning: Cognitively grounded evaluation with a clear, quotable dissociation (misremembering vs. forgetting) from credible researchers; the released benchmark adds lasting value, though the scale of evaluation is modest.

items.title: Towards Reinforcement Learning for Space Robotics: Fast Training and Reliable Real-World Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2610.24241v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work demonstrates the use of a fast simulation-based training framework to learn control policies using reinforcement learning. The hardware requirements are minimal and the simulation-learned policies transfer reliably to the real world. With this setup, we show that a quadruped robot can learn to traverse diverse real-world terrains reliably---including in a lunar-analog facility---after less than 20 minutes of training on a single consumer-grade GPU. These results provide a glimpse of a future where reinforcement learning is a crucial tool in developing more capable and robust space robotic systems. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/vUFJiZdJaQ0.
items.author: Abhishek Naik, Michael Wu, Michael O'Sullivan, Colin Bellinger, Yunli Wang
items.summary: This work demonstrates a fast simulation-based RL training framework with minimal hardware requirements whose learned policies transfer reliably to real robots. It showcases practical sim-to-real RL for space robotics applications.

items.title: Cooperation Without Shared Rewards via Reciprocal Q-Augmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24793v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
items.author: Francesco Morri, Adel Abusitta, Quentin Cappart, Margarida Carvalho
items.summary: This multi-agent RL paper introduces Reciprocal Q-Augmentation (RQA), which uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment an agent's Q-function with estimates of how its actions affect others, enabling sustained cooperation in general-sum games without access to other agents' rewards or internal states. It targets the well-known failure mode where a single defection collapses agents into welfare-suboptimal Nash equilibria.
items.reasoning: Addresses a realistic and underexplored constraint (no reward observability) in general-sum multi-agent settings with a principled method; the contribution is solid but sits within an established multi-agent RL literature and its evaluation breadth from the abstract is unclear.

items.title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2610.25134v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.
items.author: Xiaoyu Wu, Zhaoxin Yu, Xinglin Xiao, Nan Xu
items.summary: TIRE is a framework for scalable synthesis of physics reasoning training data that instantiates problems top-down from reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions, with reliable execution producing verifiable numerical answers. This avoids hallucination risks of pure LLM text-based synthesis while retaining expert-style control over laws, conditions, and scenarios.
items.reasoning: Addresses the important bottleneck of verifiable physics training data for reasoning LLMs. Combining formula-driven instantiation with executable answer verification is a solid contribution, though data-synthesis pipelines of this kind are becoming relatively common.

items.title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
items.content: arXiv:2610.25211v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. We introduce NeuroAct, an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding. NeuroAct implements dual-loop autonomous research across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles use evidence on signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics to test hypotheses, select analyses or interventions, and refine candidates using performance, stability, and cost feedback. An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.
items.author: Wei Xiong, Jiangtong Li, Han Zhao, Linxiao Yang, Jie Li, Changjun Jiang
items.summary: NeuroAct is an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding that runs dual loops over EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. An inner loop of research, development, and review roles uses evidence on signal structure, representations, and training dynamics to test hypotheses and select interventions, aimed at explaining performance and generalization gaps rather than blind search.
items.reasoning: Part of the growing wave of domain-specific autonomous research agents, with a differentiated emphasis on evidence-driven hypothesis testing over reward-driven search. Domain application to EEG/BCI is valuable, though general-agent methodology is borrowed rather than novel.

An inner loop of research, development, and review roles uses evidence on signal structure, representations, and training dynamics to test hypotheses and select interventions, aimed at explaining performance and generalization gaps rather than blind search.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.25211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. We introduce NeuroAct, an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding. NeuroAct implements dual-loop autonomous research across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles use evidence on signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics to test hypotheses, select analyses or interventions, and refine candidates using performance, stability, and cost feedback. An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.

items.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
items.content: arXiv:2610.25512v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
items.author: Mingcong Ding, Chenyan Zhang, Zhuojiang Cai, Dongyang Guo, Babette B\"uhler, Enkelejda Kasneci
items.summary: This controlled study examines whether interpretation records carried in an AI assistant's memory influence later predictions in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Findings show free-form interpretations amplify historical influence in both helpful and harmful directions, while evidence-bounded interpretation formats preserve distinguishing behavior and reduce harmful influence of wrong histories.
items.reasoning: An interesting and well-controlled empirical study of memory contamination in assistive AI, with actionable design implications (favor evidence-bounded interpretations in agent memory). Niche domain, but the core question about persistent interpretive memory is broadly relevant to agent design.

items.title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
items.content: arXiv:2610.25652v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.
items.author: Joseph Turnbull, Berkan Ottlik, Jamie Simon
items.summary: Proposes a simplified ordinary differential equation, the feature ODE, meant to describe the gradient-flow learning dynamics of two-layer MLPs on anisotropic Gaussian data, and shows empirically that real MLPs learning Hermite polynomials and staircases roughly follow its loss trajectories. The surprisingly close agreement despite large simplifications is discussed and speculated upon.
items.reasoning: Interesting theoretical-empirical bridge in the theory of neural network training dynamics, but confined to shallow networks and simple target functions, so the broader significance is still speculative.

items.title: AirMPA: A Meteorology-to-Pollution Adapter for Global Air Quality Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.25797v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate real-time forecasting of atmospheric pollutants is essential for reducing exposure risks and improving public health. Traditional numerical forecasting systems suffer from incomplete parameterizations, uncertain inputs, and high computational cost. Existing deep learning approaches improve efficiency, but often entangle meteorological and pollutant variables within unified forecasting frameworks, limiting flexibility and pollutant-specific representation learning. To address these challenges, we propose AirMPA, a decoupled autoregressive framework for meteorology-to-pollution forecasting. AirMPA predicts 13 atmospheric pollutants at 0.4{\deg} spatial resolution and 12-h temporal resolution using meteorological fields, emission priors, and historical pollutant concentrations. The model is built on an improved Swin-Transformer architecture with zonal release attention and dual-branch fusion, enabling more effective modeling of global transport continuity and heterogeneous pollutant dynamics. During training, AirMPA uses the fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ERA5) as meteorological forcing, while during inference it directly ingests forecast fields from external meteorological models, enabling stable autoregressive prediction up to 5 days ahead. Experiments show that AirMPA consistently outperforms Aurora and surpasses the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in approximately 90% of pollutant-lead-time evaluation cases over the 5-day forecast horizon, while outperforming CAMS on all variables beyond 48 h. These results demonstrate the potential of decoupled meteorology-to-pollution forecasting for global air quality prediction.
items.author: Yiheng Wang, Kai Zheng, Yuetan Lin, Fanglu Fan, Chenliang Tao, Guochao Chen, Hongliang Zhang, Hao Li
items.summary: Presents AirMPA, a decoupled autoregressive deep learning framework that forecasts 13 atmospheric pollutants globally at 0.4-degree resolution by adapting meteorological fields and emission priors to pollution prediction, rather than entangling meteorology and pollutants in one model. It aims to overcome the cost and parameterization limits of numerical forecasting systems.
items.reasoning: Applied science contribution with clear public-health relevance and a sensible decoupling design; Google's WeatherNext line shows the value of learned atmospheric forecasting, but this is an academic-scale system whose operational quality needs validation.

items.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2610.25932v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
items.author: Minoo Ahmadi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
items.summary: This work improves sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for masked diffusion language models by preserving particle lineage diversity during resampling, avoiding the duplication-and-discard failure of multinomial resampling. It works with both internal confidence rewards and external process reward models and requires no post-training. It matters because diffusion LLM inference is an emerging area needing better decoding methods.
items.reasoning: Technically sound refinement of SMC decoding for a relatively novel model class (diffusion LLMs); the diversity-preservation insight is useful, but the contribution is incremental within inference-time decoding and empirical breadth is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Correctness-Dependent Asymmetric Target Distributions for Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.25973v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Self-distillation policy optimization provides dense token-level supervision for LLM post-training through feedback-conditioned self-teachers. However, directly matching the self-teacher can disrupt successful behaviors on correct rollouts while providing insufficient correction on incorrect ones. We propose Asymmetric Policy Optimization via Self-Distillation (APSD), which constructs correctness-dependent targets by mixing student and self-teacher distributions: interpolation preserves successful behaviors on correct rollouts, while extrapolation beyond the self-teacher strengthens correction on incorrect ones. We analyze APSD through divergence decomposition, reverse-KL barycentric geometry, and gradient analysis, highlighting the importance of gradient flow through student-dependent targets. Experiments under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and rich feedback show that APSD achieves strong overall performance against reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines and matches SDPO performance with 2.6x fewer training steps on average across Qwen3 model scales.
items.author: Suwan Yoon, Seongryong Jung, Changhee Lee
items.summary: APSD improves self-distillation policy optimization for LLM post-training by mixing student and self-teacher distributions asymmetrically based on rollout correctness: interpolation preserves successful behaviors on correct rollouts, while extrapolation beyond the self-teacher strengthens correction on incorrect ones. The paper supports the design with divergence decomposition and gradient analysis. It targets a real failure mode of naive self-teacher matching.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated refinement of dense token-level post-training supervision with theory (reverse-KL geometry, gradient analysis) backing the design; contributions are within the crowded RL-free post-training space, so novelty is moderate.

items.title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness
items.content: arXiv:2610.26059v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.
items.author: Caixin Kang, Sitong Gong, Tianyu Yan, Kaipeng Zhang, Yoichi Sato, Yifei Huang
items.summary: ZhenhuanBench is a 1,592-item benchmark for detecting mock politeness (polite form, hostile intent), built from expert commentary on a Chinese drama, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and listener uptake. GPT-6 Astra, an existing OpenAI model released in September 2026, leads at 73.48% overall with weaker listener-reaction performance at 58.37%. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model beat teacher distillation, and subsequent RL saturated, with chance correction shrinking the estimated recoverable gap substantially.
items.reasoning: Creative culturally grounded benchmark for pragmatic/social reasoning with honest statistical treatment (chance correction) and interesting training findings; value is niche-language and cultural specificity, and the top model reference is to an already-released system rather than a new launch.

items.title: ALIGN: Aligning Condition Estimation and Expression in Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning
items.content: arXiv:2610.26455v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy's action-vector-field prediction. Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field. We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies. ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time. We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories. ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, compared with 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline. These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.

This strengthens the conditioning signal in both construction and incorporation into the action vector field. The result is better exploitation of retries, recoveries, and failures in manipulation datasets.

items.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
items.content: arXiv:2610.26695v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
items.author: Murat Guney Kemal, Robert Lieck
items.summary: This work studies whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone, introducing a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively composes sequences into multi-level representations. Using unsupervised grammar induction as a testbed where hierarchies can be explicitly evaluated, the authors probe whether reconstruction objectives favor compositional structure. It speaks to a core representation-learning question about emergent hierarchy without structural supervision.
items.reasoning: Addresses a fundamental scientific question with a clean evaluation substrate (grammar induction), but the scope is exploratory and results are confined to controlled settings rather than demonstrating broad practical impact.

items.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.26852v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.
items.author: Zehao Wang, Jianpeng Yao, Yuping Wang, Yiping Li, Jiaqi Li, Zhixu Li, Kanghoon Lee, Jinfeng Wang, Cong Liu, Zhaowei Tan, Jinkyoo Park, Jiachen Li
items.summary: Proposes a multi-robot social navigation framework combining uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting across robots with robust decision making, targeting safety under occlusions and out-of-distribution scenarios. Cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion predicts future occupancy grids to improve coordination. Addresses a known weakness of naively extending single-robot RL navigation to multi-robot settings.
items.reasoning: Solid robotics systems work combining uncertainty quantification with multi-agent forecasting; valuable for safe deployment but incremental relative to the substantial prior literature on social navigation and occupancy prediction.
