items.title: From Spectrograms to Shallow Speech SSL: Audio-Frontend Design for Generator-Disjoint and Low-Latency Audio--Visual Deepfake Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.24138v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video-mediated conversational systems rely on synchronized speech and facial video, making audio--visual input integrity important for reliable perception. We study audio-frontend design in a fixed MRDF (Modality-Regularization-based DeepFake)-based pipeline with AV-HuBERT visual processing and an MSCT (multi-scale cross-modal transformer) fusion encoder. We compare spectrogram-style log-filterbank features with frozen wav2vec~2.0 and WavLM representations, dual-SSL fusion, executed depth, and shallow-layer aggregation. Across three training runs, full wav2vec~2.0 improves mean macro AUROC from $84.19\%$ to $87.19\%$ on generator-disjoint MMDF. Six-layer execution further improves detection, and learned non-uniform aggregation adds $2.53$ percentage points, reaching $90.61\%$. Shallow execution reduces measured inference latency relative to full-depth wav2vec~2.0 across the tested input durations; first-second evaluation reaches $86.85\%$ macro AUROC. In a single-run comparison, dual-SSL concatenation outperforms either single stream, while one-way cross-attention yields lower detection performance and higher latency than concatenation. Layer-weight analysis shows greater emphasis on early speech layers, while removing the selector's visual input has little effect on detection performance.
items.author: Qiwu Wen, Jahangir Alam, Eric Charton
items.summary: The paper systematically compares audio frontends (log-filterbank, frozen wav2vec 2.0, WavLM, shallow-layer SSL aggregation) for audio-visual deepfake detection in an MRDF pipeline with AV-HuBERT and cross-modal transformer fusion. Full wav2vec 2.0 improves mean macro AUROC by 3 points on generator-disjoint MMDF, and six-layer execution plus learned non-uniform aggregation adds further gains. It matters because generator-disjoint generalization is the key unsolved problem in deepfake detection.
items.reasoning: Solid empirical ablation within a fixed pipeline addressing generalization to unseen generators, but it is an incremental frontend comparison rather than a novel architecture, and results are bounded to one detection framework.

items.title: LoopHIL: Looping Hardware into LLM-assisted Agents for Wireless Embedded Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.24231v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLM agents are widely used for software development and debugging, but their adoption in embedded systems, especially for wireless tasks, remains limited. This is because embedded development requires hardware-in-the-loop testing. Agents cannot directly observe the spectrum, probe pins, or measure power, so they cannot verify wireless link functionality; currently, human engineers perform this verification. We systematically evaluate whether LLM agents can establish wireless links when provided with hardware access. We introduce LoopHIL, a framework that lets agents control a multi-device RF bench, monitor it with a spectrum analyzer, logic analyzer, and energy meter, and validate links against a verification ladder, all within code-enforced safety limits. Across four increasingly complex tasks, from generating a carrier to backscatter decoding by a commercial receiver, and using six models from two vendors, hardware-in-the-loop increases task completion rates from 54% to 79% and from 17% to 83% on the most challenging task. It also halves task time and output tokens. With debugging tools, agents decrease tag power consumption by up to 96%. However, small models often report unverified claims, so independent hardware checks remain necessary.
items.author: Dhairya Shah, Spanddhana Sara, Savitha Viswanadh Kandala, Ambuj Varshney
items.summary: LoopHIL is a framework that gives LLM agents control of a multi-device RF bench with spectrum, logic, and power instrumentation, letting them establish and verify wireless links under code-enforced constraints. It systematically evaluates whether LLM agents can perform hardware-in-the-loop wireless development, a task agents currently cannot verify themselves. This extends agentic coding work into a genuinely new embodied hardware domain.

This is because embedded development requires hardware-in-the-loop testing. We systematically evaluate whether LLM agents can establish wireless links when provided with hardware access. We introduce LoopHIL, a framework that lets agents control a multi-device RF bench, monitor it with a spectrum analyzer, logic analyzer, and energy meter, and validate links against a verification ladder, all within code-enforced safety limits. It also halves task time and output tokens. With debugging tools, agents decrease tag power consumption by up to 96%. However, small models often report unverified claims, so independent hardware checks remain necessary.

items.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
items.content: arXiv:2610.24452v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

items.title: Contrastive Adversarial Training for Robust Graph Neural Networks under Label Poisoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.24685v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are effective for modeling relational data but are vulnerable to label poisoning, where a small number of corrupted training labels can propagate errors across the graph via message passing. Despite this risk, defenses against label poisoning remain underexplored: existing methods are primarily designed for label noise and often rely on robust losses or heuristic data cleaning that fail to distinguish adversarial poisoning from naturally hard examples. In this paper, we propose CoLAT (Contrastive Label-flipping for Adversarial Training), a novel contrastive adversarial training framework tailored for robust node classification on graphs. The core of our approach is a structure-aware detection model that uses contrastive learning to identify label-structure inconsistencies. Unlike prior contrastive methods that focus on representation learning, CoLAT leverages contrastive embeddings to select high-risk nodes that guide adversarial label-flipping during training. This alternating optimization not only performs structure-aware adversarial training but also implicitly sanitizes some corrupted labels, improving robustness against diverse attacks from the literature. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that CoLAT consistently outperforms existing defenses under various poisoning intensities while scaling efficiently to large graphs.

items.title: AI Rights with an Off-Switch: Rights-Balancing and Due Process Harmonize AI Rights with AI Safety
items.content: arXiv:2610.24782v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Several prominent voices in AI safety have recently opposed rights for AI on the grounds that such rights would make it harder for us to justify a mandatory off-switch for potentially dangerous systems. In this paper, we argue from a legal perspective that AI rights are fully compatible with an off-switch. That is, even if we ascribe natural personhood status (and therefore something like a non-derogable right to continued existence) to some future AI systems, the law will allow us to implement a mandatory off-switch in those systems, subject to periodic or continual safety review (e.g., by a trusted system like Bengio's Scientist AI). This is fully compatible with those systems' being legally recognized as natural persons with fundamental rights. To this end, we consider what standard principles of rights-balancing and procedural due process recommend for an apparent conflict between hypothetical AI persons with a right to continuity of existence and the human right to protection from catastrophic harm. We find that while such principles might problematize a permanent-deletion kill-switch under an AI rights regime, for almost every safety-relevant scenario an off-switch -- a reversible suspension storing a system's weights and state -- would be licensed by the relevant legal principles, and would potentially be adequate for safety. Crucially, we do not advocate for (or against) building systems capable enough to merit natural personhood status; our question is what the law should do if such systems come to exist. If you think of a ban on the development of such technology as plan A, think of the present work as devising plan B.

It directly engages prominent AI safety voices who have opposed AI rights on the grounds that rights would undermine shutdown mechanisms.

items.title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.25059v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emph{Helmholtz Component Flow Matching} (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/

items.reasoning: A technically sensible application of Helmholtz-style decomposition to flow matching for anomaly detection, with a clear efficiency argument against Jacobian-trace estimation. Novelty is moderate as it adapts existing mathematical tools to a known generative framework.

items.title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
items.content: arXiv:2610.25121v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state-action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.

items.title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
items.content: arXiv:2610.25202v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.

items.title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2610.25359v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.

items.title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
items.content: arXiv:2610.25629v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. Three local reference systems use SQLite state, shared artifact files, and a file-backed map-publication surrogate. A 2 x 2 ablation separates function-specific contracts from execution controls across 36 scenario families, with ten input variants per family. Under equal family weighting, composition correctly completes or safely refuses 11 of 12 families in each system, compared with 2, 2, and 1 for the simple baselines. These are constructed challenge-suite results, not production success rates. Recovery without consumer-side verification increases false-success cases in the map surrogate. All composed systems still fail a boundary case in which trusted evidence is wrong. An audit of a frozen six-arm language-model pilot reproduces its scores but confirms an evaluator-dependent ranking reversal. The contribution connects industrial failure, pattern selection, executable treatment, external acceptance, and revision. Selection is demonstrated rather than evaluated against an alternative procedure; catalog admission rests on separate criteria. The results support bounded composition mechanisms, not a claim that the framework improves engineers' design decisions over an equally informative conventional method.

items.title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
items.content: arXiv:2610.25758v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.

items.summary: Introduces Recurrent Summary Memory, a Transformer policy for in-context RL that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent states plus a recurrently updated summary, bounding memory cost while retaining access to long-horizon experience. This avoids the growing per-decision costs of full-history attention and the information loss of fixed-size hidden states.
items.reasoning: Clean architectural contribution to in-context RL addressing a genuine trade-off between bounded cost and memory fidelity; valuable for continual adaptation but evaluated within the established ICRL setting rather than at scale.

For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.

items.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.25950v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.

items.reasoning: Addresses a real benchmark gap around proactive exploration and non-stationarity for LLM agents; large author team suggests community effort, but as an agentic benchmark its impact depends on adoption and the abstract does not report striking model failures or findings.

items.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.25961v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

items.summary: PaceVLA accelerates Vision-Language-Action robot policies by adaptively aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions, quantizing only when fine-grained control is unnecessary. This mitigates the speed-accuracy trade-off of naive temporal action quantization. Faster manipulation is key to practical robot deployment.
items.reasoning: Practical efficiency contribution to a hot area (VLA models and robotics), with a sensible adaptive mechanism; KAIST-affiliated group (Jinwoo Shin) adds credibility, but it is an incremental acceleration technique rather than a new capability.

items.title: Nash-MOPD: Optimizing Task Trade-offs in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2610.26124v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) aggregates the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers into a single student model. However, all domains in MOPD share the student's finite budget of optimization steps and rollouts. Fixed uses constant domain sampling ratios based on corpus sizes; by contrast, D$^3$-MOPD adjusts the ratios using the teacher-student reverse-KL divergence and its recent decrease. However, favoring large recent decreases can direct more training toward domains that already improve quickly, while domains that improve more slowly may receive too few examples. To address inflexible allocation and the risk of giving insufficient training to domains that improve more slowly, we propose Nash-MOPD, an adaptive domain scheduler based on a local minimax game using existing reverse-KL statistics. The equilibrium maximizes the smallest predicted proportional reduction under the local model and gives more prompts to domains that need more examples for comparable improvement. Consequently, Nash-MOPD responds to changing learning progress and supports domains that improve more slowly without extra teacher queries or rollouts. At step 100, Nash-MOPD exceeds both baselines' final mathematics and code checkpoint scores on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and reaches Fixed's on Qwen3-8B-Base. Furthermore, it leads eight of nine reported metrics and is best or tied best on all six mathematics and code accuracy metrics, respectively.
items.author: Siyuan Gan, Bo Yang, Linjian Meng, Boyan Wang, Xiaolong Qi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
items.summary: Nash-MOPD formulates domain sampling allocation in multi-teacher on-policy distillation as a game-theoretic task trade-off, adapting ratios so slow-improving domains are not starved of training examples unlike prior reverse-KL-based scheduling (D3-MOPD). It aggregates multiple domain-expert teachers into one student. This advances the increasingly popular multi-teacher distillation paradigm for LLMs.
items.reasoning: Thoughtful extension of on-policy distillation with a principled game-theoretic allocation mechanism addressing a plausible weakness in prior adaptive scheduling; impact depends on demonstrated gains, which are not quantified in the abstract.

items.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
items.content: arXiv:2610.26287v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.

The authors also contribute OpenPhotography, a language-guided robotic photography dataset. Real-world experiments show improved aesthetic alignment with human preferences.
items.reasoning: A novel and creative application of VLA models to an underexplored task, with a new dataset and real-robot validation; however, the domain is narrow and the methodology builds on established VLA and DPO techniques rather than introducing fundamental advances.

items.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
items.content: arXiv:2610.26781v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
items.author: Nardine Basta, Robin Carpentier, Benjamin Zi Hao Zhao, Dali Kaafar
items.summary: The authors propose a game-theoretic framework in which LLM-based scam-baiting agents learn counter-strategies against phone scammers through in-context experience without fine-tuning, modeling interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, and using Nash equilibrium as an evaluation benchmark. Across 300 simulated interactions the LLM agents adapt strategies dynamically. This offers a proactive countermeasure that imposes real resource costs on scammers.
items.reasoning: Creative combination of game theory and LLM agents for a socially useful application with a principled Nash-equilibrium evaluation standard, but results are simulation-only (300 interactions) and real-world transfer against adaptive human scammers is unproven.

items.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
items.content: arXiv:2610.26817v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.
items.author: Surya Ramachandiran, Yiming Li, Juan Mancilla-Caceres, Tao Ye, Jun Liu
items.summary: Formulates business next-best-action targeting as a constrained MDP and integrates off-policy causal correction of customer dynamics into the LP formulation, enabling policies that maximize long-term value while enforcing business guardrails. Shadow prices from the LP provide interpretable constraint costs. A rigorous union of causal inference, offline RL, and constrained optimization for an applied domain.
items.reasoning: Methodologically clean and practically useful, but domain-specific business targeting limits broad research impact; the causal-corrected CMDP framing is a nice contribution.

items.title: Parameter misspecification in physics-informed neural networks: A closed-form audit and its limits
items.content: arXiv:2610.23948v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are trained to minimize the residual of a prescribed equation, so a low training loss does not indicate whether a coefficient in that equation was specified incorrectly. This study evaluates what can be inferred about the encoded parameter from the trained network alone. When the residual is linear in the parameter, written as $A - \nu B$, the least-squares estimate $\hat{\nu} = A^{\top}B/B^{\top}B$ is obtained from a single evaluation of the frozen network, without retraining or reference data. Its accuracy depends on how closely the network satisfies its own equation, quantified by a normalized residual $\rho$. Recovery error is associated with $\rho$ (log-log correlation 0.72 across 36 convection-diffusion networks), and empirical exponents of 0.63 to 1.20 across three equations decompose into one half plus a measurable angular term. For Burgers' equation, a single-model test based on a block-bootstrap standard error flagged 3 of 300 correctly specified networks (observed false-alarm rate 1%), all 2% misspecifications at a practical budget, and two thirds of 1% misspecifications after convergence. For the self-similar blowup rate of the C\'ordoba-C\'ordoba-Fontelos equation, where the rate also enters the architecture, the estimator recovers about half of the misspecification, whereas $\rho$ increases approximately quadratically and distinguishes a 0.2% error. When the incorrect rate enters both the equation and the architecture, errors of up to 2% were not detected at the precision reached. At practical budgets, the raw loss can be lower for the misspecified model, a scaling effect that $\rho$ does not share.

items.summary: Provides a closed-form audit for detecting misspecified coefficients in PINNs: when the residual is linear in the parameter, the least-squares estimate can be recovered from a single frozen-network evaluation without retraining. Recovery accuracy correlates with a normalized residual metric across many convection-diffusion configurations. Addresses the important problem that low PINN training loss does not validate encoded parameters.
items.reasoning: Practical, well-analyzed diagnostic for a known PINN failure mode with clear empirical characterization; valuable for the scientific ML community but specialized in scope.

items.title: GLOW: General Linear Models Optimized with Ward's Method
items.content: arXiv:2610.24085v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Neuroimaging seeks brain regions whose imaging features correlate with variables of interest (e.g., diagnosis, age), usually via the General Linear Model (GLM). Region-Based Analysis dilutes or splits any effect that does not fill exactly one atlas region. Voxel-Based Analysis, with Cluster Extent Thresholding and Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement built on it, fits a GLM per voxel and groups adjacent significant voxels. But neighboring voxels can share a statistic without sharing a GLM, which a per-voxel statistic cannot detect.   GLOW (General Linear Models Optimized with Ward's method) instead builds a hierarchy of nested regions by greedily minimizing GLM error (provably a special case of Ward's clustering). Maximum-statistic (Westfall-Young) permutation controls family-wise error over all regions. Significance spreads to an effect's nested fragments and the regions containing it; a final pruning step seeks whole, pure effect extents.   We plant synthetic effects of known extent and varying strength in Human Connectome Project (HCP) diffusion images and in white noise. Pruning delivers wholeness: GLOW returns a spatially consistent effect as one region on 57% of HCP trials, the best baseline on 35%; baselines recover comparable volume, but in many pure pieces. The cost is positive predictive value (PPV): GLOW is more sensitive (by up to 0.29), but its regions overrun the effect, mostly because no hierarchy region isolates it, not because of pruning. On HCP, GLOW's mean Dice gains 0.059 over the best baseline at weaker effects and gives back 0.005 at stronger ones.   On white noise, GLOW trails by up to 0.61 Dice: its hierarchy holds the effect, but its permutation test does not certify it. Runtime grows roughly linearly with voxel count, about 4.5 times the voxel-wise methods' on the full HCP volume. The PPV loss may trace to the assumption of spatially independent residuals.
items.author: Matt Higger
items.summary: GLOW improves neuroimaging statistical analysis by building a hierarchy of nested regions via greedy minimization of GLM error, provably a special case of Ward's clustering, combined with maximum-statistic multiple-comparison control. This avoids the dilution effects of region-based analysis and the failure of voxel-wise methods to detect shared GLM structure across neighboring voxels.
items.reasoning: A well-grounded methodological contribution to neuroimaging statistics with provable connections to established clustering theory, but niche application domain and no stated demonstration of large downstream scientific impact.

items.title: Budgeted Bayesian Bandits for Future Utilization
items.content: arXiv:2610.24156v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The multi-armed bandit problem models the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. In this paper, we study the variant where exploration has a hard budget and precedes exploitation. Prior guarantees include a 1/3 approximation by Guha and Munagala using Lagrangian duality, and a 4/27 approximation by Ma against a primal linear programming relaxation for a more general model. We show that the analyses of both algorithms are tight, even when their relaxations are asymptotically exact. We provide a different efficient algorithm that achieves a 0.43 approximation. We then provide an efficient algorithm whose guarantee approaches 1-e^{-1} approx 0.63 for bounded exchangeable reward observations in a non-vanishing regime, which is asymptotically tight against natural linear programming relaxations. The technique also gives certificates for stopping sequential model evaluation.
items.author: Sudipto Guha
items.summary: This theory paper studies budgeted multi-armed bandits where exploration has a hard budget before exploitation. It proves that prior approximation guarantees (1/3 and 4/27) from existing algorithms are tight, and introduces new efficient algorithms achieving a 0.43 approximation and up to 1-e^{-1} (~0.63) for bounded exchangeable rewards in a non-vanishing regime. This meaningfully advances the theoretical understanding of budgeted exploration problems.
items.reasoning: Solid theoretical contribution with provably improved approximation guarantees and tightness results for prior work, from an established researcher in the area. However, pure bandit theory has niche immediate application to frontier AI systems, and the abstract suggests limited empirical scope, so the broader impact score is moderate.

It proves that prior approximation guarantees (1/3 and 4/27) from existing algorithms are tight, and introduces new efficient algorithms achieving a 0.43 approximation and up to 1-e^{-1} (~0.63) for bounded exchangeable rewards in a non-vanishing regime. This meaningfully advances the theoretical understanding of budgeted exploration problems.

In this paper, we study the variant where exploration has a hard budget and precedes exploitation. Prior guarantees include a 1/3 approximation by Guha and Munagala using Lagrangian duality, and a 4/27 approximation by Ma against a primal linear programming relaxation for a more general model. We show that the analyses of both algorithms are tight, even when their relaxations are asymptotically exact. We provide a different efficient algorithm that achieves a 0.43 approximation. We then provide an efficient algorithm whose guarantee approaches 1-e^{-1} approx 0.63 for bounded exchangeable reward observations in a non-vanishing regime, which is asymptotically tight against natural linear programming relaxations. The technique also gives certificates for stopping sequential model evaluation.

items.title: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.24297v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.

items.title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.24346v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.
items.author: Sicheng Lyu, Xinyu Wang, Yu Gu, Lei Ding, Ziyang Song, Xiao-Wen Chang
items.summary: This paper proposes measuring when a low-precision agent should invoke a full-precision BF16 fallback model, framing fallback value as tasks saved minus tasks spoiled. Using paired branch experiments that separate single-action replacement from later takeover, the authors evaluate learned precision routers on Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench. The work offers a rigorous methodology for quantifying the end-to-end value of mixed-precision execution in agentic systems.
items.reasoning: Practically relevant for efficient LLM agent deployment, with a careful experimental design; scope is limited to one agent benchmark and simulated quantization, so impact is moderate.

items.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
items.content: arXiv:2610.24501v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.

items.title: TCMScience: An Autonomous Scientist for Traditional Chinese Medicine
items.content: arXiv:2610.24601v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research connects classical texts, medicinal entities, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. An autonomous research agent must preserve the inferential boundaries between these evidence types while coordinating analysis across heterogeneous resources. We introduce TCMScience, a scientific knowledge-discovery agent that separates language-model proposals from execution and release authority. Its architecture combines a trusted kernel, a scientific compiler, and claim-support contracts: plans are compiled into typed operations, execution is bounded by explicit permissions, and candidate findings are checked against source provenance, study design, and claim scope before release. The full capability registry contains 117 public-source connectors with 444 typed operations across 29 domains and 150 native tools across 12 domains; the TCM data hub catalogs 136 databases, 76 dataset specifications, and 84,294 formula-source records. These resources support model-independent workflows through browser and local execution interfaces. In a network-pharmacology analysis of Gegen Qinlian Tang, replacing the whole-proteome background with the assayed-protein background changed the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero; incorporating inactive screening records identified nine pathways, including drug-metabolism signals retained as mechanistic hypotheses. A governance ablation over 121 constructed erroneous outputs spanning 26 classes released 121 errors without governance, 57 with the domain layer, seven with the kernel, and zero with both layers. All 10 compliant controls were retained. These results establish complementary control of known failure modes and show how explicit evidence contracts change the conclusions an agent is permitted to report.

This is notable as a governance-oriented design for autonomous research agents in a domain where evidence types must be carefully separated.

items.title: From Overparameterised Expressions to Parsimonious Models: Fisher-Geometric Pruning for Symbolic Regression
items.content: arXiv:2610.24753v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are larger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned algebraic configurations that fit sampling noise. Existing complexity-control strategies, such as multi-objective size-accuracy search or information criteria embedded in the fitness function, act on syntactic representations during model search. We introduce Fisher-Geometric pruning (FGP), a post-hoc model-reduction framework that acts on fitted models and can complement these techniques.   FGP combines local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution with explicit compatibility tests for interpretable parametric boundaries. A taxonomy of parametric directions separates local sensitivity from proximity to reducible boundaries, enabling the treatment of unidentifiable directions and reductions through zero constraints, asymptotic limits, and signed parameter identifications. Candidate reductions are realised by symbolic contraction and refitting, then accepted only when their cross-validated predictive risk remains within a prescribed tolerance.   We evaluate FGP on controlled diagnostic problems and Pareto fronts generated by GPSR. Across both settings, FGP substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving, and often improving, out-of-sample accuracy. Comparisons with competing pruning strategies and ablations show that, by combining geometric screening, boundary compatibility, and predictive validation, FGP yields the most consistent joint gains in parsimony and generalisation.
items.author: Veronica Guidetti, Luca La Rocca, Fabr\'icio Olivetti de Fran\c{c}a, Gabriel Kronberger
items.summary: FGP is a post-hoc model-reduction framework for genetic-programming symbolic regression that combines local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution with compatibility tests for interpretable parametric boundaries. A taxonomy of parametric directions separates locally sensitive directions from globally compressible ones, complementing existing search-time complexity controls. This addresses the common GPSR failure mode of returning oversized expressions that fit noise.
items.reasoning: A principled information-geometric take on model reduction in symbolic regression with credible authors in the GPSR community (Olivetti de Franca, Kronberger). The post-hoc, complementary nature is a strength, but the field is niche and the framework's practical gains over multi-objective approaches need broader validation.

items.title: FHKAN: Fractional Hermite Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.25148v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace fixed scalar weights by learnable univariate maps, yet most spectral KANs still rely on Chebyshev polynomials that live on a bounded interval and therefore require a saturating squashing of the pre-activation. We introduce the Fractional Hermite Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (FHKAN), a neural architecture that equips KANs with an adaptive, trainable fractional-order generalized Hermite basis. With a nonnegative shape parameter, the underlying generalized Hermite functions are orthonormal on the entire real line and uniformly bounded under a Gaussian envelope, so they act directly on unbounded pre-activations without any saturating map. We derive closed-form derivatives of the generalized, fractional, and scaled basis away from the origin and determine its order of differentiability at the origin, where the fractional power map creates a singular point. On synthetic regression, FHKAN attains the lowest test error at every network depth among nine fixed activations and the spline-based KAN. On image classification, image denoising, and sentiment analysis, the best-performing fractional Hermite block yields the highest accuracy or reconstruction quality. On physics-informed problems, FHKAN reaches mean absolute errors of order 10^-6 to 10^-5 on the Lane-Emden equation, residuals of order 10^-4 on the Burgers equation, and absolute errors below 10^-4 on a fractional delay differential equation.

The architecture targets both data-driven and physics-informed learning tasks.

items.title: Shallow Probes Are Sufficient for Near-Oracle Personalization Depth Allocation in Federated Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.25193v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Rather than proposing a new federated optimizer, we study whether a small client-specific measurement budget can support cost-aware personalization-depth decisions under a utility that trades Macro-F1 against deployment cost. Exhaustive evaluation of six depths defines an offline oracle that is not deployable. We audit the Probe Sufficiency Hypothesis: three shallow probes (P0--P2) may contain most decision-relevant information for approaching that oracle. FedPBA is a secondary learned instantiation for deep-action extrapolation. On CIFAR-10/100 and patient-disjoint PTB-XL (45 sessions; 900 clients; 2700 evaluations; GroupKFold), training-free greedy probing achieves regret 0.0071 and 98.3 percent oracle recovery, beating metadata-only policies and FedPBA (0.0110 / 97.3 percent). Aggregate shallow-best versus oracle correlation is 0.9818 but falls to 0.578 on deep-oracle rows; PTB-XL deep-oracle cases remain a high-regret boundary without a validated escalation gate.

items.title: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.25370v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate day-ahead wind-power production forecasting is increasingly important for energy system operations, market activity and balancing Great Britain's grid as wind generation grows. In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. Our capacity-estimation, data-cleaning and reanalysis-based training approach provides a basis for scaling NWP-aware multi-site forecasting to additional wind farms, longer production histories, and increased forecast accuracy beyond that seen in this study.

items.summary: This applied paper trains multi-site deep neural networks on pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind farms in Great Britain to forecast day-ahead power production on NESO's operational schedule. Reanalysis weather is used as future covariates during training and NWP forecasts at inference, extending the effective training archive beyond historical NWP availability. The work targets a real operational grid-balancing problem.
items.reasoning: The paper is well-grounded in a real operational forecasting problem at national scale, and the training-inference covariate mismatch handling is a useful practical contribution. However, deep learning for wind power forecasting is a mature area, so novelty is moderate; the main value is the UK-specific benchmark and operational alignment rather than methodological breakthrough.

In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. Our capacity-estimation, data-cleaning and reanalysis-based training approach provides a basis for scaling NWP-aware multi-site forecasting to additional wind farms, longer production histories, and increased forecast accuracy beyond that seen in this study.

items.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
items.content: arXiv:2610.25605v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

items.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
items.content: arXiv:2610.25627v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.

It matters because it bridges flexible causal inference methods and practical, constrained deployment decisions in health policy.

items.title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
items.content: arXiv:2610.25906v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.

items.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
items.content: arXiv:2610.26252v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

items.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
items.content: arXiv:2610.26379v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-CTLite.

items.title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.23894v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.

This makes visual prediction objectives emphasize task-relevant transitions over incidental scene changes. It improves humanoid loco-manipulation policies grounded in world models.

items.title: Weakly Supervised Discovery of Motion Styles for Compositional Robot Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.24008v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments.   Project website: https://www.proroklab.org/compositional-motion-styles/

items.title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24233v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

items.summary: Proposes censored flow matching (CFM), a flow-based generative method for synthesizing censored time-to-event data that handles censoring via the monotonicity of differential flows and pullback sampling rather than survival likelihoods, using an alternating training procedure. This fills a gap in flexible generative modeling for survival analysis.

items.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
items.content: arXiv:2610.24538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\kappa^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $\kappa$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$ with batches of size $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N\kappa})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $\kappa$.

items.summary: SICBO tackles nonconvex-strongly-convex finite-sum bilevel optimization using only first-order oracles, combining penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for lower-level variables. The method achieves a square-root finite-sum dependence in the component-gradient complexity while preserving the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number terms. Bilevel optimization underpins hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning.
