items.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2610.26040v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/

By considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule and inter-token dependencies, BPD accelerates parallel decoding while preserving quality.

items.title: SNO-PI: Label-Scarce SNOMED CT Entity Linking with Pre-trained Encoders and Curated Terminology Knowledge
items.content: arXiv:2610.26425v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present SNO-PI, the top-performing submission on SNOMED International's SNOMED CT Entity Linking Benchmark as of 18 October 2026. SNO-PI achieves a macro character IoU of 0.5387, outperforming the organisers' reference system (0.4582; based on the 2024 challenge winner's approach) by 18% relative. Linking clinical mentions to SNOMED CT is a zero- and few-shot problem over a very large label space: the 272 annotated MIMIC-IV discharge summaries cover only 6,595 of the roughly 219,000 eligible concepts, and a third of those occur only once. This motivates a design built on transfer from pre-trained models and human-curated knowledge. SNO-PI combines high-recall span proposal, SapBERT candidate retrieval and listwise ensemble reranking with three BERT-family encoders, each further pre-trained with masked language modelling on unlabelled MIMIC-IV notes and then on SNOMED CT synonyms and hierarchy before task fine-tuning. We find that curated knowledge helps most on concepts never seen in training, yet these concepts remain the main source of error.

items.title: Information Theory of Random Composition Trees
items.content: arXiv:2610.24788v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Random composition trees model the hierarchical semantic structures of meaningful texts as a statistical ensemble generated by recursively splitting texts into coherent chunks. A recent study shows that different text types can be described by random composition trees with distinct branching factors, and that the entropy rates of these trees exhibit a similar dependence across text types as the entropy rates of the actual texts. Motivated by this correspondence, we analyze information-theoretic properties of this stochastic splitting model. First, we demonstrate that the entropy of random composition trees grows linearly with the root size, and we derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. Second, we prove that large trees exhibit typicality: with high probability, they belong to a typical set in which each tree is approximately equally likely. Our analysis reveals that the random composition tree model shares two key information-theoretic properties of language when modeled as a stationary and ergodic stochastic process: linear entropy growth and typicality.

items.title: Label Authority in Speech Emotion Recognition: Intended and Perceived Ground Truth in Emozionalmente
items.content: arXiv:2610.26446v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Ground truth in Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is often presented as a single categorical fact, yet an acted emotion and the emotion heard by listeners describe different aspects of the same recording. We examine this distinction in Emozionalmente, an acted Italian corpus that provides both an elicited production label and five listener judgements for every clip. Using frozen XLS-R, HuBERT, and WavLM representations with matched probes, we compare three label authorities: the expressed condition, the listeners' hard plurality, and their complete vote distribution. The results tell a consistent story. Recovering the expressed condition is easier than predicting a tie-broken listener plurality, but that gap compares two different questions rather than revealing a general loss of SER ability. As listener agreement weakens, the plurality becomes an increasingly brittle hard target. Training on the full vote distribution does not substantially change which class wins the model's hard decision, but it produces probability assignments that more closely follow the alternatives selected by listeners, especially for ambiguous clips. No authority therefore replaces the others. Expressed labels describe how speech was produced, pluralities provide an operational single-class decision, and vote distributions preserve perceptual uncertainty. For human-facing Internet of Sounds applications, evaluations should state which authority is being predicted, retain its aggregation rule and agreement information, and use distributional scores when disagreement is part of the target.

items.title: Toward AI-Driven Phytoplankton Event Detection from Image Classification: Temporal Aggregation Under Domain Shift
items.content: arXiv:2610.23932v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Imaging FlowCytobot (IFCB) systems generate large volumes of phytoplankton imagery that exceed the capacity of manual expert analysis. Although machine-learning approaches achieve high image-level classification performance, it remains unclear whether their predictions can provide ecologically meaningful temporal information for monitoring. This study investigates whether AI-derived phytoplankton classifications can reproduce temporal occurrence patterns and elevated-occurrence signals under realistic sampling and independent-domain transfer. A monitoring-oriented framework was developed using MedPlanktonSet and evaluated on an independent IFCB dataset from the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI). Eight biologically comparable taxa were selected as targets, while all remaining observations were retained as background to preserve the full image-stream denominator. Session-aware partitioning prevented temporal leakage, and alternative preprocessing strategies and convolutional neural network architectures were evaluated. Cross-domain experiments showed that preprocessing strongly affected generalisation. EfficientNet-B0 provided the strongest target-versus-background discrimination and was selected for temporal analysis. Despite residual image-level errors, AI-derived target-occurrence rates closely reproduced expert-derived signals after aggregation (mean absolute error = 0.0432, Pearson $r$ = 0.9696, Spearman $\rho$ = 0.9568). Agreement remained strong across multi-session windows, and elevated, strong, and persistent occurrence proxies were recovered in held-out testing. These results show that AI-based phytoplankton classification can support monitoring-relevant temporal indicators beyond image-level identification and support future operational early-warning development.

items.title: Spatons: Spatiotonally Localized Building Blocks for Efficient XR Predistortion
items.content: arXiv:2610.24400v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Spatons, a family of compositional, spatially localized neural operators for computationally efficient XR (extended reality) predistortion and distortion compensation. XR displays (AR, VR, and MR) suffer from spatial (e.g., geometric) and tonal (e.g., colour) distortions. Frames can be pre-distorted so that the projected image looks as intended. Distortions vary with manufacturing tolerances and projection systems, motivating programmable compensation. Untethered, battery-operated XR systems also require low energy and latency. A Spaton is a hybrid patch-to-pixel block combining tiny Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with fixed-function interpolation. Using Spatons, we build programmable, computationally efficient pipelines for varied distortion scenarios. On the full spatiotonal Scenario 5, Sequential-5' matches CompenNet++ in SSIM (0.944 vs. 0.944) and closely matches its PSNR (27.5 vs. 27.7 dB), with substantially lower complexity. We demonstrate a flexible Spaton solution with 6 times fewer FLOPs and 106 times fewer parameters than CompenNet++, and 4-10 times fewer memory transfers than UNet++. We characterize software implementations and analytical hardware estimates, including optimizations across target XR platforms. The distortions considered are drawn mostly from see-through, near-eye displays, where the spatial light path governs local intensity and spectral response. This early systems-level exploration uses closed-form differentiable distortions and one real projector-camera capture set for training and evaluation, rather than through-the-optics measurements. Testing on a wider range of real XR devices remains future work. Chromatic dispersion (color fringes) remains the main artifact where Spatons trail monolithic baselines.

The design targets low energy and latency while remaining programmable across different projection systems and manufacturing tolerances.
items.reasoning: An interesting efficiency-oriented architecture for a practical deployed-hardware problem in AR/VR, from a group including Steve Mann with deep expertise in wearable computing. Niche application area limits broad impact, but the hybrid neural/fixed-function design pattern could generalize to other low-power perception pipelines.

items.title: Predicting Individual Differences in Lipreading From Eye-Tracking and Pupillometry During Silent Visual Speech
items.content: arXiv:2610.24898v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lipreading ability varies widely, including among people who are hard of hearing. Although mouth-directed attention is linked to speechreading outcomes, it remains unclear how much lipreading skill can be inferred from viewing behavior and which signals carry this information. We examine whether individual differences in lipreading ability are reflected in viewing behavior during silent speech and quantify the contributions of gaze dynamics, pupil-linked signals, and spatial viewing allocation. We introduce the Lipreading Perception Study (LiPS) dataset and a tracker-independent preprocessing pipeline that synchronizes SR Research EyeLink gaze and pupil recordings with the stimuli. Twenty-four adults (age 32 $\pm$ 10 years) completed a four-alternative forced-choice silent lipreading task. An extreme-groups protocol yielded 18 participants labeled as stronger or weaker lipreaders. Each participant-trial included four aligned views: lip-region images, frame-level gaze, pupil summaries, and spatial viewing proportions. A four-branch neural network with cross-modal attention predicted labels using participant-disjoint splits and systematic ablations. The full model reached accuracy 0.680 $\pm$ 0.040 across five folds, outperforming naive fusion baselines in accuracy. The pupil and viewing-summary branch was most informative: removing it caused the largest degradation (0.618 accuracy, 0.623 AUC), while it alone achieved 0.675 accuracy. The lip-image stream contributed little to participant-level discrimination. Individual differences in lipreading are reflected in pupil-linked and frame-level gaze signals rather than in how much time a viewer spends looking at the mouth. Synchronized gaze and pupillary measures may provide objective markers of visual speech perception, warranting investigation in larger, clinically diverse populations. LiPS provides a resource for extending this work.

items.title: GeoART: Geometry-Aware Refinement via Test-Time Scaling for Camera-Conditioned Video Diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.25273v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Camera-conditioned video diffusion models often suffer from inaccurate camera control and geometric inconsisten- cies because camera constraints and estimated geometry are only weakly enforced during denoising. Existing reme- dies often require costly geometry-aware fine-tuning or ad- ditional 3D supervision. We introduce GeoART, a training- free self-refinement framework that improves camera con- trollability through geometry-aware test-time scaling. At selected denoising steps, GeoART generates multiple can- didates within the Predict-and-Perturb cycle and eval- uates them using a geometry prior, without directly modify- ing the denoising trajectory. A confidence gate suppresses unreliable geometric evidence, while rank-calibrated prob- abilistic selection combines score magnitude and relative rank to choose the next refinement state. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in camera controlla- bility, multi-view consistency, and visual quality over exist- ing sampling and self-refinement methods, without training or modifying the pretrained video diffusion model

items.title: Only Means Only: what a harmonization benchmark score averages over
items.content: arXiv:2610.25387v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four confirmed near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns.

items.title: From Label Priors to Task Evidence: Efficient Long-Video Frame Selection via Bayesian GRPO
items.content: arXiv:2610.25418v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.

items.title: Where Do the Gaussians Go? Foreground Attraction for Camera-Based Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy
items.content: arXiv:2610.25631v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy models can be trained without 3D labels by rendering their predictions into the images and supervising them with 2D pseudo labels. In sparse Gaussian representations trained this way, Gaussian positions are learned only through pixel-wise rendering losses, which we hypothesize give small foreground objects little weight. In trained GaussianFlowOcc models, the Gaussian density on foreground voxels is on average only 1.62 times that on background voxels. We propose a training-only foreground attraction loss that back-projects foreground pseudo-label pixels with pseudo depth and pulls nearby Gaussians toward these 3D points, favoring Gaussians that already predict the target class; the inference network is unchanged. On Occ3D-nuScenes, the loss raises this concentration to 2.40 over three seeds. Over three seeds, the mean foreground IoU increases from 6.29 to 6.96 and is higher for each seed, whereas the change in mean mIoU (13.53 to 13.82) is within the seed-to-seed variation of the baseline. Single-run ablations further indicate that pseudo-label targets outperform targets placed at ground-truth voxels and that acting on the Gaussian positions alone is not sufficient, and a single-seed test shows that the model degrades less when fewer Gaussians are kept at inference.

items.title: See the Future, Classify the Present: Stochastic Latent World Modeling for Hyperspectral Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.25781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hyperspectral image classification (HSIC) relies on static spatial-spectral representations learned from labeled samples, limiting its ability to model structured dependencies in the latent representation space. To address this limitation, this work proposes Stochastic Latent World Modeling (LWM), a trajectory-based representation-learning framework that enriches classification through stochastic latent-state prediction. Given a hyperspectral patch, LWM tokenizes and encodes spectral and spatial information separately using dedicated transformer branches, then fuses their outputs into a unified representation. This representation is further organized into an environment state that captures center, neighborhood, spectral, and global contextual information. A stochastic latent transition module then predicts multiple future latent states through Gaussian parameterization and reparameterization, with recurrent refinement used to model dependencies across successive states. The resulting latent trajectory is adaptively aggregated by a rollout planner to construct a planned representation, which is integrated with the base representation for final classification. By extending static spatial-spectral encoding with stochastic multi-step latent-state modeling, LWM enables the classifier to exploit structured dependencies in the representation space and provides richer features for HSIC. Across five benchmark datasets, LWM achieves overall accuracies ranging from 89.21% to 99.52%, demonstrating consistent classification performance under limited-label settings.

items.title: Multi-scale Fusion of Fast Vision Mamba and Foundation Model Features for Patch-Level Gleason Grading in Computational Pathology
items.content: arXiv:2610.25904v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate whole slide images (WSIs) enables faster and more consistent cancer risk stratification. However, it remains a challenging task due to the subtle morphological differences between grades, the severe class imbalance arising from rare patterns, and the diagnostic features that span multiple spatial scales. Pathology foundation models (FMs) extract strong patch representations but often operate at a single-scale, which limits spatial context and disproportionately affects classes that depend on broader context. The challenge of fusing multiple scales and complementary models, with minimal data and computational resources, remains unresolved. We propose a multi-scale classifier built on state-space models. Our method combines two complementary feature sources: a frozen foundation model, and a lightweight FastVim, pre-trained on ImageNet and distilled from the foundation model, that reads the raw image crops. At each scale, a Mamba model encodes the features from both sources with linear-time spatial context, and a jointly trained head fuses the encoded representations into one prediction. On the PANDA dataset, our method reaches macro F1 of 0.894 and Gleason 5 F1 of 0.802 under 5-fold cross-validation, a 12% and 21% relative improvement over the best single-scale model. A controlled study over 5 foundation models, 5 base classifiers and 3 scales confirms that the gain holds across encoders, with larger improvements observed at smaller scales.

items.title: DCR-TSF: Dual-Level Compositional Reasoning with Triadic Spherical Fusion for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2610.26078v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image that reflects an intended textual modification while maintaining semantic consistency with a reference image. Existing training-free ZS-CIR methods typically rely on fine-grained generated target descriptions, which often overemphasize reference-specific visual details and lead to appearance-biased retrieval. Moreover, since these descriptions are generated through multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the direct influence of the original image-text query can be weakened in the final retrieval representation. In this paper, we propose DCR-TSF, a training-free ZS-CIR framework that combines Dual-level Compositional Reasoning (DCR) and Triadic Spherical Fusion (TSF). DCR generates fine- and coarse-grained descriptions from the reference image and modification text, capturing complementary target-side semantics across different granularities. To preserve the original image-text query information, TSF constructs a composed-query anchor by spherically interpolating the reference image feature and modification text feature, and fuses it with the fine- and coarse-grained representations using a weighted Karcher mean on the unit hypersphere. The resulting final query representation balances detailed visual evidence, high-level semantic abstraction, and direct preservation of the original composed query. Extensive experiments on CIRCO, CIRR, and Fashion-IQ demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods.

items.title: RGB--Event Object Detection Across Operating Frequencies via Reliability-Supervised Routing and Asymmetric-Resolution Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.26090v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous vehicles must detect objects faster than a frame camera delivers images. Event cameras record brightness changes with microsecond resolution, so RGB--event detectors can decide between frames, at an operating frequency, the rate of decisions, far above the frame rate. As this rate rises, each decision receives a sparser event window, and the reliability of the events relative to the frame varies over the scene and over time. Existing detectors weight the sensors per sample and encode the frame at the reduced event resolution. Reliability-supervised routing assigns a fusion weight to every location and supervises it with targets from the losses of two single-modality classifiers used only in training, moving loss-based supervision of fusion weights from whole samples to individual locations. Asymmetric-resolution fusion lets the frame carry the decision where the events fail: it encodes the frame at native resolution and pools every feature level onto the event grid, reusing all pretrained weights. On the DSEC-Det dataset, routing halves the accuracy loss from 20 to 180 Hz, from 6.3 to 3.1 mAP, and lowers it in every seed. The resulting detector, ERA-Det, sets a new state of the art at 63.2 mAP, 3.7 mAP above FlexEvent, leads at every operating frequency, and at 180 Hz is more accurate than FlexEvent at 20 Hz. On two DAVIS346 datasets, the router lowers the frame weight at night and in low light and raises it when the events vanish. ERA-Det upgrades released FlexEvent weights in 5,000 iterations on one GPU.

items.title: From Legacy to Contemporary: Scalable Color Modernization for Long Video
items.content: arXiv:2610.26391v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Bringing legacy video back to contemporary screens does not necessarily make it look contemporary. Earlier imaging pipelines often leave color casts, muted chroma, weak con- trast, and tonal imbalance, while correcting these character- istics still relies heavily on expert colorists and scales poorly to long, multi-shot videos. We formulate long video color modernization, a task that updates the chromatic and tonal appearance of legacy color footage while preserving scene content and coherence across frames and shots. We introduce a scalable, training-free framework that jointly modernizes grids of temporally adjacent keyframes using a pretrained text-guided image editing model, producing coherent con- temporary references without paired supervision. Compact shot-specific color transforms then propagate these adjust- ments throughout each shot, preserving spatial structure and temporal stability. We conduct a multidimensional evaluation on diverse legacy videos spanning five decades. We combine a human evaluation of perceived modernness with quantita- tive measures of content fidelity, temporal stability, percep- tual quality, and efficiency, and introduce Source-Weighted Inter-shot Grade Consistency (SW-IGC) to assess grade co- herence across shots. On our evaluation set, our frame- work achieves the highest perceived modernness while re- maining competitive across complementary measures, open- ing a path toward the systematic study of long video color modernization. Code is available at https://github.com/jiwoomood/ Video_Color_Modernization.git

It addresses a task that currently relies on expert colorists and scales poorly.

items.title: CaptionFuse: Training-Free Composed Product Retrieval Via VLM Intent Captioning and Weighted Embedding Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.26661v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) retrieves products matching a reference image modified by natural language---a core capability for eCommerce search. Existing training-free methods fuse CLIP embeddings via arithmetic, but we identify a fundamental limitation: user text modifications are attribute-sparse---a user who types ``make it red with shorter sleeves'' specifies what to change but not what to keep (the floral pattern, the V-neck, the fit-and-flare silhouette). We introduce language-space fusion: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) jointly interprets the reference image and modification to generate a visually grounded product-title caption---e.g., ``Red floral fit-and-flare dress with short sleeves and V-neck''---that fills in the missing attributes from the image. Our method, CaptionFuse, requires no task-specific training and is model-agnostic. A controlled experiment confirms that attribute content--- not linguistic style---drives the gains: imperative and descriptive captions with identical attributes achieve equal R@10, while both outperform raw modifications by +6.5 points.

It identifies a fundamental limitation of arithmetic CLIP fusion when user text specifies changes but not what to preserve. The approach is practical and directly deployable for product search.
items.reasoning: Clever, simple insight (attribute-sparse modification text) with a training-free, immediately usable solution for a commercially important task. Limited scientific depth, and gains hinge on VLM captioning reliability, but the framing is genuinely useful.

items.title: An Anatomy-Aware Staged Pipeline for Vessel-Specific Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation in CT and MR Angiography
items.content: arXiv:2610.24011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The TopAneu 2026 challenge requires intracranial aneurysms to be segmented at the voxel level and assigned to one of more than fifty vessel-specific classes, on CT and MR angiography alike. We address it with a six-stage anatomy-aware pipeline rather than a single segmentation network. A logistic-regression classifier routes each scan to a modality-specific branch; networks segment the vasculature, first as a binary mask and then over the full 36-class arterial taxonomy; a candidate localiser turns raw angiography and vessel priors into suspicious regions; a candidate-centred network segments the lesion in each crop; connected components become instances; and a per-instance classifier assigns each its anatomical location. Two principles organise the design. Whenever an upstream model output becomes a downstream training input it is generated out-of-fold, so no stage trains on unrealistically clean predictions of itself. And the anatomical decision is made once per lesion rather than once per voxel, which fits the data: of 406 connected aneurysm components in the full release, 405 carry exactly one location label. Task 1 is read off the Task 2 mask, making the two consistent by construction. We report stage-wise performance and a five-part ablation isolating what vessel priors and class-aware sampling contribute at each stage.

items.title: Implicit Neural Models for Direct Multi-Shell Diffusion MRI Signal Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24034v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging is a noninvasive technique that is sensitive to the motion of water molecules in human tissue. The image signal is commonly described in q-space; however, a complete coverage of this space is often infeasible due to hardware and acquisition time limitations. In this work, we propose to represent the entire diffusion signal using an implicit neural representation network with wavelet activation functions. The signal space is encoded using Fourier features and spherical harmonics basis functions for a continuous output distribution of the raw diffusion data, enabling both super-resolution and q-space interpolation. Additionally, we introduce a pretraining strategy using a group template, enabling faster per-subject optimisation when combined with nonlinear registrations of subjects into template space. We tested the method with 10 subjects from the Human Connectome Project and 26 subjects from in-house data (multidimensional diffusion MRI from a Parkinson's disease cohort). The results show that the proposed method yields high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly reduced memory requirements compared to raw diffusion-weighted images. The pretraining scheme showed good generalisability properties on data acquired with very different protocols. We further assess the method on downstream metrics relevant to diffusion MRI data from the learned representations.

A group-template pretraining strategy enables faster per-patient fitting. It addresses a fundamental acquisition-efficiency problem in neuroimaging.

items.title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2610.26457v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. items.title: Evaluating Lightweight Contact Feedback in Dual-Operator Collaborative Humanoid Teleoperation
items.content: arXiv:2610.24257v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dual-operator humanoid teleoperation enables collaborative manipulation through two separate robots, but operators lack direct awareness of robot-object contact that is normally available during physical interaction. To address this, we present eXtended Reality Teleoperation (XRT), an extended reality teleoperation framework that returns a robot's fingertip contact through lightweight vibrotactile and/or auditory feedback, and a synchronized dual-humanoid testbed built on it for two operators. Sixteen dyads performed a collaborative crate lift-and-flip under vision only and the three feedback conditions in a counterbalanced within-subject design with verified feedback-channel delivery. Three results follow. First, operators rated our finger-localized vibrotactile display as more effective than our open-ear sonification: all 32 ranked it above the sonification, 18 ranked it most effective, and its cues were rated far easier to perceive and interpret than the auditory cues. Second, completion time, failures, workload, discomfort, and partner awareness showed no detected condition differences, with wide completion-time intervals and smaller meaningful effects unresolved. Third, performance changed substantially with practice, especially on the harder flip-over task: completion time improved across blocks, and attempt-to-attempt variation within a dyad (SD x1.51) was larger than the largest condition contrast (x1.16). Exploratory analyses detected no difference in immediate grip or motion responses between feedback conditions. For novice collaborative teleoperation, our fingertip vibrotactile cues were rated more effective and easier to interpret than our auditory cues, while their effect on task performance remains unresolved.

items.title: Scalable, Intuitive, Mixed Reality-Based Semi-Autonomous Robotic Telemanipulation for the Execution of a Fine-Grained Bimanual Task
items.content: arXiv:2610.25006v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.

items.summary: This paper presents a mixed-reality semi-autonomous telemanipulation system for fine-grained bimanual tasks, aimed at reducing operator fatigue during large-scale demonstration collection. By blending autonomy with human control, the system improves the scalability and quality of demonstration data used for robot learning. The work targets the bottleneck that manual teleoperation imposes on dataset creation.

However, the contribution appears to be systems integration rather than a novel algorithmic advance, and evaluation details are limited in the abstract.

items.title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
items.content: arXiv:2610.26043v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

items.title: Robot Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models for Agricultural Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.26717v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots. In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and pretrained policy adaptation. A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation, with a low-level controller used to execute robot actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and $\pi_{0.5}$, are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations. The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Results show that $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.

items.summary: This work develops a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that combines task-specific demonstration collection with adaptation of pretrained vision-language-action policies, using a MuJoCo-based agricultural environment. It targets challenges such as plant geometry variation, occlusion, and camera viewpoint changes while reducing costly real-robot demonstrations.
items.reasoning: A reasonable application of existing sim-to-real and VLA adaptation techniques to agriculture, a valuable domain, but the methodological novelty appears limited; the abstracted framework largely assembles known components.

items.title: Human vs AI in Go in 2026: Lessons for superintelligence?
items.content:
In July 2026, Korean Go player Shin Jin-seo defeated KataGo 2-1, with only[1] a 2-stone handicap (favoring Shin). I thought this was very surprising, and posted on LessWrong and Twitter asking how to interpret this. I didn’t get any entirely satisfactory answer, so I decided to spend ~one day looking into it and writing up my understanding.

To preface this post: I don’t know all that much about Go and I'm a quite bad Go player (like, no better than 20 kyu or something like that). But in 2022 I did an interpretability project on a Go-playing model and have spent quite some time thinking about Go-playing AIs.

# Why I found this surprising

Go is the canonical domain where AI models are considered to be vastly, vastly superhuman. We heard it from the best Go players themselves, who have faced off and been defeated by these Go-playing AIs. Ke Jie, the professional Go player then ranked world No. 1, said in 2017 after losing to AlphaGo that “AlphaGo to me is 100 percent perfection, to me AlphaGo is the god of the Go game”.

I've been interested in Go-playing AIs partly because it serves as an intuition pump for me for superintelligence in other domains: Just imagine if an AI model became as superhuman in software/math/business strategy/persuasion as Go models in fact are. I specifically thought this of Go, and not necessarily chess or other games. It seems like many other people share this intuition.

Noam Brown on Dwarkesh Podcast in September 2026 saying Go models are "orders of magnitude stronger than any human alive".

And yet in 2026, a human defeated the best Go model, with only a 2-stone advantage. How is this possible? Do I have the wrong impression of just how superhuman Go models are?

And if I’m wrong about this, are my beliefs about superintelligence therefore suspect?

# The case for “unimaginably, orders of magnitude stronger than any human alive”...

items.summary: The author analyzes Shin Jin-seo's July 2026 match victory over KataGo with only a 2-stone handicap, probing what this surprising result implies about AI superhuman claims in Go and about superintelligence forecasts generally. The post surveys possible interpretations and their implications for how much we should trust domain-level superhuman benchmarks as evidence of general AI superiority.

items.title: Twitch Plays: AI Interpretability of Bonsai-8B
items.content:
# Quick Links

Watch the Twitch stream.

Check the status of the interpretability map.

Do your own parallel research and submit pull requests to fill out the map.

# What is this?

Let's Play Interpretability is a Twitch livestream where you can help Claude semi-autonomously interpret the neurons, connections and circuits in the Bonsai-8B LLM.

Your help comes in at various stages in the interpretation pipeline. The audience and the agent collaborate to:

- Pick the neuron to work on
- Suggest sentences on which to test activations
- Explicitly test various hypotheses, and attempt to falsify them
- Branch out to nearby (upstream and downstream) neurons whose ablation most impacts the activation, to better solidify the interpretation
-... and more.

View and participate in the stream.

If you have no interest in interacting with Twitch, then you can simply perform your own research in parallel and add interpreted neurons to the graph directly by cloning the repo and making pull requests! Help fill in the graph directly. With sufficient effort, we could fully characterize the entire LLM.

Current progress. Pick a neuron and get started!

# Why did you build this?

I have always been fascinated by direct AI interpretability efforts, starting in the long ago time of the melting dogs, the more recent work on monosemanticity and its application to larger models, and the very recent and provocative Neural Networks Are Already Clean. I simply find it interesting.

However, undertaking such research efforts myself has been prohibitively difficult - until recently. Now, it's relatively trivial to set your sights on some particular interpretability or alignment-type problem and dive in, with assistance from frontier models.

I suspect concrete value might emerge from this project:...

items.title: Capital Ownership Will Make You Go Crazy First
items.content:
People worried about a “permanent underclass” often assume that owning capital will protect them from disempowerment, or at least that they will be disempowered last, after the jobless masses dependent on UBI. I think something else is more likely: owning large amounts of capital will get you disempowered sooner than average, just by a different path, namely going crazy.

How? The basic mechanism is actually easy to understand on a human level. One of the things difficult about being a billionaire is staying true to your values and keeping good epistemics. Why? Because a growing number of people are optimizing against your mind. Not “against” in an adversarial sense, but in the sense that your specific mind believing or doing something is part of their optimization objective. People see you as a source of resources and try to befriend you so you’ll fund them, invest in their startups, donate to their causes, or have sex with you. Nearby egregores extend their tentacles to convert you.

Staying sane gets harder. You often see countermeasures, like billionaires setting up family offices or small organizations that also act as filters, shielding them from part of the pressure (“I do philanthropy only through my foundation and don’t make personal donations, please don’t reach out”).

In my view most billionaires lose in this game, the question is just to what degree. 

Now imagine a hypothetical future with the ultra-rich (or, as people usually imagine it, with you as the billionaire), where the rest of the world consists of the permanent underclass and countries of geniuses in datacenters. In this world, the content of your mind is the key to an absurdly large share of resources. Unless some magical social realignment happens, the countries of geniuses will optimize against your mind, and millions of desperate people with no better game in town will be happy to help them (or the other way around)....

The post analyzes why staying sane and value-coherent becomes harder as one's capital grows.

items.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
items.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues.

As I said a few times in the speech - some of which was ad libbed and not captured here - I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously

But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. These capabilities will not stop at coding; the same thing will happen to science and robotics. It has already begun to happen. And it means some important properties of the global economy may change - like the rate of innovation, or the frequency with which we invent entirely new general purpose technologies that create new industries around themselves, like the internet, phones, and artificial intelligence.

In biology, researchers have used AI to design viruses from scratch, to identify new drug candidates for testing, and there are already drugs in trials today which have been in large part designed by AI.

Taken individually, each of these examples is exciting. But the profound fact is that they all relate to the same underlying technology - and for most of these use-cases, the same single underlying frontier model. We now have singular entities - AI systems like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini - which can carry out work at the frontier of multiple scientific disciplines.

One such metric is the score of AI systems at a test called Humanity’s Last Exam - I didn’t choose the name!

This ominously named test was developed in response to the profound advances seen in prior years by AI systems at a variety of difficult and varied scientific challenges, covering topics as varied as advanced chemistry, computer science, mathematics, classical literature, and ecology.

Another example is FrontierMath, a test released in November 2024 that sought to assess how well AI systems could solve hundreds of challenging math problems, curated and evaluated by professional mathematicians. When it launched, the best scoring systems got 2%. Now, they get 94%.

More broadly, it looks like this everywhere. Pick your favorite part of science and go looking for a test and you’ll find this pattern - sudden and steep increases in capability, everywhere you look.

This is a paper that tests out how well AI systems can solve unpublished problems in theoretical physics. The 50 questions in the paper were compiled by physicists around the world.

Unsurprisingly, AI systems got high scores. But what is surprising is how they got the high scores. Here, I am going to quote from Indian physicist Suvrat Raju, who wrote a post commenting on the results.

“I don’t know of any individual who can solve any significant fraction of our final collection of problems without AI assistance,” he said. “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).”

Think about this for a moment. Some of the world’s scientific experts built a test out of problems an AI could never have possibly read the answer to. And when they tested the AI, not only did it score high, but it got a higher score by finding errors in the answers that the humans had worked on!

There is a scene in films, usually two thirds of the way through, when the young protagonist finally proves to their mentor that they have what it takes to go out into the world and succeed independently. It is a narrative trope - when the teacher becomes the student. That is what is happening here.

So, why am I telling you this? Why does it matter that AI systems are getting better at science?

I believe it is because doing true frontier science - being capable of making breakthroughs that extend the frontier of knowledge - implicitly tests for one of the last frontiers of AI capability: creativity. My view is that if AI systems can creatively problem solve to succeed at science, we should expect this to be a sign of their ability to generalize into many domains, including certainly AI research itself, which could have an explosive effect on innovation.

Therefore, if AI systems get better at science, this will strongly drive the growth and shape of the future economy, which means that you can make decisions today to set up your nations and people to benefit from this trend in the future.

Science and growth

Let’s talk about growth. One of the main sources of growth is in research yielding new ideas. One of the things that drives growth is our stock of human capital - the people all over the world who ask questions and conduct scientific research and thus help the world move forward.

But we also know that, as some economists have said, “good ideas are getting harder to find.” The cost of breakthroughs is going up, and we’ve had to pour an ever-rising amount of resources into research to keep going at the same pace.

As I said at the beginning, when I listed my credentials, there is one of me and it took me about 40 years to get here. What would it mean to be able to run hundreds or thousands of copies of me simultaneously? What would it mean if new versions of me could be created instantly, rather than waiting 40 years? How would my work change if I could make copies of myself and order them to do work under my supervision? That is what the next few years will be like for large swathes of the economy - we will be able to augment human labor in frontier disciplines, like science, in a way we’ve never been able to do before.

This will likely change the rate at which we find good ideas, because we’ll be able to add 100s or 1000s of times as many researchers to any problem, force multiplying our human scientists.

We can also do this very quickly. If you wanted to train a new generation of researchers in a certain area, it might take you 10 or 15 years of targeted education, and millions of dollars, to even get a small cohort. On the other hand, these AI systems can be created immediately, in arbitrary numbers, as long as there is enough computing capacity - and they can be used across domains to benefit from new scientific insights near instantaneously, and they can combine existing knowledge in new and surprising ways to make discoveries. This means that we can rapidly augment humans in domains that show promise by generating large amounts of virtual scientists to work alongside them.

This means that in the coming years, every human scientist on this planet will become more important and more powerful, as they gain the ability to supervise hundreds or thousands of like-minded experts on any problem they find interesting.

We have done some of our own modeling here, where we have tried to simulate different versions of the economy according to different trajectories of the technology. If you assume that models will be able to autonomously complete a broad range of tasks and will diffuse quickly in the economy, then under these singularity-esque conditions, we could see an unprecedented economic transformation, with US GDP reaching 44 trillion by 2030. This sounds outlandish, but it’s implicated by the technology continuing to get better. If GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such major economic expansion - and that is exactly what is implied by this notion of having AI systems be capable of autonomous scientific inquiry.

So, what do we do about this? How do we set up the world broadly to benefit from these advancing capabilities? How do we balance this opportunity for progress with appropriate caution?

We need to both plan for success so that humanity can take advantage of this technology and use it to create abundance, and be prepared to make wise choices about how to use the technology itself - just because AI will be a capable scientist, that does not mean we should use it for absolutely everything.

On planning for success, I’ll start with a story from my own experience.

For the last ten years, I have gone to governments around the world and tried to convey a very simple but important fact: that AI systems are getting far more powerful and useful, and that these systems require large amounts of computers. Therefore, I said, the single best thing a government could do to position itself to take advantage of the AI revolution was to build enough electricity capacity and data center space to be able to host the kinds of powerful AI systems discussed here, and to invest in the AI supply chain.

Therefore, just as we did with compute and power, we will want to use much more scientific equipment and robotic systems or we will run very quickly out of capacity. But infrastructure alone will not be enough. If discovery becomes abundant, we need to avoid bottlenecking ourselves downstream - an avalanche of new proposed drugs is of little use if only a handful can ever be tested. The policymakers and their colleagues in this room will need to help us find ways to accelerate our ability to move discoveries out of the lab and into the clinic, the factory, and the field.

The better we prepare for this world, the better able we will be to translate the gains of AI to gains for the world.

We have many choices to make, and it’s only by recognizing this technology for what it is - for how powerful it is - that we will see the urgency behind making these choices.

The first choice is about where we should direct this technology. Just because we have an AI system that can do science, that doesn’t mean that it should be left to do science unattended. One such use case is biological research, where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety.

Another is AI research itself, where labs like Anthropic will need to make decisions about how much oversight we apply to AI-driven research. This could let us make more progress on the technology but also introduces risks. We will need to move extremely carefully here, because otherwise we could lose control of the technology. We will also likely need rules to govern this.

I was in Tokyo earlier this week, and a student at a university there said they worked in the physics department, and they said AI was already beginning to be able to do many experiments. What experiments should they spend time on as a person, and what experiments should they let the AI system do itself? This is a subtle question to which I don’t know the answer, but it is a question each discipline of science will need to answer.

The second choice is about how much we need to understand about what these AI systems do. As we have seen this year with the rise of AI in mathematics, we are already dealing with a world where the advances made by AI systems are sufficiently creative that we as humans are now spending time trying to decode them - trying to understand what they mean and how to apply these insights for ourselves.

How much should we understand? Again, the answer here is going to be subtle, and it relates to fundamental questions of meaning in the age of the singularity - for what parts of scientific progress do we want to have true understanding? We are only a few short years from AI systems not only doing science, but inventing their own new scientific equipment built for the ways AI systems work, rather than human minds. Do we need to understand that equipment? Should we? This is another choice we will need to make.

When I was a teenager, I read a lot about the world, and I was afraid. I believed that the 21st century was going to be difficult - that population growth, climate change, resource extraction, and other crises would add up to cause a malthusian collapse of the human species. That after rising to invent computers and the internet, we might consume ourselves into the ground.

And then over the subsequent years, I saw time and time again how technology could allow us to fundamentally alter these odds: how solar panels came along and became much cheaper, much faster than people expected. How our growing understanding of the human body allowed us to invent cures for things that had killed many people - including some of my own family.

How we could do things I had never even imagined but find utterly amazing, like how we are now using AI systems to decode the speech of animals, or how companies have built rockets that take off and then land back on this planet.

I work on AI because it can help us do more of that. I work on AI because whether it does that is about choices we make - choices people here in this room will make - about how we direct it and how we govern it. Choices I need to make. I work on AI because it is the most important technology our species has built.

It is a technology that, if we are able to use correctly, will let us deal with problems that might otherwise doom us as a species. But it is also a technology that has danger woven into it. For us to get through this - to chart a course through the singularity – we are going to need to work together to create unusual and serious rules for this technology and the companies building it, and to exercise the hardest and I think most noble quality of people - restraint.

We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development. We need to constantly differentiate between the things we can do and the things we should do. And we will need to invest today in the scientific capabilities to make that progress possible.

I am reminded in all of this by the great Carl Sagan, who said in The Pale Blue Dot, that the humans who may one day reach other stars, will be “a species very like us, but with more of our strengths and fewer of our weaknesses… more confident, farseeing, capable, and prudent.”

That is what AI demands from us. And where Sagan thought we had hundreds of thousands of years to achieve this - to become a better and wiser people - we instead have a handful of years. I believe we can do it. But it is only by treating AI with the seriousness it deserves that we will succeed. Thank you.

This will likely change the rate at which we find good ideas, because we’ll be able to add 100s or 1000s of times as many researchers to any problem, force multiplying our human scientists.

We can also do this very quickly. If you wanted to train a new generation of researchers in a certain area, it might take you 10 or 15 years of targeted education, and millions of dollars, to even get a small cohort. On the other hand, these AI systems can be created immediately, in arbitrary numbers, as long as there is enough computing capacity - and they can be used across domains to benefit from new scientific insights near instantaneously, and they can combine existing knowledge in new and surprising ways to make discoveries. This means that we can rapidly augment humans in domains that show promise by generating large amounts of virtual scientists to work alongside them.

This means that in the coming years, every human scientist on this planet will become more important and more powerful, as they gain the ability to supervise hundreds or thousands of like-minded experts on any problem they find interesting.

We have done some of our own modeling here, where we have tried to simulate different versions of the economy according to different trajectories of the technology. If you assume that models will be able to autonomously complete a broad range of tasks and will diffuse quickly in the economy, then under these singularity-esque conditions, we could see an unprecedented economic transformation, with US GDP reaching 44 trillion by 2030. This sounds outlandish, but it’s implicated by the technology continuing to get better. If GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such major economic expansion - and that is exactly what is implied by this notion of having AI systems be capable of autonomous scientific inquiry.

So, what do we do about this? How do we set up the world broadly to benefit from these advancing capabilities? How do we balance this opportunity for progress with appropriate caution?

We need to both plan for success so that humanity can take advantage of this technology and use it to create abundance, and be prepared to make wise choices about how to use the technology itself - just because AI will be a capable scientist, that does not mean we should use it for absolutely everything.

On planning for success, I’ll start with a story from my own experience.

For the last ten years, I have gone to governments around the world and tried to convey a very simple but important fact: that AI systems are getting far more powerful and useful, and that these systems require large amounts of computers. Therefore, I said, the single best thing a government could do to position itself to take advantage of the AI revolution was to build enough electricity capacity and data center space to be able to host the kinds of powerful AI systems discussed here, and to invest in the AI supply chain.

Not many policymakers listened. Now, we deal with the consequences of that. In today’s world, data center capacity is concentrated in the United States, China, and increasingly the Middle East, and the supply chains are concentrated and are under such contention that prices are going up.

That buildout remains important, but it was just the first phase of this economic and scientific revolution implied by AIs continued advance. Now, there is more to be built, and I believe more countries can participate in this - if they choose to.

The next phase of the AI revolution is about the expansion into the physical world, specifically by having AI systems increasingly operate robots, and to perform scientific experimentation, sometimes together. Therefore, just as we did with compute and power, we will want to use much more scientific equipment and robotic systems or we will run very quickly out of capacity. We must build this capacity now to let us take maximum advantage of converting this boom in science into benefits for us all.

According to estimates by UNESCO, there are approximately ~10 million scientists in the world. Even with only 10 million scientists, we have too few human scientists to oversee the work, too few laboratories to do materials science analysis, too few biological labs to develop and test new drugs, and too few large pieces of scientific equipment in space or on the earth for the experiments we want to run.

What happens when instead of ~10 million scientists, we have a billion virtual scientists directed by our own ten million? Or ten billion? That is the world that is coming right for us. We have to get ready.

If we do get ready, we are going to be in a better position to translate the intelligence of AI systems into gains for us all: longer, healthier lives, more energy, more food, more wealth. And just as with the data centers, the nations which build and develop this supply chain, will be the ones that will benefit the most.

This is an opportunity for everyone: if you are a developed country with a rich scientific ecosystem, you have an opportunity to make all of your scientists more productive. If you are a developing country that supplies the basic ingredients into the AI and scientific enterprise, like raw materials, then you have an opportunity to leapfrog: you can both build scientific testing facilities that, paired with human scientists and digital AI scientists, will let you grow a scientific community, and continue to develop your contribution to the supply chain, which will become more valuable in the future.

But infrastructure alone will not be enough. If discovery becomes abundant, we need to avoid bottlenecking ourselves downstream - an avalanche of new proposed drugs is of little use if only a handful can ever be tested. The policymakers and their colleagues in this room will need to help us find ways to accelerate our ability to move discoveries out of the lab and into the clinic, the factory, and the field.

The better we prepare for this world, the better able we will be to translate the gains of AI to gains for the world.

We also need to prepare ourselves as a global community to make choices about the future. Because as I have said, there is risk here. Being able to use AI for science, opens us up to the misuses of science as well - biological and cyber weapons, and things we can not yet imagine.

We have many choices to make, and it’s only by recognizing this technology for what it is - for how powerful it is - that we will see the urgency behind making these choices.

The first choice is about where we should direct this technology. Just because we have an AI system that can do science, that doesn’t mean that it should be left to do science unattended. One such use case is biological research, where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety.

Another is AI research itself, where labs like Anthropic will need to make decisions about how much oversight we apply to AI-driven research. This could let us make more progress on the technology but also introduces risks. We will need to move extremely carefully here, because otherwise we could lose control of the technology. We will also likely need rules to govern this.

I was in Tokyo earlier this week, and a student at a university there said they worked in the physics department, and they said AI was already beginning to be able to do many experiments. What experiments should they spend time on as a person, and what experiments should they let the AI system do itself? This is a subtle question to which I don’t know the answer, but it is a question each discipline of science will need to answer.

The second choice is about how much we need to understand about what these AI systems do. As we have seen this year with the rise of AI in mathematics, we are already dealing with a world where the advances made by AI systems are sufficiently creative that we as humans are now spending time trying to decode them - trying to understand what they mean and how to apply these insights for ourselves.

How much should we understand? Again, the answer here is going to be subtle, and it relates to fundamental questions of meaning in the age of the singularity - for what parts of scientific progress do we want to have true understanding? We are only a few short years from AI systems not only doing science, but inventing their own new scientific equipment built for the ways AI systems work, rather than human minds. Do we need to understand that equipment? Should we? This is another choice we will need to make.

Most importantly, taking AI’s progress seriously means we should give ourselves license to imagine a fundamentally different world

When I was a teenager, I read a lot about the world, and I was afraid. I believed that the 21st century was going to be difficult - that population growth, climate change, resource extraction, and other crises would add up to cause a malthusian collapse of the human species. That after rising to invent computers and the internet, we might consume ourselves into the ground.

And then over the subsequent years, I saw time and time again how technology could allow us to fundamentally alter these odds: how solar panels came along and became much cheaper, much faster than people expected. How our growing understanding of the human body allowed us to invent cures for things that had killed many people - including some of my own family.

How we could do things I had never even imagined but find utterly amazing, like how we are now using AI systems to decode the speech of animals, or how companies have built rockets that take off and then land back on this planet.

I work on AI because it can help us do more of that. I work on AI because whether it does that is about choices we make - choices people here in this room will make - about how we direct it and how we govern it. Choices I need to make. I work on AI because it is the most important technology our species has built.

It is a technology that, if we are able to use correctly, will let us deal with problems that might otherwise doom us as a species. But it is also a technology that has danger woven into it. For us to get through this - to chart a course through the singularity – we are going to need to work together to create unusual and serious rules for this technology and the companies building it, and to exercise the hardest and I think most noble quality of people - restraint.

We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development. We need to constantly differentiate between the things we can do and the things we should do. And we will need to invest today in the scientific capabilities to make that progress possible.

I am reminded in all of this by the great Carl Sagan, who said in The Pale Blue Dot, that the humans who may one day reach other stars, will be “a species very like us, but with more of our strengths and fewer of our weaknesses… more confident, farseeing, capable, and prudent.”

That is what AI demands from us. And where Sagan thought we had hundreds of thousands of years to achieve this - to become a better and wiser people - we instead have a handful of years. I believe we can do it. But it is only by treating AI with the seriousness it deserves that we will succeed. Thank you.

items.title: SAR: Learning Global Item-Space Matching and Geometry-Aware Placement Ranking for Buffered Online 3D Bin Packing
items.content: arXiv:2610.25795v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a bounded buffer requires irreversible item-selection and placement decisions under limited knowledge of future arrivals. Feasibility alone is insufficient, as feasible actions can produce different residual-space structures and subsequent packing opportunities. A central architectural question is how to allocate spatial reasoning between item selection and placement evaluation. We propose Spatial Affordance Retrieval (SAR), a novel learning-based framework that coordinates global item-space matching with geometry-aware placement ranking. A voxel-token spatial encoder represents 3D container occupancy, enabling a picker to match buffered items to the residual space without requiring item-specific placement proposals as inputs. After item selection, a loader ranks feasible rotation-position candidates using candidate geometry, local geometric features (LGF), and inter-candidate comparison, without directly accessing global spatial tokens. The feasible candidate set connects the two stages, which are jointly optimized under a shared long-horizon packing return. On the Random, JD, and SF datasets, the best SAR variants improve utilization over the strongest evaluated online baselines by 0.96-4.20 percentage points under the no-buffer setting (K=1). With a buffer (K=5), the best utilization rates across SAR variants reach 93.55%, 91.04%, and 90.41%, respectively. Ablations support the complementary roles of global item-space matching and geometry-aware placement evaluation, counterfactual analysis suggests that learned item selection favors greater future packing potential, and experiments demonstrate compatibility with multiple candidate generators.

items.summary: SAR is a learning-based framework for online 3D bin packing with a bounded buffer that coordinates global item-space matching with geometry-aware placement ranking, using a voxel-token spatial encoder to represent container occupancy. It addresses how to allocate spatial reasoning between item selection and placement evaluation under irreversible decisions with limited future knowledge.
items.reasoning: A competent learning-based approach to a well-defined combinatorial/logistics problem with real industrial relevance (packing and warehousing). The architecture choice is sensible but the problem domain is specialized, and the contribution is primarily an application-level advance rather than a general method.
