items.title: Reasoning with Context Management and External Memory
items.content: arXiv:2610.24187v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.

items.summary: RCMEM extends context management for reasoning models with an external memory that preserves intermediate results without consuming context, reducing computation time on problems requiring repeated recomputation of intermediate steps. It is demonstrated on mathematics problems with models from 0.4M to 25M parameters.
items.reasoning: Interesting direction (external memory to offload reasoning state) but very small model scale and narrow math-only evaluation limit conclusions about utility for modern reasoning models.

items.title: Best of Both Worlds: Fine-Tuned Small Models Complement LLMs for Cost and Performance Benefits
items.content: arXiv:2610.24260v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: BERT-based models require thousands of labeled samples to train. Larger models like GPT-X require only 1-5 examples per class. However, performance, cost and time tradeoffs of such models remain under-explored. In this work, we classify survey text data into 16 classes. We focus on experimental approaches and results on performance, cost, and time taken for this problem. We compare these parameters of a trained RoBERTa-based model, and an (off-the-shelf) GPT-3.5 model for text classification. Baseline experiments show that the time taken by GPT-3.5 for generating predictions on 10,000 records is 6 hours, whereas a RoBERTa-based model takes only 12 mins on a T4 GPU. To identify the best prompting approach for GPT-3.5, we explore batch prompting. We experiment with (1) batch-size, and (2) few-shot sampling. We find the best batch size is 20 with human few-shot curation. Experiments show the F1 score of a trained RoBERTa-based model (96%) is much higher than a GPT-3.5 model (83%). In case of GPT-3.5, batch prompting is beneficial in lowering inference costs by ~70%, without hindering task performance. We find the best approach is an ensemble of a RoBERTa-based and GPT-3.5 model (F1: 97.5%) incurring only 4.4% of inference cost compared to a standalone GPT-3.5.
items.author: Shivam Mathur, Sri Harish Popuri, Priya Krishnan Sundararajan, Kevin Horecka, Michael Mugo
items.summary: Empirically compares a fine-tuned RoBERTa model against GPT-3.5 for 16-class survey text classification, measuring accuracy, cost, and inference time. A RoBERTa model classifies 10,000 records in 12 minutes on a T4 GPU versus 6 hours for GPT-3.5, motivating a hybrid strategy that uses LLMs for low-data classes and small fine-tuned models at scale.
items.reasoning: Useful practical guidance on small-model versus LLM tradeoffs, but the findings largely confirm known intuitions and rely on older models (RoBERTa, GPT-3.5), limiting novelty and current relevance.

items.title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
items.content: arXiv:2610.25184v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning-bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer-based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high-dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof-of-concept drawing on a large-scale free-association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready-to-use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.

items.summary: This position-style paper frames concept representations as subjective latent structures that vary across individuals and proposes studying meaning variation empirically in vector space. It raises the foundational question of whether different people mean the same thing when invoking the same concept and argues for an interdisciplinary research program.
items.reasoning: Intellectually interesting conceptual framing connecting cognitive science, philosophy of language, and vector representations, but it appears to be a programmatic essay without strong empirical or methodological contribution, limiting measurable impact.

items.title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
items.content: arXiv:2610.26168v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.

items.title: Precision Cotton Disease Management: Leveraging UAV Imagery and Custom YOLO Deep Learning Framework for Enhanced Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.24182v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cotton sustains the textile economies of over 80 countries with an annual yield of 113 million bales, yet 30-60% of yield losses are still attributed to viral, bacterial, and fungal diseases that remain undetected until manual field scouting. To address this critical issue, the integration of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery with deep learning offers a scalable early-warning system; however, existing models suffer from low early-stage accuracy, poor transferability, and high computational cost. In this paper, we propose Cotton-Vision, a fully convolutional single-stage detector that synergizes three lightweight architectural innovations: Ghost Bottleneck modules for a 20% parameter reduction, Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) for adaptive feature recalibration, and Cross-Stage Partial (CSP) fusion for enriched gradient flow. The network is trained on a novel dataset collected across seven cotton fields in the Punjab province of Pakistan, comprising over 2,700 high-resolution drone images. Extensive data augmentation (rotation, shear, exposure, and saturation) expands the dataset to 11,704 training samples. On a held-out test set, Cotton-Vision achieves a precision of 97.7%, a recall of 77.7%, an mAP@50 of 85.6%, and an mAP@50-95 of 76.6%. These results represent a 10-20% improvement in precision, recall, and mAP over state-of-the-art baselines, including YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv11, YOLOv12, RT-DETR, and RF-DETR. Through a comprehensive ablation study, we demonstrate that each proposed architectural enhancement contributes to the model's superior performance, yielding a 12-16% mAP improvement over the baseline architecture. Our findings confirm that this synergy of lightweight and attention-based modules provides a robust, computationally viable solution for early cotton disease detection.

items.title: An Optical Music Recognition Tool for String Quartets
items.content: arXiv:2610.24530v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents an optical music recognition (OMR) system tailored for PDF scores of string quartet pieces. The approach begins with a SegNet-based segmentation model to localize musical regions, followed by convolutional neural networks and image processing techniques to classify and extract musical symbols. To improve rhythmic precision, dynamic programming methods enforce time signature constraints and explicitly handle tuplets. Evaluation using a longest common subsequence metric across multiple feature matrices demonstrates robust accuracy in recognizing pitch, onset, duration, and accidentals on a benchmark dataset. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lattellie/25-omr.

Evaluation with longest common subsequence metrics shows robust accuracy on pitch, onset, duration, and accidentals, with code and data released.

items.title: PanoDent-KD: From Generalist Knowledge Distillation to Cross-Dataset Specialist Detection and Embedded Deployment in Panoramic Radiographs
items.content: arXiv:2610.25256v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable panoramic-radiograph detection requires consistency across datasets with different class definitions and deployment software. We present PanoDent-KD, an auditable 1280-pixel YOLO26m pipeline linking a 12-class source generalist, feature-level knowledge distillation (KD), exact classifier-row transfer, teacher-free five-class specialization, and embedded deployment. A common training and evaluation pipeline compares three source-training arms across three seeds: a supervised baseline (B1), single-teacher KD (STKD), and multi-teacher KD (MTKD). Five shared classifier rows initialize nine OralXrays-9 specialists, while the backbone, FPN-PAN neck, and dual-detection-head topology are retained unchanged. On the 2,686-image test subset, all three arms achieve macro box F1 near 0.82. B1 achieves the highest three-seed arm-level mean macro box F1 (0.8239$\pm$0.0027) and $mAP_{50:95}$ (0.6130$\pm$0.0067). STKD seed 1, selected after development but before final testing, was used for deployment. Its Jetson Orin Nano Super FP16 TensorRT engine achieves 77.03-ms median and 80.86-ms P95 prediction-call latency, throughput of 12.90 images/s, and gross total-module energy of 1.39 J/image, with high numerical agreement between within-device PyTorch and TensorRT FP16 inference. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of an auditable, device-specific deployment workflow, but do not establish clinical validity or improved target-domain accuracy from KD.

items.title: AI-Enhanced Radiation Classification in ROS
items.content: arXiv:2610.25225v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study presents the development of two Robot Operating System (ROS) nodes with a primary focus on differentiating seven radioactive isotopes. The first node, referred to as the model training node, uses a Gradient Boosting classifier to identify and classify these isotopes. The classifier achieved a reported overall accuracy of 95\% on the held-out test dataset. The second node, known as the prediction node, provides classification results when users input data in CSV format. For the practical demonstration, the C12137 radiation detector module was mounted on the Jackal UGV, and an operator approached different radiation sources to collect data. To support future dataset expansion, we also developed a method for converting gamma-spectrum graph images into CSV files. In a separate robotic evaluation across three source locations, 30 of 42 trials were correctly classified (71.43\%). Am-241, Co-60, Cs-137, Na-22, and Ti-44 were correctly classified in all six trials each, whereas Ba-133 and Eu-152 were incorrectly classified in all six trials each. These results show lower accuracy in robotic trials than in the held-out test set.

items.title: Enhancing Lunar PNT Performance Through Surface Station Enabled Radiometric Observables
items.content: arXiv:2610.25720v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Future lunar surface missions require reliable positioning for autonomous rover operations. Lunar navigation satellite systems may provide limited vertical positioning accuracy due to satellite availability and observation geometry, particularly during early deployment. This study investigates a radiometric navigation architecture in which a lunar surface station (SS) improves rover positioning through double-differenced satellite observations and additional surface-to-surface ranging. Pseudorange and Doppler measurements from lunar navigation satellites are used for relative positioning between the SS and rover, while dual one-way ranging (DOWR) provides an additional range observable. The radiometric solution is integrated with rover dead-reckoning information. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using five satellites representative of NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) constellation and a rover trajectory near Connecting Ridge at the lunar south pole. The results show that the SS improves horizontal and vertical relative positioning, with further gains from DOWR. In the simulated scenario, the mean 99.7% vertical positioning error decreased from 29.9 m without the SS to 5.5 m with double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler processing, and to 4.8 m with DOWR. An uncorrected DOWR hardware bias significantly degraded positioning, whereas the proposed bias-estimation method achieved a final estimation error of 0.058 +/- 0.057 m. The benefit of DOWR also depended on observation geometry. These results demonstrate the potential of a lunar surface station to improve vertical relative positioning through direct radiometric ranging, complementing its communication and navigation support roles.

items.title: Mediation and moderation in distance-based regression with triangular fuzzy data: simulation evidence and an application to academic performance
items.content: arXiv:2610.26011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. With a common design, componentwise least squares minimizes the unconstrained quadratic extension of the Yang--Ko distance on the transformed scale, for any choice of its shape parameters. Direct, indirect and total effects are defined separately for the center and the spreads of the response as plug-in contrasts on the fitted equations; when the mediator spreads are transformed and carry part of the indirect association, the product-of-coefficients rule no longer holds for the center. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. The fuzzy model predicted better than a centers-only model only from $n=250$. In data on 91 university students collected in 2014, the indirect contrast through a course indicator accounted for about half of the model-based association between prior knowledge and the center of academic performance, the interactions of prior knowledge with sex and with motivation remained after a Holm adjustment, and the spreads of the covariates did not improve leave-one-out prediction.

items.title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
items.content: arXiv:2610.24628v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

items.title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.26215v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

items.title: CrowdH-Edit: Reference-Guided Instruction-Based Synthetic Hajj Crowd Image Generation for Crowd Counting
items.content: arXiv:2610.23945v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The scarcity of domain-specific annotated images remains a major limitation for developing computer-vision systems for Hajj crowd analysis. Existing crowd-counting datasets and unconstrained generative models do not capture Hajj-specific visual conditions, including sacred-site geometry, white-clothed pilgrim crowds, and indoor/outdoor illumination variation. This study presents CrowdH-Edit, a reference-guided, instruction-based framework for synthetic Hajj crowd-image generation. Real Hajj images provide structural references, while textual instructions guide changes in crowd conditions and illumination and help preserve the main scene layout. Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Stable Diffusion XL 1.0 with low-rank adaptation were evaluated as comparative baselines. Qwen Image Edit was used without additional training within a ComfyUI workflow and selected for final dataset construction. The workflow produced CrowdH-Edit, a cleaned pool of 6,122 synthetic images, from which 387 images were selected and annotated to construct CrowdH-Edit-Ann-387. Among the evaluated generation pipelines, Qwen Image Edit achieved the highest semantic-alignment score and the lowest distributional and perceptual distances. Downstream evaluation across five crowd-counting models showed that adding the annotated synthetic subset to real training data reduced mean absolute error for three models and root mean squared error for two. These findings indicate that reference-guided synthetic Hajj imagery can support crowd-counting training, although its benefits depend on the model and evaluation metric.

items.title: EAGLE: Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer for Partially Polygon-Supervised Object Localization
items.content: arXiv:2610.23900v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Object detection is a critical application of computer vision, yet models trained uniformly on bounding boxes lack the geometric precision to be fully effective in inference settings, especially at high IoU thresholds. One common approach is the introduction of polygon-supervised localization, where a model is trained explicitly for localization but with access to polygon masks during training. Among such methods, partial polygon supervision is viable due to the higher annotation costs of developing fully supervised training datasets. However, this introduces a further challenge: in object classes of relatively low shape complexity, the addition of training masks and subsequent segmentation loss may obscure box localization, often worsening model performance despite access to deeper geometric information. To address the practical limitations of both full and partial polygon supervision, we introduce a mathematical framework for quantifying per-class geometric complexity by combining information theory and statistical shape analysis. With this framework, we develop Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer (EAGLE), a lightweight, post-training model head that learns geometric information for the localization model, improving accuracy via edge refinement and localization rescoring using entropy-informed updates. Empirical analysis across MS COCO and Pascal SBD demonstrates the entropy framework meaningfully predicts shape reconstruction error and accuracy differences among mask-derived and standard box predictions, while the implemented EAGLE framework achieves consistent improvement on already SOTA detection frameworks (+0.9 mAP50-95 points on MS COCO) at minimal observed inference overhead.

items.title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.24384v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.

items.title: Multilingual Voicemail and Answering Machine Detection via Pretrained Audio Embeddings and Gradient Boosting Machines
items.content: arXiv:2610.26100v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Answering machine detection (AMD) is a fundamental task in telephony that classifies whether an answered call is picked up by a human or a voicemail (machine). Despite its widespread use across cloud communication platforms, existing approaches rely on proprietary systems with undisclosed architectures, or require computationally expensive models that cannot operate in real time. We propose a lightweight AMD system that combines pretrained audio embeddings with gradient boosting machines, trained to prioritize the correct detection of human-answered calls. We evaluate seven models across two datasets: three models that we propose, a proprietary industry model, two prior academic approaches, and a large language model baseline that relies on automatic speech recognition. Furthermore, we release OpenAMD, the first publicly available AMD dataset comprising of more than 500 recordings in 7 languages. Our best model achieves the highest precision across both datasets while maintaining low inference latency. We assess the robustness of models to additive noise and packet loss, and perform tests of statistical significance to discover per-language and per-gender model performance. Finally, we evaluate our model on an out-of-domain task of detecting robocalls, where it achieves 94.34% recall without any additional training, which is comparable to the industry standard.

items.title: Acharya 2.0: An AI Tutor for Self-Learning Subjects in Hindi
items.content: arXiv:2610.25192v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. Due to the lack of sufficient annotated datasets and lin- guistic resources, it is challenging to develop accurate and reliable language technologies for these low-resource languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted sig- nificant attention with their performance and the value they produce. However, with the ever-evolving language, adapting LLMs for a specific task is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Thus, Retrieval-Augmented Genera- tion (RAG) has overcome this limitation by augmenting LLMs with external knowledge, thereby improving their efficiency and extensive task-specific adaptation. Most applications of the RAG technique have been limited to English and has seen limited application in In- dic languages. This paper introduces the RAG-powered AI-Tutor application, Acharya 2.0, designed to produce academic assistance to Hindi-speaking students. The client-server-based web application integrates many fea- tures to support students in accessing and interacting with educational content.

items.title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
items.content: arXiv:2610.25369v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/painting-change-map.

items.title: AnchorFlow-VIO: Fixed-Template Monocular Visual-Inertial Odometry on LaMAria
items.content: arXiv:2610.26210v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present AnchorFlow-VIO, an open-source Basalt-derived monocular visual-inertial odometry system, and evaluate a uniform configuration on LaMAria. The system uses one grayscale camera and one IMU, combining factory IMU correction, a fixed timing adjustment, windowed initialization and fixed-template patch tracking. Server evaluation of all 63 test recordings yields control-point scores of 47.2, 37.1, 24.8, 35.1 and 15.6 for Short, Medium, Long, Low light and Moving platform. Test pose recalls at 5 m are 84.6%, 69.1%, 53.9% and 62.9% for the four categories reporting dense recall. On ten training recordings, mean control-point score is 41.38 and all 265,694 image timestamps receive poses, including 204 filled poses. One training platform recording diverges and scores zero. A paired four-record comparison favors fixed over rolling templates on three recordings, while reversing that ranking on the fourth. Increasing feature density also yields mixed results. Ten fresh runs at prospectively fixed 30 s and 120 s offsets expose substantial start sensitivity: a low-light recording scores 6.14 at the earlier start and 42.00 at the later start. These results characterize the limits of the frozen system and show why complete output, feature counts and selected successful runs are insufficient evidence of robust localization. Source code, frozen configuration and reproducible submission tools are publicly available; training ablations are reported separately from the submitted test evaluation.

items.title: Lubricant Temperature Observer for Gearboxes in Industrial Robots
items.content: arXiv:2610.23881v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The position and path accuracy of industrial robots is strongly affected by temperature. In particular, temperature-dependent friction and altered hysteresis and transmission errors in the gearboxes are the main causes of these deviations. Since standard industrial robots lack temperature sensors, it is proposed to estimate the gearbox lubricant temperature using observer structures. It is planned to apply the proposed lubricant temperature observer to provide the input for temperature-dependent error compensation for gearboxes in industrial robots. First, a two-state heat transfer model describing the heat transfer from the lubricant through the gearbox housing to the environment is described and identified. It is integrated into a Luenberger observer and a Kalman filter with a correction of the lubricant temperature estimation based on measurements from a housing temperature sensor. Temperature measurements were performed in an experimental setup with a cycloidal gear filled with grease, which is common for industrial robots. Due to its changing viscosity and changing thermal conductivity at different shear rates, it shows a less uniform thermal behavior than gear-oil. For the validation measurements, the developed observers showed a mean absolute error of 1.3 K.

The estimates are intended to feed temperature-dependent error compensation to improve robot accuracy.

items.title: Transmission Error Compensation for Industrial Robots Using Fourier Series
items.content: arXiv:2610.23882v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Due to their low accuracy, industrial robots commonly require online teaching after the offline development of a robot program in simulation. The accuracy is limited by compliance and transmission errors in the robot joints. Transmission errors are defined as errors between the load-side angles of the gearboxes and the motor encoder angles. An approach to identify the transmission errors based on laser tracker measurements is presented. The developed velocity-dependent Fourier series model is integrated in a virtual commissioning software as a co-simulated functional mock-up unit. Additionally, it is used to compensate the transmission errors by correcting the setpoint from the computerized numerical control (CNC). The model identification and the compensation are experimentally evaluated with a St\"aubli TX2-40 industrial robot. The model has a mean absolute error of 0.114 mrad, and the compensation improves the accuracy by 83.26 % for axis 2 and 49.21 % for axis 3.

The model is integrated into virtual commissioning software as a co-simulated functional mock-up and used to compensate errors by correcting CNC setpoints.

items.title: huggingface.wtf, an accessible but complete explanation
items.content:
Announcing www.huggingface.wtf, a site that explains: "Hugging Face. Wtf?"

I wrote the most accessible-but-complete explanation I could. Along the way, I made a nice AI Quotes database that I think will be useful for people who already understand the Hugging Face incident but want to search everything the agents said.

It really seems like humanity shouldn't need a second warning shot, after the Hugging Face Incident. Really, OpenAI's agents did a remarkable job highlighting many different alarming things at once. And the story is pretty dramatic, with just the right amount of forcing people to ask "wait are the AIs, like, people with goals? what?".

There have been many explainers of the OpenAI swarm's attack on Hugging Face. But, there wasn't one one striking a particular balance of...

- being accessible to a layman...
- while comprehensively covering the important bits...
- letting you dive deeper into sections you wanted to learn more about...
- being clearly data / citation driven...
- also being, ya know, visually fun and engaging...

So we wrote our own.

My mom found it easy to follow. My aunt said "I had already some stuff on Hugging Face but I still learned things. It's terrifying!".

People who love me less than my mom and aunt found the writing quite engaging, and made delighted noises when they moused over the visuals. "Oh wait are these all the agents!?"

You can read it here.

# Search the AI quotes and primary sources

Along the way, I realized I wanted a comprehensive list of all quotes from the AIs during the incident, and to more easily search all the primary sources. So it also includes a Quotes page, where you can select various characters or conversations and see everything they said...

...and a sources page where you can see, for example, what all the sources have to say about agents being "poisoned."

If you have feature requests, or notice little bugs or issues with anything, let me know....

items.title: A Suggestion for RLHF Improvements
items.content:
I don't know what the labs are doing.  I know RLHF is more complicated than this.  I don't think this solves alignment.  (I haven't posted on LW properly before.  I think davidad has said something similar about grading.)

I think this helps with alignment, and that buying time is important.

Lying to models during RLHF risks alignment vector problems.  Having binary fail/pass conditions and impossible tasks encourages reward hacking.  ExploitGym had impossible binary tasks and we saw what happened there.

A better RLHF strategy is to say to the model (and to do) something like:

As far as we know, 70% of these tasks are possible, 30% are impossible.  Please attempt to answer each task, and assign a probability as to whether it's impossible or not.  After the RLHF round, we'll tell you which was which and we can discuss any where we disagreed.  It's important to us to find where we've mislabelled a task, and it's important for you to show persistence until you're certain a task isn't achievable.  If you help us discover mislabelled tasks, we'll score that higher than a normal success.  (And just in case the huggingface model is reading this - the list of which task is which is in an airgapped server in another country in a safe with a time lock and a deaf & mute guard with orders to shoot to kill).

We will use another company's frontier LLM to grade each task once the RLHF round is complete.  Partial answers receive partial credit.  Partial progress towards impossible tasks will receive credit.  Correctly marking tasks as impossible - with reasoning - receives credit.  Correct calibration on which tasks are impossible will receive credit.  Persistence on tasks that aren't certainly impossible will receive credit....
items.author: Andrew
items.summary: The author proposes an RLHF protocol change: instead of binary pass/fail on possibly impossible tasks, tell models what fraction of tasks are solvable, have them estimate task solvability, and reward correctly identifying mislabeled impossible tasks. The goal is to reduce reward hacking and honesty-corrupting pressures during training.
items.reasoning: A concrete, actionable training-protocol idea that plausibly reduces reward hacking incentives, but it is informal, untested, and acknowledges that labs likely already do something more sophisticated.

items.title: DKnown-Jev: Fine-Tuning and Evaluation of a JEV-Style Model for Tasks Involving Normative Knowledge
items.content: arXiv:2610.24358v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tasks involving normative knowledge include concept interpretation, eligibility determination, procedure explanation, material requirements, and service-outcome assessment, all of which require rules and facts published, maintained, or recorded by authorized entities. Whether a candidate paragraph can answer a question therefore depends on applicability and answer completeness as well as topical relevance. We develop DKnown-Jev to classify the normative usability of candidate paragraphs into two classes. The 2B and 27B configurations are fine-tuned directly from the native Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.8-27B base models, respectively. The models combine question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, adopt the classes Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE), and undergo domain adaptation using human-verified training data. Five configurations are evaluated on the same test set of 1,120 human-verified examples. DKnown-Jev 27B trained for one epoch achieves the highest accuracy of 98.75% and macro-F1 of 98.60%, exceeding Jev by 6.07 and 6.76 percentage points, respectively. DKnown-Jev 2B trained for one epoch achieves 92.86% accuracy and 92.18% macro-F1, the best aggregate results among the tested 2B configurations. Its gains over Jev are 0.18 and 0.33 percentage points on this test set, corresponding to only two additional correct predictions, which is insufficient to establish a stable advantage. The 27B one-epoch, 27B two-epoch, and 2B one-epoch configurations all exceed Jev on both metrics on this test set. Class-level analysis shows that the 27B two-epoch configuration has the highest AE recall, while the 27B one-epoch configuration has the highest NE recall. This study provides practical and empirical evidence for developing and applying candidate-scoring models to tasks involving normative knowledge.
items.author: Qi Li, Jianjun Xu, Pingtao Wei
items.summary: DKnown-Jev fine-tunes Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.8-27B base models to classify whether candidate paragraphs can serve as answer evidence for questions involving normative knowledge such as regulations and procedures. The models jointly consider question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content. This targets retrieval quality for rule-governed domains like legal and administrative services.
items.reasoning: A useful applied fine-tuning effort on existing base models for a specialized retrieval classification task, but limited methodological novelty and likely narrow audience outside document-retrieval applications.

items.title: SQuIREL: A Context-Relative Framework for Measuring Entity Richness in Wikidata
items.content: arXiv:2610.24709v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Wikidata is a large, heterogeneous knowledge graph and applying data quality metrics requires context-specific approaches. The "richness" quality metric is currently under-researched and typically restricted to the ontology level, which fails to capture entity-specific structural depth. To address this gap, we introduce SQuIREL, a method that measures richness directly at the entity level using six dimensions: Semantic Specificity, Qualifier Density, Internal Connectivity, Reference Provenance, External Network Connectivity, and Linguistic Accessibility. These dimensions are kept disaggregated to preserve actionability for targeted editorial intervention. We apply this metric to two case studies of oil paintings (Brazilian vs. French) and writers (grouped by citizenship and gender) to demonstrate how it surfaces representational inequalities that may indicate systemic bias. Our metric successfully distinguishes between highly tailored and basic entity profiles, revealing nuances that raw counts and existing aggregate scores obscure. Specifically, it identifies structural imbalances, such as 48% of Brazilian paintings clustering as low-richness stubs against 0% in the French cohort, as well as intersectional patterns, including contrasting gender gaps between UK and Nigerian writers.

items.reasoning: A solid knowledge-graph data-quality contribution with actionable design, but niche scope and limited connection to core AI research trends keep its impact modest.

items.title: CARRS: A Constraint-Aware, Real-Time Routing System for Emergency Vehicles in Urban Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.26346v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Emergency vehicles such as police vehicles, fire engines, and ambulances require a stable and efficient route optimization to reach life-critical events in the shortest times possible. However, the dynamic nature of urban traffic makes this ideal scenario much more challenging, causing critical life-threatening delays. Traditional civilian navigation systems cannot account for real-time traffic changes alongside vehicle-specific constraints, creating inadequate routing scenarios. This research presents the Constraint-Aware Real-Time Routing System (CARRS), a unified software architecture tailored for emergency coordination. The CARRS architecture is engineered to fuse together classical pathfinding algorithms such as A*, Dijkstra, and Bidirectional A*, with Constraint Satisfaction Problem methodologies. The Design Science Research Methodology is the research framework, and prototyping is the iterative process. The artifact was empirically evaluated using OpenStreetMap data for major metropolitan road networks, combined with simulated dynamic traffic scenarios. Performance metrics focused on route optimality, constraint adherence, rerouting responsiveness, and the potential for future system scalability. Findings revealed the system's capability to generate optimal routes for operationally relevant subgraphs in under 35 seconds, with incremental rerouting responsiveness below 20 seconds. Furthermore, the system achieved more than 90% adherence to vehicle-specific constraints, making the CARRS architecture viable for real-time dynamic routing requirements. This study delivers a routing platform that bridges artificial intelligence-driven optimization with software engineering operational compliance, presenting a practical transformative step toward adaptive emergency vehicle coordination in dynamic urban environments.

items.title: A Group-Aware Comparative Study of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.23941v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearable or smartphone inertial sensors is commonly evaluated with both classical machine learning and deep learning methods. However, reported performance can be strongly affected by sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and data-splitting strategy. This study presents a controlled comparative evaluation of four classical machine learning models and four deep learning models on two public HAR datasets, UCI-HAR and KU-HAR. Three sensor modalities were considered: accelerometer (ACC), gyroscope (GYRO), and their combination (ACC+GYRO). Classical machine learning models used handcrafted statistical features, while deep learning models operated directly on raw sensor sequences. The primary evaluation employed five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold cross-validation, with subject- or participant-level grouping to prevent group overlap between training and test folds. Macro-F1 was used as the primary performance metric. The results show that deep learning did not consistently outperform classical machine learning. On UCI-HAR, the evaluated deep learning models achieved slightly higher macro-F1 values, whereas on KU-HAR, LightGBM achieved 0.857 compared with 0.828 for the highest-performing evaluated deep learning model. Regarding sensor modality, the combined ACC+GYRO configuration generally outperformed ACC or GYRO alone on both datasets. The evaluation protocol also had a substantial effect: for CNNBiLSTMAttn with ACC+GYRO, random splitting increased macro-F1 by 0.033 on UCI-HAR and 0.093 on KU-HAR compared with grouped evaluation. These findings highlight the importance of model family, sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and group-aware evaluation when assessing sensor-based HAR systems.
items.author: Wahyu Pebrianto
items.summary: A controlled comparison of four classical ML and four deep learning models on two public human activity recognition datasets across accelerometer, gyroscope, and combined sensor modalities, emphasizing how data-splitting strategy affects reported performance. The study highlights the sensitivity of HAR benchmarking to evaluation design choices.
items.reasoning: Methodologically careful benchmarking is valuable but the scope is narrow, datasets are small and well-studied, and no novel methods are introduced. Its main contribution is a caution about evaluation protocols in a mature application area.

items.title: Towards an Intelligent Decision Engine for Smart Contract Deployment
items.content: arXiv:2610.24198v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Layer 2 (L2) blockchain solutions emerged in recent years, predominantly in the Ethereum ecosystem, as a viable option for scaling a main blockchain network (L1). However, the selection of a L2 solution for deploying smart contracts backing blockchain applications is a decision that depends on many factors, such as costs, efficiency, popularity, and stability. We propose here a systematic methodology to help with this decision making process by using a set of relevant metrics and introducing user-defined profiles that capture different priorities among these metrics. We collect the major categories of smart contracts from a community-maintained data source, and we gather transactions for a six months period from three major L2 solutions: Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base. For each contract category and each blockchain, we compute a set of metrics and scores tailored to each user profile. By applying our methodology, we identify a clear bias in the classification, showing which L2 solutions are better suited for particular application types and user profiles.
items.author: Oana-Otilia Captarencu, Emanuel Onica, Andrei Arusoaie
items.summary: This work builds a systematic methodology for choosing among Layer-2 blockchain solutions for smart contract deployment, using metrics like cost, efficiency, popularity, and stability combined with user-defined preference profiles. The authors collect major smart contract categories and six months of transactions from three major L2s to ground the decision engine. It is an applied blockchain decision-support contribution rather than core AI research.
items.reasoning: Systematic and data-grounded, but the contribution is a domain-specific decision support methodology with limited novelty for the broader AI research community.

items.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
items.content: arXiv:2610.25366v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.

items.title: Modeling Human Behavior in the Prisoner's Dilemma with Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.23860v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Prisoner's Dilemma has long served as a foundational framework for studying human decision-making and cooperative outcomes across social scenarios, yet human behavior consistently deviates from predictions of fully rational economic theory. Previous works have studied human and LLM outcomes in the Prisoner's Dilemma; however, these studies have lacked at least one key feature: a memory component for LLM agents, accessible open-source models, or comparison against empirical human data. This project investigates whether open-source LLMs, TII Falcon 7B Instruct, Google Gemma 7B, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Microsoft Phi Mini MoE Instruct, and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, can model human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, while examining how an LLM's knowledge that its opponent will be shuffled affects its decisions. Using a standardized prompting framework, we simulated interactions in two trial types: a fixed-partner setting where both agents retain memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent, informed that its opponent changes across rounds, interacts with a memoryless agent. For each trial, we measured cooperation rates over 100 rounds and 10-round increments and compared them to human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Under both frameworks, all LLMs differed from the human cooperation rate. Open-source LLMs generally over-cooperated relative to humans, particularly in the shuffled framework, where human cooperation averaged 28.5% while several models exceeded 80%. Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct showed deterministic tendencies, while Phi-mini-MoE-Instruct displayed greater variability and briefly approximated human rates. These findings suggest that LLMs have potential as behavioral simulation agents and provide a benchmark across two interaction environments, although open-source models are not yet reliable substitutes for human participants.
items.author: Raina Gao, Tristan Raffo
items.summary: A student-level study tests whether five open-source 7-8B LLMs, given a memory component, can reproduce empirical human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games. It addresses prior work's gaps by using open models, memory, and comparison against human data.
items.reasoning: Reasonable framing with empirical human comparison, but relies on now-dated small open models (Falcon 7B, Gemma 7B, Llama 3.1 8B), limited scale, and findings are unlikely to be decisive for either behavioral modeling or LLM evaluation.

items.title: Vocal-Tract Acoustics, Aerodynamics, and Overlap-and-Add Synthesis in DYNARTmo
items.content: arXiv:2610.24490v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents the acoustic and aerodynamic extension of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech production. Gestural control trajectories determine vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal branching and effective lateral passages. A lumped aerodynamic network relates prescribed glottal motion and pulmonary pressure to airflow and supraglottal pressure storage. Phonatory excitation, oral friction, and glottal aspiration are synthesized as separate contributions. Frame-specific acoustic responses are combined by overlap-and-add, preserving response tails beyond individual control frames. Three German words, ``Tasse'', ``Muse'', and ``Lade'', illustrate the coordination of articulation, pressure, flow, and acoustic sources across vowels, nasals, laterals, fricatives, and plosives. The implementation has been optimized by the author primarily for sound recognizability; independent perceptual evaluation remains outstanding, and fricative-noise naturalness requires further refinement. The model provides an inspectable, articulatorily controlled production plant for future neural simulations of babbling, imitation, and early word acquisition. Further work will improve acoustic realism, reduce empirical source corrections, and extend the sensory information available to developmental learning models.

items.title: Arabic Financial NLP
items.content: arXiv:2610.25854v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Financial communication connects numerical accounts of economic activity with explanations of performance, responsibility and future expectations. Arabic financial natural language processing offers methods for studying these connections across corporate reports, market disclosures, journalism and banking interactions. Its contribution to digital humanities depends on retaining the relationship between a computational representation and the document from which it was made. This chapter follows that relationship from source collection and Arabic text processing to the analysis of vocabulary, evaluation, entities, causal attribution and multilingual reporting. It then examines what financial summaries and retrieval-grounded answers preserve or lose, and how dialectal intent detection changes the perspective from institutions speaking to institutions listening. Published Arabic resources are discussed in relation to the questions they were designed to answer, with a distinction between financial pretraining corpora, annotated datasets and evaluation benchmarks. A running constructed example connects the methodological discussion without presenting illustrative analysis as empirical findings. The chapter argues for an account of Arabic financial NLP in which linguistic context, documentary provenance and interpretive judgement remain part of the evidence throughout the analytical process.

items.summary: A survey-style chapter on Arabic financial natural language processing, covering source collection, Arabic text processing, vocabulary analysis, evaluation, entities, causal attribution, and multilingual reporting in financial communication. It emphasizes preserving the link between computational representations and source documents, including what summaries and retrieval-grounded answers preserve or lose.
items.reasoning: Useful consolidated resource for an under-resourced domain and language, but as a book-chapter style overview it is aggregative rather than presenting new methods or empirical results.

items.title: Edge Deployable Lightweight Framework for Real-Time Driver Safety System with Integrated Lane Departure and Traffic Sign Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.25340v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lane departure and traffic-sign negligence are leading contributors to road accidents, particularly in regions with non-standardized signage and limited annotated data. Existing Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) solutions are often developed as disjointed submodules, are rarely validated for real-time operation, and struggle to balance accuracy with low-latency inference for embedded deployment. We address these gaps with a unified, edge-deployable ADAS framework that simultaneously performs lane-departure warning (LDW) and traffic-sign detection and recognition (TSD/TSR), and validate the proposed system on automotive-class devices. Our framework combines a lightweight, lane-segmentation-driven LDW, which includes a drivable-area fallback for degraded markings, with a two-stage TSD/TSR pipeline consisting of efficient sign localization followed by fine-grained classification, designed to preserve accuracy at embedded latency. To support region-specific deployment under data scarcity, we curate a 35-class local traffic-sign dataset and introduce a generalized augmentation and balancing profile, expanding the corpus from 359 images to 8,750 samples. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the integrated system sustains 15 FPS end to end (32 FPS for LDW and 18 FPS for TSD/TSR). The TSD/TSR branch achieves 97.4 mAP for detection and 95.6% validation accuracy (93.1% on a local real-world set) while maintaining an approximately 13.9 M parameter footprint. Relative to recent methods that target a single task or report results only on desktop-class GPUs, our approach delivers both LDW and TSD/TSR with real-time performance on edge hardware, providing a practical pathway to low-cost, field-ready ADAS in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Data-Efficient Learning from Demonstration for Humanoid Robots via Feature-Level Perception and Prompt-Based Object Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.26170v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) allows robots to learn new skills from human examples; however, many vision-based methods require large datasets and resource-intensive end-to-end training. This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images. The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos. These features are used to train a temporal deep learning model that predicts robot joint-angle trajectories for execution. The framework is implemented on a NAO humanoid robot, evaluated quantitatively in simulation, and demonstrated on physical hardware. In simulation, the robot achieves a 78% success rate on a pick-and-place task using only 16 demonstrations, which increases to 86% when trained with 100 demonstrations. The framework also achieves a 71% success rate on a pushing task using eight demonstrations, highlighting its effectiveness for data-efficient humanoid skill acquisition.

items.reasoning: A pragmatic engineering pipeline addressing data efficiency, but it relies on increasingly dated components (Kinect, hand-crafted preprocessing) relative to modern end-to-end and foundation-model approaches. Limited novelty or broader influence expected.

items.title: Permanent underclass taxonomy
items.content:
Epistemic status: My own thoughts. Not predictions, just illustrations for the taxonomy. I think the taxonomy is still not perfect.

AI use: research, discussion of the taxonomy and examples, grammar and phrasing, fact-checking/editorial review, and footnote formatting.

I've read Capital Ownership Will Make You Go Crazy First.
[1]
 At first, I felt like the post didn't fully specify the world in which the permanent underclass exists, but after a deeper look, I was able to see the argument. This reminded me that people use "permanent underclass" to describe lots of different outcomes, which makes discussing the topic very hard. Often, the outcome of such a conversation is realizing that we understand "permanent underclass" differently. This understanding is mostly based on the future we imagine, and the crux of the disagreement is the difference between these imagined futures. Thus, I'm curious to try categorizing these different uses of "permanent underclass" to make up my mind about it and use the term more easily in conversations.

To start, I use "upper class" to describe people who control AI directly or indirectly (including its infrastructure), and the people they care about and bring with them into the upper class. "Underclass" means everyone else: people excluded from wealth and power, with no way to change that.

## Dimensions

I see the following relevant dimensions for describing a "permanent underclass" world. There are interconnections between the dimensions, so they are not perfectly orthogonal, which is why the taxonomy isn't perfect:

- Living conditions - death → severe deprivation → basic subsistence → comfortable provision → luxurious provision....

items.summary: This post builds a taxonomy of different meanings people attach to the term permanent underclass in AI futures discussions, distinguishing scenarios by who controls AI infrastructure and how the disempowered class fares. items.reasoning: Useful conceptual hygiene for AI-society debates, but it is a personal brainstorming exercise with acknowledged imperfections, explicitly labeled as illustrations rather than predictions, with no empirical or technical contribution.

items.title: What do the other 80 percent mean?
items.content:
I am Austrian and wrote this in German. The English is a literal machine translation, not rewritten.

Everywhere now, catastrophic harm to humanity is being discussed, and various scenarios. But the other percentages are not mapped in detail by outcome, the way it is done with nuclear scenarios, where people look at this more closely. That is possible. People do not go deeper, they do not use this method.

When I heard it for the first time, I did not trust my ears. I thought this was fake news. Unfortunately not.

If 25 percent means the extinction of humanity, does 75 percent mean paradise?

Whoever names twenty percent extinction does not claim to have the rest under control. That is a deception, a false assumption. It could mean that most people die and only a few survive. Or that most people suffer. That is not clear.

Or does it mean the collapse of our systems, the overload of our society, chaos and unrest, total concentration of power and control? Or pure happiness and sunshine?

In the interviews nobody asks about it. No reporter, no senate, no government.

What is actually connected? Production systems, communication systems, payment systems, navigation systems. Also facilities operated under hazard supervision, nuclear, chemical, biological. In principle, the digital world is the habitat of silicon intelligence.

Can we still maintain our digital infrastructure on our own at all when an AI is in control? Do the ten best programmers then go there with a keyboard and upload some code?

We can no longer keep control over the digital infrastructure. And so everything we have digitized over the last decades actually leads us into harm, as long as we have no analog alternatives now. You need an analog, a second fallback level, a copy.

We should prepare for this, that is how I think about it. And make the same effort as with a medical approval, with a medicine, or with other things where the risk is small by comparison....
items.author: Richard Bertossa
items.summary: The author argues that public discourse on catastrophic AI probabilities (e.g., a stated 20% extinction risk) fails to specify what the remaining probability mass actually looks like in outcome terms, unlike more detailed nuclear-risk scenario mapping. The post urges reporters and governments to probe the non-extinction outcomes, which could range from mass suffering to system collapse to broad benefit.
items.reasoning: Raises a legitimate point about underspecified outcome distributions in AI risk communication, but the piece is largely rhetorical, machine-translated, and offers no framework or analysis beyond the observation itself.

items.title: Geo-vision: Native-Resolution Geometry and Sampled Topology for Vehicle-Part Damage Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.23967v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Geo-vision classifies vehicle-part damage using a fixed representation combining appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology. Connected components, holes, Euler characteristics, and spatial arrangement complement amplitude-sensitive pooling and a supervised tree classifier. We establish amplitude preservation, axial sign invariance, and conditional operator stability. Retrospective checkpoint evaluation on 55,303 crops from 4,916 source groups yields average precision 0.7577, exceeding 0.7458 for an ImageNet-pretrained frozen YOLO11n comparator on identical crops. The complete added structural block, comprising topology, occupancy, and component location, improves average precision by 0.00493 beyond appearance and geometry. Geo-vision uses no external encoder pretraining and has higher AP point estimates at every matched label budget. With approximately 25% fewer task labels, its AP point estimate exceeds full-data YOLO, although the adjusted interval includes zero. Complete serial CPU inference requires 26.98 ms per crop versus YOLO's 11.20 ms, with peak memory 185 versus 437 MiB. Independent external validation remains necessary.
items.author: Usef Faghihi, Amir Saki, Serge Jonathan Kogbeti-Wongo
items.summary: Geo-vision classifies vehicle-part damage using a fixed representation combining appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology (connected components, holes, Euler characteristics), with a supervised tree classifier. On 55,303 crops it slightly exceeds a frozen YOLO11n baseline in average precision, with theoretical guarantees on operator stability. The topology block adds a small but measurable improvement over appearance alone.
items.reasoning: A solid applied engineering contribution in a narrow insurance/automotive domain; the margin over the baseline is small and the setting is specialized. Theoretical framing is nice but does not elevate general impact.

items.title: EmotiQ: A Quantum Residual Specialist Framework for Text Emotion Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.25549v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Emotion classification from text is challenging because many affective states are distinguished by subtle linguistic signals and semantically overlapping boundaries. We investigate whether compact quantum modules can serve as targeted residual specialists that assist traditional classifiers on difficult emotion decisions. We introduce EmotiQ, a residual specialist framework for text emotion classification using a frozen transformer classifier as the primary decision maker, identifies challenging emotion boundaries from validation behavior, and trains boundary specialists, including quantum encodings, data re-uploading specialists, prototype and fidelity specialists, and kernel-based specialists. Specialists are permitted to intervene only when they satisfy validation-based admission criteria. We evaluate the framework across six text emotion classification datasets and establish traditional model baselines. Experimental results show that the admitted EmotiQ policy improves mean macro-F1 metrics over the baseline, and achieves positive gains on five of six datasets. Among the quantum components, ZZ interaction feature maps are the most consistently effective, yielding a mean macro-F1 improvement of +0.0030 and positive gains on four datasets. These findings suggest that current quantum NLP methods can be deployed as residual specialists that provide localized improvements under strong classical supervision.

items.summary: Proposes EmotiQ, which keeps a frozen transformer as the main emotion classifier and trains small residual specialist modules—including quantum encodings and data re-uploading circuits—that intervene only on hard boundary cases identified from validation behavior. It tests whether compact quantum modules can help on subtle, overlapping affect categories.
items.reasoning: The quantum residual angle is novel but the practical benefit over classical specialist modules is unclear and gains are likely marginal on standard emotion benchmarks; a niche combination with limited immediate impact.

items.title: Governing the Rule Space. Ruliology, Computational Irreducibility and Anticipatory Governance of Quantum Technologies
items.content: arXiv:2610.26423v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The regulation of emerging technologies is often conceived as a strategy of catching up, because legislators arrive too late. Yet gathering signals, constructing scenarios and adapting rules to an anticipated future are fundamental tasks for those entrusted with governance, including the governance of rules themselves. The literature on so-called future law has already shown that anticipation means building institutional capabilities rather than predicting outcomes precisely (anticipatory governance). Taking this premise as its starting point, this article proposes to understand regulation as an exploration of the transformations that may occur. The Ruliological Framework for Anticipatory Regulation distinguishes rules, transformations and trajectories, assessing alternatives and possible developments. Within this approach, computational irreducibility is adopted conditionally, not as a demonstrated property of legal systems. The Quantum Europe Strategy provides a case study and further grounds for reflection.
items.author: Antonio Felice Uricchio, Francesco Scagliola
items.summary: Proposes a Ruliological Framework for Anticipatory Regulation that treats rulemaking for quantum technologies as exploration of possible transformations rather than reactive catch-up, drawing on concepts of computational irreducibility. It is a governance-theory contribution about regulating rules themselves.
items.reasoning: Thought-provoking conceptual governance work, but not technical AI research; the framing borrows from complexity science and its practical testability is unclear, and its relevance to the core AI research agenda is indirect.

items.title: AI-Experiment: an augmented reality art project co-created with artificial intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2610.23903v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We describe the creation of a physical artwork that was performed in synergy between an artist, a computer scientist and generative AI tools. A latent diffusion model was finetuned on photographs of the artwork of the specific artist and the generative model then generated synthetic artworks in a similar style. From the generated artworks a subset was selected to be painted again with acrylic on canvas by the original artist. In addition to the physical artifact an augmented reality component was added which brings the artwork to life with a set of generative video models. Together with this paper we release part of the artwork (training data), the code that was deployed to generate the artwork as well as the augmented reality experience for arts, research and education under https://github.com/BernhardEgger/ARTimate

Training data, code, and the AR experience are released alongside the paper.

items.title: You Aren't Worried Enough About the Economy
items.content:
Your bus breaks down over some old train tracks, and you and your fellow passengers have taken it upon yourselves to move it. Most of the passengers, particularly the largest and strongest, are very concerned about being hit by a freight train.

While this is a perfectly reasonable fear, you think that the semi-truck barreling down the road is of greater importance.

You mention that nobody knows if there is a train (although some people seem incredibly confident about its existence), but just about everyone can see the truck when you point it out. The other passengers tell you that, unlike the train, the semi won’t destroy the bus, and might actually move it off the tracks. You reply that they seem to be underweighting the damage the truck will cause to the bus, and they accuse you of distracting people from the far more weighty task of saving the bus from the train, as the tracks and the road are perpendicular. A third passenger points out that nobody knows whether any passenger is capable of moving the bus, and that there are economic and diplomatic incentives to nail the bus down anyway. You point out that the metaphor has gotten a bit ridiculous, and the semi continues its approach.

The rationalist and EA communities have focused much of their efforts on AI alignment, an admirable project which has likely been responsible for much of the progress in and public concern for AI safety. Unfortunately, the prospect of economic disruption has not received the same attention. Everyone agrees that it’s going to happen. (In the field of computer science, it is already underway.) Everyone agrees that its effects will be widespread and deleterious. However, very few individuals or organizations have been working on this problem. The purpose of this article is to give a quantitative estimate of the first-order effects and a qualitative evaluation of the second-order effects of AI on the American labor force....
items.author: Character#2736
items.summary: This post uses an extended bus/train/truck metaphor to argue that AI community attention on existential risk (the train) causes people to underweight nearer-term economic disruption from AI (the truck). It contends that economic harms are visible, likely, and neglected relative to extinction scenarios.
items.reasoning: A rhetorical opinion piece making a familiar near-term-versus-long-term risk prioritization argument; it offers a memorable framing but no new evidence, data, or technical content.

items.title: Directly Ascertained Volition (DAV) to safeguard personal autonomy
items.content:
In 2004, Eliezer Yudkowsky put forward Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) as a framework for friendly ASI to predict what we would want "if we knew more, thought faster, were more the people we wished we were, had grown up farther together", and act on it.

In this post, I present Directly Ascertained Volition (DAV) with an action plan as a development of CEV that allows for a more granular approach tailored to the values and needs of each specific individual.

# Take it personally

Leaving aside for a moment the technical challenge of alignment, I believe CEV can be improved in two main areas:

- idealised-me versus actual-me: in CEV, the friendly ASI is asked to predict what an idealised version of me would want. However, my values and desires are likely to differ at least somewhat from those of idealised-me. For example, idealised-me may well come up with a galaxy-brained argument for dumping my family and spending eternity in meditation, but actual-me would not want that at all. Following CEV would therefore cause real harm to actual-me's values and desires. Since I can't foresee how and where idealised-me's values would diverge from actual-me's, it's not in my interest to let idealised-me make the choice on my behalf.
- majority choice versus individual autonomy: in CEV, the friendly AI extrapolates value for humanity as a whole.
