items.content_html:
In 2004, Eliezer Yudkowsky put forward Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) as a framework for friendly ASI to predict what we would want "if we knew more, thought faster, were more the people we wished we were, had grown up farther together", and act on it.

In this post, I present Directly Ascertained Volition (DAV) with an action plan as a development of CEV that allows for a more granular approach tailored to the values and needs of each specific individual.

# Take it personally

Leaving aside for a moment the technical challenge of alignment, I believe CEV can be improved in two main areas:

  • idealised-me versus actual-me: in CEV, the friendly ASI is asked to predict what an idealised version of me would want. However, my values and desires are likely to differ at least somewhat from those of idealised-me. For example, idealised-me may well come up with a galaxy-brained argument for dumping my family and spending eternity in meditation, but actual-me would not want that at all. Following CEV would therefore cause real harm to actual-me's values and desires. Since I can't foresee how and where idealised-me's values would diverge from actual-me's, it's not in my interest to let idealised-me make the choice on my behalf.
  • majority choice versus individual autonomy: in CEV, the friendly AI extrapolates value for humanity as a whole. However, different cultures, even different individuals, don't share the exact same values. Many people would be unhappy if radically different (yet still human) values were imposed on them. This should be avoided by directly ascertaining the volition of each individual and acting on it to the extent possible.

items.title: A Video by Adam Conover and the “A.I. Distraction Narrative”
items.content:
Introduction

I recently watched the video "'AI Existential Risk' Was Invented to Distract Us" by Adam Conover of Adam Ruins Everything where he expressed his views on why he believes the claim of the extinction threat posed by AI is being used as a diversion from other harms caused by AI. I’ve seen this narrative being tossed around a bit so I figured I’d take the opportunity to investigate some of the claims being made and offer counterpoints. This is also a bit of a personal endeavor for me as I credit Adam Conover in propagating the critical thinking skills necessary for survival in the corporate internet world that we find ourselves in. 

This article works best when in companion with the attached video but still doesn't function as well as a stand alone piece. I will not be addressing every point made in the video or every point I’ve seen made in favor of this argument. I will focus on four points that I believe to be the most important. For clarity's sake, I’m going to employ the use of a numbered list where the name of each item is the claim I’m addressing.

----------------------------------------------------------

- The threat of existential risk exists to further the AI race

In the video, Conover gives the claim that the threat of existential risk is being used by the AI companies to create a sense that these companies must be the ones to build AI. I disagree with this for a number of reasons. Firstly, before all of this went down, these companies were already on the good-side of the US government [1], were already raking in billions in investment [2]-[4], and were already making extremely fast progress on AI. It doesn’t seem clear to me why solidification of their place in the market would be necessary....

items.summary: The author critiques Adam Conover's video arguing that AI extinction risk claims are a distraction from nearer-term AI harms, addressing four of its central claims with counterpoints. The post aims to engage seriously with a popular public-facing anti-xrisk narrative.
items.reasoning: A point-by-point rebuttal of a public video that engages an important discourse but contains no original research, data, or technical analysis; its value is mostly rhetorical and community-facing.

items.title: Analysis of Binary O-type Star Systems Using Recurrent Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.24015v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This work presents an initial analysis of the estimation of effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated O-type binary systems using a recurrent neural network. The proposed system uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical region of a stellar spectrum. Two methods were applied to observed IACOB spectra before normalization: the addition of a blackbody continuum and the addition of a second observed spectrum. The first method produces only small differences in the normalized line profiles and in the estimated physical parameters over 3700-7000~\AA. In the second method, the secondary spectrum is added with contributions of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 75 per cent, as defined relative to the original primary spectrum. The general comparison includes 192 simulated systems and 1152 modified spectra. For most of these spectra, the estimated effective temperature and surface gravity decrease as the contribution of the secondary component increases. Individual examples using HD14947, HD190429, HD48099, and HD206267 show that this behavior is not the same for every combination: some estimated effective temperatures fall below the estimates for both isolated spectra, and some surface gravity estimates increase. Comparisons with previously published values also depend on the physical parameter and reference considered. The results show that the proposed system is sensitive to the addition of a secondary spectrum, but do not establish a unique contribution for the secondary component of an observed binary.

items.summary: The authors use a recurrent neural network to estimate effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated binary O-type star systems from 34 equivalent-width measurements in optical spectra, testing robustness to continuum additions and spectral contamination from a secondary star. The approach is validated on observed IACOB spectra.

items.title: A Flexible ROI Analysis Tool for Spatially Consistent Vegetation Index Extraction from Turfgrass Imagery
items.content: arXiv:2610.26719v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Time-series multispectral imaging is widely used to assess turfgrass condition; however, extracting plot-level vegetation index (VI) values remains labor-intensive when camera positions vary between acquisitions and automated plot tracking is unreliable. We developed an open-source software tool comprising (i) a graphical user interface (GUI) for the interactive placement of orientation-adjustable regions of interest (ROIs) with $N$-way subdivision to match plot geometry and (ii) a batch-processing script that computes plot-level mean VI values from single-band floating-point rasters and exports measurements and ROI coordinates in JSON format for reuse. Saved coordinates can be reapplied to measure NDVI, NDRE, and SAVI from identical pixel regions within a single time point without re-delineating ROIs. In a demonstration using rail-mounted multispectral turfgrass imagery (18 images), plot-level mean values were extracted in a single session, with coordinates reused directly for NDRE and SAVI rasters. The system reads non-georeferenced pixel-coordinate rasters natively, does not require GIS expertise, and supports reproducible VI quantification where static sensor deployment is impractical.

items.summary: This paper presents an open-source GUI tool and batch-processing script for interactively placing orientation-adjustable regions of interest on multispectral turfgrass time-series imagery, computing plot-level NDVI, NDRE, and SAVI values with reusable JSON coordinate export. It solves a practical workflow problem when camera positions vary between acquisition sessions. Useful domain software rather than a research advance.

items.title: How I got my non-tech friends to learn about AI safety
items.content:
TL;DR: I built an open-source, two-hour interactive presentation on AI safety for non-technical audiences. Here’s a recap of what it covers, how it went, and how you can use it yourself.

Epistemic status: personal experience from one session with six close friends, plus impressions from conversations with people inside and outside the field over the past six months.

I've been a machine learning engineer for almost 10 years, working in scale-ups and startups, even as a CTO. And not once during all those years did I really realise how dangerous AI could be. Not until a friend actually showed me.

Six months ago, I quit my job to transition into AI safety, after realising that AI might be one of the most critical dangers we're facing. Today I’m launching my own AI safety non-profit.

But this post is not about me.

It's about something I've been realising over the past six months: most people outside of AI safety simply don't understand the risks of AI. And I think one of the main reasons is that they don't even realise how powerful AI already is. Or at least, that’s my impression when I talk to people around me. Polls in the US show that many people say they are worried about AI, but in my experience, few of them understand why it could actually be dangerous.

When I talk to some of my non-technical friends or family (my stepmother, for example), I sometimes realise that, for them, AI is still basically a chatbot. Something you ask a question to, then copy-paste the answer to help you write an email.

And at the same time, I've spent the past six months discovering how little is actually happening around AI safety, especially politically.

But how could anything happen politically if most people don’t really understand the problem?

## Why I built this...

items.title: Reconstruction and Discrete-Event Simulation Assessment of an Analytical
items.content: arXiv:2610.25967v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This article presents an analytical-DES benchmark for intra-aisle robotic picking in automated warehousing. The investigated cycle combines horizontal shuttle travel, tote handling and item picking at storage locations. Simulation results are compared with the analytical formulation of Lerher et al. under the same rack geometry, shuttle-motion, handling and picking conditions, and the same definitions of cycle time and derived item throughput. Reproducing the published analytical tables requires the distance interpretation dES = 1.5 m and dTB = 0 m. The analytical-DES benchmark comprises 180 scenarios formed from three rack lengths, two paired motion profiles and n = 1 to 30 visited picking locations, with ten simulation replications per scenario. The six n = 1 cases are reported separately because no travel-between component is present. Across the remaining 174 scenarios, the mean absolute relative cycle-time discrepancy is 0.8655%, the median is 0.6758%, and the maximum is 7.0370%. The mean absolute error is 2.411 s and the RMSE is 2.744 s. The simulated scenario-mean cycle time is below the analytical value in all 174 principal scenarios. The results therefore show close numerical correspondence under the tested conditions, but not exact agreement, formal statistical equivalence, or validation against an operating warehouse.

items.summary: This paper builds an analytical and discrete-event simulation benchmark for intra-aisle robotic picking in automated warehousing, comparing simulation results with the analytical formulation of Lerher et al. across 180 scenarios of rack geometry, motion profiles, and picking locations. It is a validation and reproduction study for warehouse robotics throughput models. Its relevance to mainstream AI research is limited.

items.title: Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
items.content: arXiv:2610.24492v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date. Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.

items.title: Improving the flow of interesting things
items.content:
I believe the flow of interesting things to people who would be interested in them is not currently as effective as it could be. I also believe (a) that such a system could be built and (b) it would have important implications for society.

I will now attempt to describe what such a system could look like, and some of the ways it could impact society.

Think of such a system as containing four layers.

On the first layer you have 'knowledge for knowledge's sake'. These are things you're interested in knowing but don't really affect your daily life. For example, a monthly update on the latest innovations in health research for an enthusiast who doesn't work in health. Or an alert every time they find a new black hole.

The second layer is 'knowledge for value's sake'. This might be the same monthly report but tailored to someone who does work in health. Or a new finding in physics that applies to a similar problem a biologist is working on.

The third layer can be thought of as 'opportunities'. A job listing that fits exactly what you're looking for. A notification that tells you a band you like is playing nearby. You like board games and you get told there's a board games club in your area.

Already I think a system that is effective at these three layers would have a tremendous impact. I only gave a few examples for illustrative purposes, but the potential is huge. (I'm sorry I'm still unfamiliar with some of the more maths related techniques this community as good at so I can't properly quantify, even for myself, what kind of scales we're talking here. If somebody would like to offer advice I'd be very grateful)...

items.title: IWOO: Wave Optics Optimizer Improved with Hybrid Strategies for Numerical Optimization and Engineering Applications
items.content: arXiv:2610.23994v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The Wave Optics Optimizer (WOO) incorporates optical diffraction and interference into numerical optimization and has shown competitive performance in benchmarks and engineering applications. However, it can converge slowly, become trapped in local optima, and lose search effectiveness in later iterations. This paper proposes an Improved Wave Optics Optimizer (IWOO) that integrates four complementary strategies. First, a good point set and opposition-based learning are combined in GPS--OBL initialization to improve population quality and diversity. Second, an E-DM nonlinear perturbation mechanism is embedded in temporary triangle-based search to develop the TriEDM multi-path strategy and enhance search capability. Third, Correlation-Guided Groupwise Orthogonal Learning (CGOL) leverages relationships among decision variables to improve search efficiency while reducing computational overhead. Fourth, an adaptive stagnation-aware Runge--Kutta correction is introduced to mitigate premature convergence. IWOO is evaluated on the IEEE CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017 benchmark suites against representative and high-performing optimizers, with ablation studies assessing the contribution of each strategy. Within the representative algorithm group, IWOO achieves Friedman ranks of 1.8000, 1.5833, and 1.4483 on CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017, respectively. Tests on six constrained engineering optimization problems further demonstrate its competitive accuracy, stability, and practical applicability.

items.summary: IWOO enhances the Wave Optics Optimizer metaheuristic with four strategies: opposition-based initialization, a nonlinear perturbation mechanism for multi-path search, correlation-guided components, and additional refinements, targeting slow convergence and local-optimum trapping. It is validated on benchmarks and engineering applications.

items.title: First Strike
items.content:
The prairie lodge had two virtues - it was quiet and had an excellent golf course nearby. Outsiders thought the point of the trip was visiting national landmarks and airbases, insiders knew it was about taking some time off. The job might be 24/7 - but if you are the boss you will find a way. So when Agent Ortega knocked twice and uncharacteristically let herself in without waiting for an answer, the president knew before she spoke that the quiet was over.

"Sir. We've lost secure comms with the Pentagon. NMCC, State, all of it. Everything routed through the satellite relays is garbage, regular lines unpredictable."

"Garbage, unpredictable? How?"

"Static. Loops. Dropped calls. IT thinks it might be an attack on the relay infrastructure - they don't know whose. Cell reception here was always poor, now even landlines seem to drop randomly. Internet is the same."

He was still absorbing that and watching more of his crew coming into the room when his cell - his personal cell, the one only a dozen people had the number for - lit up on the desk. Danny.

"Dad..." his son's voice was wrong, too fast, climbing. "Dad, something happened. There was this — this light, and then the whole building shook. I'm not sure. Ann says..."

"Danny. Danny, slow down. Where are you?"

"I'm fine, I'm fine. I was just about to board the jet at Tacoma, but downtown, Dad, downtown is just — it's gone, there's this cloud—"

The phone cut into static then just dropped, like Ortega described. At the edge of his vision he saw the TV on the other side of the room going blank. A rerun of an old movie had been playing just the moment before, now it was all dark. A few seconds later the blank screen was replaced by a news anchor, tunes playing in the background.

"We are interrupting our broadcast with Breaking News."

The left side of the screen showed a map of the Seattle area, with concentric circles centered on the other side of the bay, north-west from downtown....

items.title: Sorry, you are still dead
items.content:
Epistemic status: A brief exploration based on court documents and contemporary reporting. My interpretation is tentative.

AI use: context research, grammar.

I don't remember how I stumbled upon the topic of legally dead people who are still alive. Basically, they are alive, but according to the government, they are dead. I was curious to examine documented examples and discovered Donald Miller's case.

In 1986, Donald Miller disappears from Arcadia, Ohio, leaving two daughters from a previous marriage without his child support. Before disappearing, he lost his job and was struggling with alcoholism. In 1994, his ex-wife obtains a court declaration of his death so their daughters can receive Social Security survivor benefits.
[1]

In the 2000s—news reports say 2005; his affidavit suggests 2008—Donald returns to Ohio, alive. In 2013, he asks the court to undo the declaration and restore his Social Security number. Without it, he says he cannot work or obtain a driver's license.
[2]
 His ex-wife objects, fearing she would have to repay the benefits.
[3]

However, the judge interprets Ohio Revised Code §2121.08(A) as allowing reversal only:

within a three-year period from the date of the decree

The clock starts when the declaration is issued, not when the deceased discovers they have been declared deceased. So the court denies Donald's request.
[4]

Despite this, in 2014 Social Security demands that his daughters repay the benefits. By December, it drops those demands.
[5]

Miller's lawyer argues that the deadline concerns estate administration and property. Miller isn't trying to recover property; he just wants to be recognized as legally alive. However, this isn't enough for the judge.
[6]...
